The preparation of financial statements requires management estimates and assumptions, including revenue allowances, inventory valuation, goodwill and intangible asset valuation, and income taxes. Revenue is recognized when a customer obtains control of promised goods or services, with sales, value-added, and other taxes excluded. Shipping and handling costs are included in cost of sales. Substantially all revenue is from product sales, representing a single performance obligation. Customers typically pay within net 30 to 60 days, and the company does not have significant financing components in its contracts. For non-custom products, revenue is recognized upon shipment to customers, including OEMs and distributors, with provisions for returns, allowances, and rebates based on historical experience. Incentive programs such as cooperative advertising and volume-based incentives reduce revenue at the time of related revenue recognition or when the program is offered. Custom products, particularly semi-custom products, are recognized over time based on a cost-based input method, which includes cost incurred plus estimated margin. Sales of semi-custom products are not subject to returns. Development and intellectual property licensing agreements may combine development services and IP licensing, and are subject to specific accounting treatment.

Custom products associated with the Company’s Gaming segment, specifically semi-custom products sold under non-cancellable purchase orders, for which the Company has an enforceable right to payment and no alternative use at contract inception, are recognized as revenue over the production period. The Company uses a cost-based input method—calculated as cost incurred plus estimated margin—to determine revenue for in-process, incomplete customer orders at a reporting date, believing this method best reflects the effort and costs incurred in satisfying performance obligations. Sales of semi-custom products are not subject to a right of return, and these arrangements generally involve a single performance obligation with no variable consideration estimates. For development and intellectual property licensing agreements, the Company evaluates whether the licensing component is distinct—defined as both capable of being distinct and distinct in the context of the arrangement. If not distinct, the development services and license are combined as a single performance obligation recognized over time; if distinct, revenue is recognized at a point in time when the customer can benefit from the license. Standalone arrangements involving the sale or licensing of patents or IP generally involve only the transfer of a license, with revenue recognized when the customer can benefit from it. There are no variable consideration estimates for either combined development and IP arrangements or standalone IP arrangements. Inventory is valued at standard cost, adjusted to the lower of actual cost or estimated net realizable value, using assumptions about future demand and market conditions. Excess or obsolescence reserves consider changes in business and economic conditions, demand declines, and technology or customer requirements, while net realizable value reserves consider historical sales, selling prices, and future price estimates. The Company fully reserves for obsolete inventory and non-cancellable purchase orders and periodically reviews inventory by comparing on-hand balances and purchase orders to anticipated usage, with potential adjustments if demand estimates decline or market conditions worsen. For business combinations, the Company applies the acquisition method, allocating purchase consideration to assets and liabilities based on fair values as of the acquisition date, with any excess recorded as goodwill. Management makes significant estimates, especially for intangible assets, including future revenue growth, technology changes, customer relationship recreation time, useful lives, and discount rates. Fair value estimates are based on market participant assumptions and are inherently uncertain, leading to possible adjustments during the one-year measurement period, which are offset against goodwill. After the measurement period or final determination, adjustments are recorded in the Consolidated Statements of Operations. Goodwill is tested annually on the first day of the fourth quarter and more frequently if events suggest impairment. The Company may first perform qualitative testing using factors such as industry trends, financial performance, share price, and company-specific events; if fair value exceeds carrying amount, no quantitative test is performed. If fair value is less than carrying value or the qualitative test is bypassed, a quantitative test is conducted using the income approach (present value of expected future cash flows) and market approach (comparable company financial ratios). Key inputs in the income approach include macroeconomic conditions, growth rates, execution ability, and discount rates; in the market approach, comparable company identification and applicable multiples are key. If fair value is less than carrying value, an impairment charge is recognized up to the amount of goodwill allocated. Long-lived and intangible assets held for use are reviewed for impairment annually or quarterly if indicators exist, with impairment tested at the lowest level of identifiable cash flows. If future undiscounted cash flows are insufficient to recover carrying value, assets are written down to fair value based on discounted cash flows or appraisals. For assets held for sale, impairment is measured as the excess of carrying value over fair value, with market conditions influencing the assessment. Cash equivalents include financial instruments convertible to cash with original maturities of three months or less. Accounts receivable consist primarily of trade receivables net of rebates, price protection, and an allowance for credit loss, plus unbilled receivables for completed development services or semi-custom products under non-cancellable orders with no alternative use, all expected to be billed and collected within twelve months. American Express Company, a globally integrated payments company founded in 1850 and incorporated in 1965 as a New York corporation, operates as a bank holding company under the Bank Holding Company Act of 1956, as amended, and is subject to supervision and examination by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. The company provides credit and charge cards to consumers, small businesses, mid-sized companies, and large corporations worldwide through its various products and services, available via mobile and online applications, affiliate marketing, customer referral programs, third-party service providers, direct mail, telephone, in-house sales teams, and direct response advertising. Its businesses are organized into four reportable operating segments: U.S. Consumer Services (USCS), Commercial Services (CS), International Card Services (ICS), and Global Merchant and Network Services (GMNS), with corporate functions and certain other businesses included in Corporate & Other. The company’s end-to-end integrated payments platform connects Card Members and merchants through direct relationships, enabling access to spending data for risk underwriting, fraud reduction, and targeted marketing, while protecting data in compliance with applicable policies and laws. It also obtains data through contractual relationships with third-party card issuers, merchant acquirers, aggregators, and processors. The company’s global proprietary card-issuing businesses are conducted through USCS, CS, and ICS, offering a broad range of card products, rewards, and services to consumers and commercial customers, with a focus on attracting Millennial and Gen Z customers and expanding SME offerings through products like business checking and consumer rewards checking, as well as digital capabilities from acquisitions of Kabbage, Resy, and acompay. The ICS organization consolidates consumer, SME, and large commercial card issuing activities outside the U.S. to better serve local priorities, with significant billed business in the United Kingdom, European Union, Australia, Japan, Canada, and Mexico. For the fiscal year ended December 31, 2022, worldwide billed business (spending on American Express cards issued by the company) was $1,338 billion, and the company had 76.7 million proprietary cards-in-force worldwide. The GMNS segment manages relationships with millions of merchants globally, including signing new merchants, setting discount rates, and handling merchant servicing, and operates through programs like OptBlue® that allow third-party acquirers to contract directly with small merchants. The company also provides fraud-prevention tools, marketing solutions, and data analytics to merchants and partners. Through its card network, American Express operates in approximately 103 countries and territories, licensing the American Express brand to third-party banks and institutions to issue local currency cards and serve as merchant acquirers. For the year ended December 31, 2022, worldwide network services processed volume (spending on American Express cards issued by third parties) was $214.5 billion, and the company had 56.5 million cards-in-force issued by third parties worldwide. The company’s diverse customer base includes consumers, small businesses, mid-sized companies, and large corporations, with a global footprint supported by partnerships. Key partners include Delta Air Lines, Marriott International, Hilton Worldwide Holdings, British Airways, Amazon.com (via Pay with Points), PayPal, i2c, BILL, BillTrust, Versapay, and Fine Hotels and Resorts. Delta is the company’s largest strategic partner, with the Delta cobrand portfolio representing approximately 10 percent of worldwide network volumes and about 21 percent of worldwide Card Member loans as of December 31, 2022. The Delta cobrand portfolio generates fee revenue and interest income from Card Members and discount revenue from Delta and other merchants for spending on Delta cobrand cards, with the current agreement running through the end of 2029 and the company planning significant investments in the partnership. Delta also participates in the Membership Rewards program, provides travel-related benefits such as airport lounge access, accepts American Express cards as a merchant, and serves as a corporate payments customer. The company’s spend-centric business model generates revenue primarily by driving spending on its cards and secondarily through finance charges and fees. As a Category IV firm, it is not subject to advanced approaches capital requirements and must maintain minimum capital ratios of 4.5% CET1, 6.0% Tier 1, and 8.0% Total capital to risk-weighted assets. The Company is subject to a dynamic stress capital buffer (SCB) of 2.5% CET1 capital, effective from October 1 each year, increasing the effective minimum ratios to 7.0% CET1, 8.5% Tier 1, and 10.5% Total capital. AENB is subject to a static 2.5% capital conservation buffer. The Company must maintain a leverage ratio of at least 4.0%. Liquidity requirements under the Federal Reserve’s enhanced prudential standards include a liquidity buffer and a minimum liquidity coverage ratio (LCR), but Category IV firms with less than $50 billion in weighted short-term wholesale funding, like the Company, are not subject to specific LCR or net stable funding ratio (NSFR) requirements. Capital distributions, including dividends and share repurchases, are limited if capital ratios fall below minimums or if the capital plan is resubmitted. The Federal Deposit Insurance Act (FDIA) imposes progressive restrictions on institutions based on capital categories, with AENB required to maintain CET1, Tier 1, Total capital, and Tier 1 leverage ratios of at least 6.5%, 8.0%, 10.0%, and 5.0%, respectively, to be considered “well capitalized.” AENB may be prohibited from accepting brokered deposits or offering interest rates above prevailing market rates unless well capitalized or adequately capitalized with a waiver. AENB is required to prepare and submit a separate resolution plan to the FDIC to enable the FDIC, as receiver, to effectively resolve the institution under the FDIA in the event of failure. The Company could become subject to the Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA), under which the Treasury Secretary may appoint the FDIC as receiver to liquidate a systemically important financial institution if the Company is in danger of default and poses a systemic risk to U.S. financial stability. Under the OLA, the FDIC has broad powers as receiver, including the ability to disregard the strict priority of creditor claims in limited circumstances, use an administrative claims procedure instead of judicial proceedings, and transfer claims to a “bridge” entity. The FDIC has developed a “single point of entry” (SPOE) strategy under OLA, whereby the FDIC would transfer AENB’s assets—including shares of its operating subsidiaries—and potentially limited liabilities to a “bridge” holding company; use the failed company’s resources to recapitalize its subsidiaries; and satisfy unsecured creditor claims and other claimants by delivering securities from new financial companies emerging from the bridge entity. Under this strategy, management of the failed holding company would be replaced, and shareholders and creditors would bear the losses. If the FDIC is appointed conservator or receiver of AENB, it has the power to transfer any of AENB’s assets or liabilities to a new obligor without creditor approval, enforce contractual terms, or repudiate or disaffirm contracts or leases deemed burdensome by the FDIC. The company’s balance sheet management objectives include maintaining a solid and flexible equity capital profile, a broad, deep, and diverse set of funding sources, and liquidity programs to meet future financing obligations and business requirements for at least twelve months in the event of a substantial weakening in economic conditions. The company manages its balance sheet in response to market volatility. Capital is allocated to growing businesses with a return on risk-adjusted equity exceeding costs to generate shareholder value. The company retains capital from net income and stock option exercises to maintain a strong balance sheet, support future growth, and distribute excess capital through dividends and share repurchases. The consolidated capital position is determined through the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process, considering business activities, marketplace conditions, and regulatory or shareholder expectations. As a bank holding company, it is subject to U.S. federal banking agency regulations, including Federal Reserve capital adequacy guidelines. Failure to maintain minimum regulatory capital levels at American Express or American Express National Bank (AENB) could affect its financial holding company status and lead to regulatory actions limiting operations. The company seeks to maintain capital levels and ratios above minimum regulatory requirements, specifically within a 10 to 11 percent target range for Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) risk-based capital ratio. Capital can be shifted across businesses as needed, such as infusing additional capital into subsidiaries to meet debt ratings and regulatory requirements, which may affect parent or subsidiary capital and liquidity positions. Capital ratios are reported using Basel III definitions and the standardized approach for risk-weighted assets. As of December 31, 2022, the regulatory risk-based capital and leverage ratios were: Common Equity Tier 1 at 10.3% for American Express Company and 11.3% for AENB; Tier 1 at 11.1% and 11.3%; Total at 12.8% and 13.2%; Tier 1 Leverage at 9.9% and 9.7%. Risk-Weighted Assets are calculated using a Federal Reserve formula that weights assets by risk, including off-balance sheet items converted to balance sheet equivalents using risk conversion factors. Common Equity Tier 1 Risk-Based Capital Ratio is calculated as CET1 capital divided by risk-weighted assets, with CET1 capital adjusted for ineligible goodwill, intangible assets, deferred tax assets, and CECL final rules. Tier 1 Risk-Based Capital Ratio is calculated as Tier 1 capital divided by risk-weighted assets, with Tier 1 capital including CET1 capital, preferred shares, and third-party non-controlling interests, adjusted for insurance subsidiary capital. The minimum Tier 1 ratio is 1.5% higher than CET1. The company has $1.6 billion in preferred shares to meet Tier 1 capital requirements. Total Risk-Based Capital Ratio is calculated as (Tier 1 + Tier 2) capital divided by risk-weighted assets, with Tier 2 capital including the reserve for loan and receivable credit losses (limited to 1.25% of risk-weighted assets) and $870 million in eligible subordinated notes, including $750 million issued in May 2022 and $120 million remaining from $600 million issued in December 2014. Tier 1 Leverage Ratio is calculated as Tier 1 capital divided by average total consolidated assets for the most recent quarter. The company uses an Enterprise-wide Risk Management (ERM) program to identify, aggregate, monitor, measure, report, and manage risks, defining risk appetite, governance, culture, and capabilities, with the Chief Risk Officer leading its implementation. Risk management is overseen by the Board of Directors through three committees: the Risk Committee, the Audit and Compliance Committee, and the Compensation and Benefits Committee, each composed entirely of independent directors and meeting regularly with senior management. The Risk Committee oversees the ERM framework, approves the ERM policy, and reviews risk appetite across credit, operational, compliance, reputational, market, funding, liquidity, model, strategic, business, country, and environmental, social, and governance risks, including limits and escalation triggers. It reviews the appointment, performance, and compensation of the Chief Risk Officer and monitors risk profile against tolerances, compliance with regulatory capital and liquidity standards, and CCAR submissions. The Audit and Compliance Committee reviews compliance policies, including the Compliance Risk Tolerance Statement, the effectiveness of the Corporate-wide Compliance Risk Management Program, financial statement integrity, internal and external auditing, and internal audit performance and independence. It approves the Chief Audit Executive’s appointment, performance, and compensation, and reviews the annual audit plan, charter, policies, budget, staffing, and risk assessment methodology. The Compensation and Benefits Committee works with the Chief Risk Officer to balance risk with business incentives, sets risk goals, reviews business unit risk profiles, and uses a risk-balanced incentive framework to determine bonus pools and senior executive compensation. The Enterprise Risk Management Committee (ERMC), chaired by the Chief Risk Officer, is the highest-level management committee overseeing firm-wide risks, maintaining the enterprise-wide risk appetite framework, monitoring compliance with limits, and overseeing risk policy implementation. The Asset Liability Committee, chaired by the Chief Financial Officer, manages capital, funding, liquidity, investment, market risk, and asset/liability activities in compliance with policies and regulations. The company follows a “three lines of defense” approach: the first line includes the Chief Executive Officer, business unit presidents, and Chief Financial Officer who initiate risk-taking; the second line includes the Chief Risk Officer, Chief Compliance Officer, Chief Operational Risk Officer, and control groups who oversee risk-taking; the third line is the Internal Audit Group, which provides independent assessments of the first and second lines. Credit risk is defined as loss due to default or changes in credit quality and is divided into individual and institutional categories. Individual credit risk arises from consumer and small business charge cards, credit cards, and term loans, involving millions of customers across geographies and industries, with risk generally correlated to economic trends like unemployment and GDP growth. Business unit leaders and Chief Credit Officers manage this risk, guided by the Individual Credit Risk Committee (ICRC), which ensures compliance with ERMC guidelines and escalates issues as needed. Sophisticated proprietary scoring and decision-making models using spending, payment history, and credit bureau data support credit risk management. Institutional credit risk arises in CS, ICS, GMNS, investment, and liquidity activities, characterized by lower loss frequency but higher severity, influenced by both economic conditions and client-specific events. Business units are supported by Chief Credit Officers guided by the Institutional Risk Management Committee (IRMC), which implements the Institutional Credit Risk Management Policy, makes investment decisions, ensures underwriting standards, monitors exposures, and determines risk mitigation actions, formally reviews large exposures, and provides guidance to optimize risk-adjusted returns. A centralized risk rating unit assesses institutional obligors. The company has significant cobrand, rewards, merchant acceptance, and corporate payments arrangements with airlines, with Delta being the largest partner, including an exclusive cobrand credit card partnership and Membership Rewards redemption. The ERM program evaluates airline and travel industry risks, including cruise lines, travel agencies, and tour operators. Debt exposure is monitored for sovereign and non-sovereign customers and counterparties by geographic region and economic sector, with a focus on credit deterioration due to economic and fiscal weaknesses; as of December 31, 2022, gross credit exposures to high-risk countries were considered individually and collectively not material. Operational risk is defined as loss due to inadequate processes, people, systems, or external environment impacts, including regulatory non-compliance and third-party relationships. A comprehensive operational risk framework, approved by the ERMC, includes operational risk event capture, a project office for issue management, key risk indicators, and process and entity-level risk assessments. The Operational Risk Management Committee (ORMC), chaired by the Chief Operational Risk Officer, coordinates risk assessments and controls, oversees preventive and responsive efforts by Operational Excellence teams, and requires root cause analysis, impact assessment (operational, financial, brand, regulatory, legal), and resolution plans. Information and cyber security risk is defined as the risk of a security incident impacting confidentiality, integrity, or availability of customer, colleague, or proprietary information. The program uses advanced technology, a trained team, and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, with controls for identification, protection, detection, response, and recovery. Information technology risk is the risk of events compromising processing, stability, capacity, performance, or resilience of IT systems, leading to financial, reputational, or regulatory impacts. The company manages IT risk through policies, procedures, governance, and controls to preserve system confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Privacy risk is the risk of financial loss, reputational damage, or legal action from violating laws, regulations, contractual obligations, or privacy policies in processing personal data. The Global Privacy Policy establishes data protection principles, and the Privacy Risk Management Committee, chaired by the Chief Privacy Officer and a sub-committee of the ORMC, provides oversight. Data management and governance risk is the risk of financial, reputational, or regulatory impacts from inadequate data governance or management practices affecting data accuracy, completeness, timeliness, comprehensiveness, or usability. The Enterprise Data Governance Policy defines in-scope critical data and lifecycle management requirements, approved by the ERMC. The Enterprise Data Committee, chaired by the Chief Data Officer and a sub-committee of the ERMC, provides governance and oversight. Third party risk is the risk from relationships with third parties or their subcontractors leading to unexpected outcomes or deviations. The Third Party Management Policy, approved by the Risk Committee and ERMC, sets procurement, risk management, and contracting frameworks, and the Third Party Lifecycle Management program guides identification, measurement, monitoring, and reporting of third-party risk throughout the relationship lifecycle. Conduct risk is the risk that colleagues fail to fulfill responsibilities in accordance with the Code of Conduct, policies, values, or laws, potentially increasing reputational risk. The Conduct Risk Management Policy, approved by the ERMC, requires annual risk assessments, preventive and detective controls, colleague training, and timely escalation of conduct issues, with consequence management for substantiated misconduct. The Conduct Risk Committee oversees conduct risk and escalates matters to the ERMC as appropriate. Compliance risk is the risk of legal or reputational harm, fines, penalties, or sanctions due to non-compliance with laws, regulations, internal policies, or ethical standards. The Global Compliance and Ethics organization manages compliance risk through assessment, control, monitoring, measuring, and reporting. The Compliance Risk Management Committee (CRMC), chaired by the Chief Compliance Officer, identifies, evaluates, manages, and escalates compliance risks and has a dual reporting relationship to the ERMC and the Audit and Compliance Committee. The company has a comprehensive Anti-Money Laundering program that monitors suspicious activity and includes an independent risk assessment of its rules, with the Internal Audit Group reviewing processes for consistency.

We define compliance risk as the risk of legal or reputational harm, fines, monetary penalties, and other sanctions arising from non-compliance with applicable laws and regulations, internal policies, procedures, and ethical standards. Our Global Compliance and Ethics organization oversees the corporate-wide Compliance Risk Management Program, which involves assessing, controlling, monitoring, measuring, and reporting legal and regulatory risks. The Compliance Risk Management Committee (CRMC), chaired by the Chief Compliance Officer, identifies, evaluates, manages, and escalates compliance risks and maintains a dual reporting relationship with both the ERMC and the Audit and Compliance Committee. We maintain a comprehensive Anti-Money Laundering program that monitors and reports suspicious activity to government authorities and includes an independent risk assessment of the rules used by the team; the Internal Audit Group reviews processes for consistency with regulatory guidance. Reputational risk is defined as the risk of negative stakeholder reactions to our products, services, client and partner relationships, business activities, policies, management, workplace culture, or responses to unexpected events, which could lead to sustained media coverage, revenue or investment decline, talent attrition, litigation, or regulatory scrutiny. We view protecting our reputation for excellent customer service, trust, security, and integrity as central to our vision of delivering the world’s best customer experience and long-term success. Business leaders are responsible for considering reputational risks in business activities and strategies and ensuring relevant subject matter experts are engaged. The ERMC ensures reputational risk considerations are included in subordinate risk policies and committees and properly reflected in decisions escalated to it. Market risk is defined as the risk to earnings or asset and liability values from movements in market prices, including interest rate risk—due to changes in the relationship between interest rates on assets (such as loans, receivables, and investment securities) and liabilities (such as debt and deposits)—and foreign exchange risk from transactions, funding, investments, and earnings in currencies other than the U.S. dollar. Market risk policies, approved by the ERMC, Asset Liability Committee, or Market Risk Management Committee, establish quantitative limits and escalation triggers and are managed by the Market Risk Management Committee. The Market Risk Oversight Officer provides independent risk assessment and oversight of market risk and Asset Liability Management policies and regulatory compliance, guided by policies on derivatives, funding, liquidity, and investments. Interest rate risk is analyzed through various scenarios to assess impacts on earnings and the value of assets, liabilities, and equity. This estimate assumes interest-rate sensitive assets and liabilities reprice by the same magnitude as benchmark rates, with certain deposits repricing at lower magnitudes depending on rate direction, consistent with historical industry and internal experience. Actual net interest income changes may differ due to timing, rate movements, and other factors. Foreign exchange risk arises from four sources: Card Member spending in non-billing currencies, cross-currency transactions and balances, cross-currency investing (e.g., foreign subsidiary equity), and foreign currency revenues and expenses. Funding and liquidity risk is defined as our inability to meet financial and business obligations at reasonable cost as they become due. Our Board-approved Liquidity Risk Policy governs liquidity risk management. The Funding and Liquidity Committee manages this risk by maintaining access to a diverse set of cash, readily-marketable securities, and contingent liquidity sources to meet business requirements and financing obligations for at least twelve months under stressed economic conditions. The committee reviews cash and financing forecasts, approves funding plans under normal and stressed conditions, establishes liquidity guidelines, and monitors positions to determine actions. Funding and liquidity risk is managed at both the consolidated and subsidiary levels. Model risk is defined as the risk of adverse outcomes—such as financial loss, poor decision-making, reputational damage, or customer harm—from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs. The Enterprise-Wide Model Risk Policy, approved by the ERMC, establishes a comprehensive framework including procedures for model development, independent validation, risk reporting, and change management to minimize errors in methodology, outputs, and misuse. Ongoing performance assessments and deficiencies are addressed promptly. Artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) models are used in various business applications, and extensive reviews and testing are conducted to reduce adverse consequences. Strategic and business risk is defined as the risk of failing to achieve business objectives due to poor strategic decisions, including mergers, acquisitions, divestitures, poor implementation, or declining demand. Strategic decisions are reviewed and approved by business leaders and committees and must align with company policies. Risk controls are embedded in these processes, and existing product performance is periodically reviewed by committees and leaders. Mergers, acquisitions, and divestitures require Executive Committee due diligence, a comprehensive risk assessment by operational, market, credit, and oversight leaders provided to the Chief Risk Officer, and approval by the Chief Risk Officer or appropriate risk committees. All new and material product or service changes are reviewed and approved by the New Products Committee and relevant credit or risk committees. Country risk is defined as the risk from economic, social, or political conditions in a country that could adversely affect us, primarily through greater credit losses, increased operational or market risk, or inability to repatriate capital. Country risk is managed as part of normal business operations, with policies and procedures setting escalation thresholds to control exposure and monitor conditions in countries where we operate. Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) and climate-related risk includes risks from the transition to a low-carbon economy—such as policy, legal, technological, market, and reputational risks—and physical impacts of climate change, such as extreme weather events and long-term climate shifts. These risks can affect customers, operations, suppliers, and business and are interconnected across all risk types, potentially manifesting as credit, operational, market, or liquidity risks. Climate-related risk is currently identified as an “emerging risk” within our risk governance framework, and we are conducting a risk identification process to assess its meaningfulness and measurability. Critical accounting estimates include reserves for Card Member credit losses, which represent our best estimate of expected credit losses in the outstanding portfolio of loans and receivables as of the balance sheet date. The Current Expected Credit Loss (CECL) methodology, effective January 1, 2020, requires estimating lifetime expected credit losses using historical loss experience and current and future economic conditions over a reasonable and supportable period (R&S Period) beyond the balance sheet date. We use a combination of statistical models and analysis to determine quantitative and qualitative components of reserves, involving significant judgment. Key judgments include selecting the appropriate R&S Period (approximately three years), modeling probability of default and exposure at default, and incorporating economic conditions. For revolving loans, future payments are allocated first to interest and fees, then to estimated higher minimum payments due to future spend, and finally to the remaining balance. For non-revolving receivables, balances are assumed to be paid or written off within 180 days past due. The R&S Period is the maximum time beyond the balance sheet date over which expected credit losses can be reasonably estimated using available information and forecasts. Beyond this period, long-term average loss rates are applied. The R&S Period includes assumptions about current and future economic conditions, incorporating multiple macroeconomic scenarios from an independent third party. Estimated credit losses from each scenario are reviewed and weighted based on management judgment. A 10 percentage point shift from a baseline to a pessimistic downside scenario as of December 31, 2022, increases estimated credit losses by approximately $120 million. This sensitivity analysis is hypothetical and does not reflect management’s judgment on scenario weighting or other adjustments, nor does it account for qualitative reserve components. Refer to Note 3 for details on macroeconomic scenario variables. The process of estimating reserves requires significant judgment, and actual losses may differ materially from estimates, resulting in higher or lower future provisions. The liability for Membership Rewards represents our best estimate of the cost of points expected to be redeemed by Card Members in the future. This liability is influenced by enrollment levels, attrition, points earned and redeemed, and redemption costs. It is estimated using the redemption rate ratio (URR) and weighted average cost (WAC) per point, applied to current enrollees. The URR is estimated using statistical and actuarial models based on historical redemption trends.

Membership Rewards points are redeemable for a wide range of rewards, including travel, shopping, gift cards, and eligible charges, with no expiration date and no cap on the number of points a Card Member can earn. The cost of these points is driven by charge volume on enrolled cards, customer participation in the program, and contractual agreements with redemption partners. A Membership Rewards liability is recorded to reflect the best estimate of the cost of points expected to be redeemed by Card Members in the future. This liability is influenced over time by enrollment levels, attrition, points earned and redeemed, and associated redemption costs. The liability is estimated using the Ultimate Redemption Rate (URR) and the weighted average cost (WAC) per point, applied to the points of current enrollees. The URR is estimated using statistical and actuarial models based on redemption trends, card product type, enrollment tenure, card spend levels, and credit attributes. The WAC per point is derived from 12 months of redemptions and adjusted for changes in redemption costs that do not reflect future expectations or shifts in redemption patterns. The company periodically reviews its liability estimates based on changes in redemption patterns, cost per point, partner contract changes, and other factors. The estimation process involves significant judgment, and actual redemptions and costs could differ materially from estimates, affecting Membership Rewards expense. An increase in the URR by 25 basis points as of December 31, 2022, would increase the liability and expense by approximately $157 million, while a 1 basis point increase in WAC per point would increase the liability and expense by approximately $190 million. Goodwill, representing the excess of acquisition cost over fair value of assets and liabilities, is not amortized but is tested annually or when events suggest a reporting unit’s fair value is below its carrying value. The impairment test includes both qualitative and quantitative assessments; if qualitative factors indicate it is more likely than not that fair value is below carrying value, a detailed quantitative assessment follows. The quantitative test uses either the income approach (discounted cash flows based on internal forecasts and terminal values using a growth rate appropriate to current economic conditions, discounted at a cost of equity derived from a capital asset pricing model) or the market approach (applying market multiples to operating results). Significant judgment is involved in forecasting cash flows, discount rates, and market comparables, and differences from assumptions could materially affect fair value. The company is exposed to increased goodwill impairment risk if future operating results or macroeconomic conditions differ from current expectations. The audit procedures included examining, on a test basis, evidence regarding the amounts and disclosures in the consolidated financial statements, evaluating the accounting principles used and significant estimates made by management, and assessing the overall presentation of the consolidated financial statements. The audit of internal control over financial reporting involved obtaining an understanding of internal control, assessing the risk of a material weakness, and testing the design and operating effectiveness of internal control based on that risk. Additional procedures were performed as deemed necessary in the circumstances. The audit provides a reasonable basis for the opinions expressed. Internal control over financial reporting is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. It includes policies and procedures that (i) maintain records that accurately and fairly reflect transactions and dispositions of assets; (ii) ensure transactions are recorded to permit financial statement preparation in accordance with accounting principles and that receipts and expenditures occur only with management and director authorizations; and (iii) provide reasonable assurance about preventing or timely detecting unauthorized acquisition, use, or disposition of assets that could affect financial statements. Due to inherent limitations, internal control may not prevent or detect misstatements, and projections of effectiveness to future periods are subject to the risk that controls may become inadequate or compliance may deteriorate. Critical audit matters include reserves for credit losses on Card Member loans and the Membership Rewards liability. Reserves for credit losses on Card Member loans totaled $3.7 billion as of December 31, 2022, and are based on management’s estimate of expected credit losses using historical loss experience and current and future economic conditions over a reasonable and supportable period (R&S Period) beyond the balance sheet date. Management uses statistically-based models involving significant judgment in determining the R&S Period, probability of default, exposure at default, and incorporating economic conditions. Beyond the R&S Period, expected credit losses are estimated using long-term average loss rates. Management also evaluates qualitative reserves for losses not fully captured in quantitative methods, considering factors such as external conditions, portfolio trends, concentration, past due accounts, and management risk actions. The audit effort involved significant auditor judgment, subjectivity, and effort in evaluating models, inputs, qualitative reserves, and assumptions, including the R&S Period and loss rates beyond it, and required professionals with specialized skill and knowledge. Procedures included testing controls related to the reserves, evaluating the appropriateness of management’s methodology, testing the completeness and accuracy of significant inputs, and assessing the reasonableness of qualitative reserves and assumptions. The Membership Rewards liability was $12.8 billion as of December 31, 2022. Key assumptions are the weighted average cost (WAC) per point and the Ultimate Redemption Rate (URR). The URR estimates future redemptions based on redemption trends, card product type, enrollment tenure, card spend levels, and credit attributes. Revenue is recognized when obligations under contracts are satisfied. Discount revenue is earned from merchant payable fees for facilitating transactions, recorded at transaction time, with contract durations varying by merchant size. Net card fees are deferred and recognized on a straight-line basis over the membership period, with unamortized balances reported in Other liabilities. Service Fees and Other Revenue are included in the income statement.

Goodwill represents the excess of acquisition cost over the fair value of assets and liabilities acquired and is allocated to reporting units for impairment testing. A reporting unit is defined as an operating segment or a business one level below an operating segment, for which discrete financial information is regularly reviewed by the segment manager. Goodwill is evaluated annually as of June 30, or more frequently if events or circumstances indicate that the fair value of a reporting unit is more likely than not below its carrying value. Before performing the impairment assessment, a recoverability test of certain long-lived assets is conducted. The company has the option to perform a qualitative assessment to determine if it is more likely than not that a reporting unit’s fair value is below its carrying value; if so, a quantitative assessment is performed. The qualitative assessment evaluates factors such as economic conditions, industry and market trends, cost factors, financial performance, and other company- or unit-specific events. If the fair value is found to be below carrying value, a quantitative assessment is conducted, which compares the reporting unit’s fair value to its carrying amount, including goodwill. If the carrying amount exceeds fair value, an impairment loss is recognized for the excess. Fair value is measured using widely accepted valuation techniques, combining the income approach (discounted cash flows) and market approach (market multiples). Discounted cash flows use internal forecasts to estimate future cash flows, discounted at the expected cost of equity derived from a capital asset pricing model, which reflects market risks and uncertainties. Market multiples apply comparable publicly traded companies’ earnings or revenue multiples to the reporting unit’s operating results. The reserves for credit losses are based on the current expected credit loss (CECL) methodology, which estimates lifetime expected credit losses over a reasonable and supportable period (R&S Period) of approximately three years beyond the balance sheet date, incorporating historical loss experience and current and future economic conditions. The process uses models for probability of default (PD), exposure at default (EAD), and future recoveries. PD models estimate the likelihood of write-off, EAD models estimate the balance at write-off, including expected repayments based on historical payment and revolve behavior, and recovery models estimate future recoveries. Beyond the R&S Period, expected credit losses are estimated using long-term average loss rates.

The company estimates expected credit losses by incorporating historical loss experience and current and future economic conditions over a reasonable and supportable period (R&S Period), which is approximately three years beyond the balance sheet date. A reserve rate is determined through judgments combined with historical data and applied to outstanding loan or receivable balances to generate a credit loss reserve. This process uses statistically-based models that include Probability of Default (PD), Exposure at Default (EAD), and future recoveries for each month of the R&S Period. PD models estimate the likelihood of an account being written off, EAD models estimate the balance at default, accounting for expected repayments based on historical payment and revolve behavior—particularly relevant in revolving portfolios due to complex assumptions about future spend and payment patterns—and recovery models estimate amounts expected to be recovered from Card Members after default, considering time of default, time since default, and macroeconomic conditions. The company also evaluates expected recoveries for previously written-off accounts based on how long ago they were written off and future economic conditions, even if such recoveries exceed expected losses. Models are developed using historical loss data across the economic cycle and consider account-specific risk factors. Future economic conditions during the R&S Period are based on multiple macroeconomic scenarios provided by an independent third party, which management reviews periodically and weights based on uncertainty. Key variables in these scenarios include unemployment rates and real GDP growth (quarter-over-quarter, seasonally adjusted to annualized rates). Qualitative reserves are assessed to cover losses not fully captured by quantitative methods or economic assumptions, and quantitative reserves may be adjusted to address model limitations or external factors such as portfolio trends, concentrations, past due account volume, or management risk actions. Lifetime losses are evaluated at a granular level, including pooled assessments for financial assets with similar risk characteristics like past spend, remittance behavior, credit bureau scores, delinquency status, and tenure. Credit losses on accrued interest are measured and reported in the Consolidated Balance Sheets and Consolidated Statements of Income, not by reversing interest income. Separate models are used for troubled debt restructurings (TDRs), which are measured individually using a discounted cash flow model. Loans and receivables are written off when deemed uncollectible, typically after 180 days past due for pay-in-full or revolving loans and 120 days for term loans, or upon notification in cases of bankruptcy or debts owed by deceased individuals. American Express periodically securitizes Card Member loans and receivables through transfers to securitization trusts, specifically the American Express Credit Account Master Trust (the Lending Trust) and the American Express Issuance Trust II (the Charge Trust, together with the Lending Trust, the Trusts). These Trusts are considered Variable Interest Entities (VIEs) due to insufficient equity at risk to finance their operations, which involve issuing debt securities collateralized by the underlying loans and receivables. American Express performs servicing and key decision-making for the Trusts, thereby having the power to direct activities that most significantly affect their economic performance, particularly the collection of the underlying loans and receivables. Additionally, American Express holds all variable interests in both Trusts, except for the debt securities issued to third-party investors. As of December 31, 2022 and 2021, American Express’s ownership of variable interests in the Lending Trust was $16.0 billion and $15.0 billion, respectively, and in the Charge Trust was $5.2 billion and $3.2 billion, respectively. These interests grant American Express the right to receive benefits and the obligation to absorb losses, which could be significant. Based on these factors, American Express is the primary beneficiary and consolidates the Trusts. The debt securities issued by the Trusts are non-recourse to American Express, and the securitized loans and receivables are available only for payment of the debt securities or other obligations arising from the securitization transactions. The long-term debt of each Trust is payable solely from collections on their respective underlying assets. The company uses derivative financial instruments to manage exposures to interest rate and foreign exchange risks, carrying derivatives at fair value on the Consolidated Balance Sheets and not for trading purposes. Market risks include interest rate risk from changes in the relationship between asset and liability interest rates and foreign exchange risk from transactions, funding, investments, and earnings in currencies other than the U.S. dollar. Market risks are centrally monitored using market risk limits and escalation triggers under the Asset/Liability Management Policy. Interest rate risk arises from funding Card Member receivables and fixed-rate loans with variable-rate borrowings and changes in benchmark rates, managed by adjusting the mix of short-term and variable-rate debt versus fixed-rate debt, and through the use of interest rate swaps to convert fixed-rate to variable-rate or vice versa. Foreign exchange exposures arise from Card Member spending in non-billing currencies, cross-currency transactions and balances, cross-currency investing, and foreign currency revenues and expenses, managed through spot agreements or hedging via derivatives such as foreign exchange forwards. Derivatives may give rise to counterparty credit risk, managed by considering current exposure and maximum potential future exposure over 12 months, with counterparties pre-approved and rated as investment grade, and centrally monitored. A majority of derivatives are subject to master netting agreements, allowing net presentation of derivative assets and liabilities with the same counterparty on the Consolidated Balance Sheets. To further mitigate credit risk, the company exercises rights under executed credit support agreements for bilateral interest rate swaps and selected foreign exchange contracts, requiring the party in a net liability position to post collateral when fair value changes exceed thresholds; all centrally cleared derivatives are fully collateralized. Certain bilateral derivative agreements include provisions allowing counterparties to terminate in the event of a downgrade of the company’s debt rating below investment grade and settle the net liability position. As of December 31, 2022, these derivatives were not in a material net liability position and there was no material risk exposure to any individual counterparty. Based on the assessment of counterparty and company credit risk as of December 31, 2022 and 2021, no credit risk adjustment to the derivative portfolio was required. The Deferred Compensation Plan for Directors and Advisors was originally effective October 1, 1973, most recently amended and restated on April 1, 2018, and further amended and restated effective January 1, 2023. Eligibility includes any Director or Advisor of American Express Company or American Express National Bank (AENB) who is not an officer or employee of the Company, AENB, or a subsidiary. Deferral elections for compensation earned in a calendar year must be made no later than the end of the preceding calendar year, except that a newly elected Director may make an irrevocable deferral election within 30 days of election, which applies to compensation earned after that date. If an election is received before initial appointment, it becomes effective upon appointment and applies to compensation earned on or after that date. If received within 30 days of appointment, it becomes effective upon receipt and applies to compensation earned after that date. If received after 30 days but before January 1 of the following year, it becomes effective as of January 1 of the following calendar year. Unless otherwise provided, a Director’s deferral election for a calendar year applies to each subsequent year unless revoked or changed. Compensation deferred is credited to bookkeeping accounts; compensation for calendar years prior to 2015 is credited to a Pre-2015 Class Year Account, and for 2015 and thereafter to separate Class Year Accounts for each year. The account for years prior to 2015 is referred to as the Pre-2015 Class Year Account; for 2015 and later, as the Class Year Account for the respective year. The Pre-2015 Class Year Account and each Class Year Account may be referred to individually as a Class Year Account and collectively as the Class Year Accounts. Compensation is credited to the account effective as of the last day of the calendar quarter to which it relates, except in the event of a Payment Event Date during a quarter where a Director has deferred all or part of compensation, in which case the deferred compensation for that quarter is credited effective as of the Payment Event Date. Investment options include an AFR-Based Option, which credits interest at 120% of the applicable federal long-term rate for December of the prior year, compounded daily or as specified, and a Share Equivalent Option, which converts deferred amounts into SEUs (shares equivalent units) by dividing the deferred amount by the average closing price of the Company’s common stock over the last 15 trading days of the quarter, or immediately preceding a Payment Event Date. On dividend payment dates, additional SEUs are credited based on the per-share dividend divided by the closing price on the dividend date, multiplied by the number of SEUs credited on the shareholder record date. In the event of stock splits, dividends, mergers, spin-offs, recapitalizations, or other extraordinary events, the number of SEUs is automatically adjusted to maintain the Director’s proportional interest.

On the date the Company pays a dividend on the Common Stock, dividend equivalents in the form of additional SEUs will be credited to a Director’s Class Year Accounts for a number of SEUs equal to (i) the per-share cash dividend divided by the closing price of the Common Stock on the dividend payment date, multiplied by (ii) the number of SEUs credited to each such Class Year Account on the shareholder record date applicable to such dividend payment. In the event of a change in the outstanding Common Stock due to a stock split, stock dividend, split-up, split-off, spin-off, recapitalization, merger, consolidation, rights offering, reorganization, combination, or exchange of shares, or any sale by the Company of all or part of its assets, any distribution to shareholders other than a normal cash dividend, or other extraordinary or unusual event, the number of SEUs credited to a Director’s Class Year Accounts will be automatically adjusted so that the Director’s proportional interest is maintained. For purposes of Section 10, the SEUs payable to a Director on a Payment Event Date will be valued by multiplying the applicable number of SEUs by the average of the closing prices of the Common Stock for the fifteen (15) trading days immediately preceding the Payment Event Date. The Administrator may, in their discretion, allow a Director to change the Investment Options for an existing Class Year SEU Award Account at any time after such Director’s separation from service, pursuant to rules and restrictions prescribed by the Administrator. A number of SEUs equal to the number of Share Equivalent Units awarded to a Director during a calendar year under the American Express Company 2003 Share Equivalent Unit Plan for Directors, as amended and restated from time to time (the “SEU Plan”), for calendar year 2015 and subsequent years, will be credited to a bookkeeping account established under this Plan for such Director for that calendar year. A Director’s SEUs attributable to awards under the SEU Plan for calendar year 2015 and each subsequent year shall be credited to separate accounts for each such year, referred to as the Director’s “Class Year SEU Award Account” for the respective calendar year (e.g., the account for 2015 is the “2015 Class Year SEU Award Account” and for 2016 is the “2016 Class Year SEU Award Account”). Each Class Year SEU Award Account may be referred to individually as a “Class Year SEU Award Account” and collectively as the “Class Year SEU Award Accounts” of the Director. If a Director has a Pre-2015 Class Year Account for compensation deferred prior to 2015, then SEUs attributable to awards under the SEU Plan for calendar years prior to 2015 shall be credited to such existing Pre-2015 Class Year Account and treated as SEUs under the Share Equivalent Option, adjusted and paid accordingly; if the Director does not have such an account, the SEUs shall be credited to a new Pre-2015 Class Year Account and treated as SEUs under the Share Equivalent Option. The SEUs credited pursuant to Section 7 for calendar year 2015 and each subsequent year shall be credited to a Class Year SEU Award Account for such year at the time specified by the SEU Plan, and thereafter shall be adjusted, valued, and paid in the same manner as SEUs credited to a Class Year Account under the Share Equivalent Option. The Administrator may, in their discretion, allow a Director to change the Investment Options for an existing Class Year SEU Award Account at any time after such Director’s separation from service, pursuant to rules and restrictions prescribed by the Administrator. A Director newly elected to the Board of Directors of the Company or AENB may make an irrevocable payment election applicable to the Director’s Class Year Account and Class Year SEU Award Account for the calendar year of election, specifying the time and form of payment as follows: (A) Time of Payment—either upon separation from service or on a specified anniversary following separation from service, but not later than the tenth (10th) anniversary; (B) Form of Payment—in cash, either as a lump sum or a specified number of annual installments (not to exceed ten (10)). To the extent permissible under Section 409A, a Director must make this payment election within thirty (30) days after election to the Board (or, if permissible under Section 409A, may make the election before election). If a Director fails to make a payment election within the permitted time or is not permitted under Section 409A, the Director is deemed to have elected to receive the accounts in a lump sum upon separation from service. The payment election (or default election) under Section 8(a) for a calendar year applies to both the Director’s Class Year Account and Class Year SEU Award Account for that year. For each subsequent calendar year following the first election, the Director may make an irrevocable payment election applicable to the Class Year Account and Class Year SEU Award Account for that year, specifying the time and form of payment from the options in Sections 8(a)(A) and (B). The Director must make this payment election no later than the end of the preceding calendar year. Unless the Administrator provides otherwise prior to the start of a subsequent calendar year, a Director’s actual (or default) payment election for a calendar year shall apply to all subsequent calendar years unless the Director makes a new payment election under Section 8(b) prior to the subsequent calendar year. The payment election (or default election) under Section 8(b) for a subsequent calendar year applies to both the Class Year Account and Class Year SEU Award Account for that year. A Director may change an existing (or default) payment election for a calendar year by making a subsequent payment election, provided that: (A) the change does not take effect for twelve (12) months following the date it becomes effective; (B) it specifies a new permissible payment date (or a new permissible payment commencement date for installment payments) that is no sooner than five years after the original payment date (or original payment commencement date); and (C) the new payment date (or new payment commencement date) is no later than the tenth (10th) anniversary of the Director’s separation from service. Any change to a Director’s existing payment election (or default election) for a calendar year applies to both the Class Year Account and Class Year SEU Award Account for that year. Upon a Director’s separation from service, the payment election in effect on that date for each of the Director’s Class Year Accounts and Class Year SEU Award Accounts governs the time and form of payment of each such account for purposes of Section 10. In the event a Director dies prior to receipt of any or all amounts payable under this Plan, except as otherwise provided, any amounts credited to the Director’s Class Year Accounts and Class Year SEU Award Accounts shall be paid to the legal representative of the Director’s estate pursuant to Section 10. The Administrator may allow Directors to designate a beneficiary or beneficiaries to receive payment of their Class Year Accounts and Class Year SEU Award Accounts upon death, and may prescribe the terms and procedures for such designations. If a valid beneficiary designation is in place at the time of death, amounts credited to the deceased Director’s accounts shall be paid to the designated beneficiary or beneficiaries in accordance with the terms of the designation (instead of to the estate). All payments under Section 9 shall be made in a lump sum. A Director’s Class Year Accounts and Class Year SEU Award Accounts will be paid (or commence to be paid in the case of installment payments) on the Payment Event Date applicable to and in effect for such account, as elected by the Director or otherwise provided by this Plan. “Payment Event Date” means the date of separation from service or a specified anniversary following separation from service, no later than the tenth (10th) anniversary, whichever is applicable under Section 8 (including Section 8(c)), or if earlier, the date of death as provided by Section 9. Payments shall be made in a lump sum or a specified number of installments, as applicable under Section 8 (including Section 8(c)), or in a lump sum if payment is made due to death under Section 9. In the case of installment payments, each anniversary of the initial Payment Event Date shall also be treated as a Payment Event Date. A payment on a given Payment Event Date shall be made or commenced as soon as administratively practicable following the Payment Event Date, but no later than 90 days thereafter (or such later date permitted under Section 409A). The amount to be paid for a Class Year Account or Class Year SEU Award Account on a Payment Event Date will be calculated as of the applicable Payment Event Date pursuant to Section 6. No interest, dividend equivalents, or other earnings will be credited on amounts payable on a given Payment Event Date between that date and the actual date of payment. If a Director elects to receive payment in a specified number of annual installments, each installment will be paid proportionally based on the number of remaining installment payments and the balance of the account, including related earnings and losses credited or debited pursuant to Section 6 and this Section 10. (For example, if a Director chooses four annual installments, the first payment shall be 1/4 of the value, the second 1/3, the third 1/2, and the fourth 1/1 of the value.) In the case of installment payments, the account shall be valued as of the Payment Event Date for each installment. Participants may not sell, transfer, assign, pledge, levy, attach, encumber, or alienate any amounts payable under this Plan.
