Participation in the Plan is limited to Employees meeting Section 4.2 and who are in Band 35 or above, unless otherwise designated by the Administrator, and the Plan must be a “top-hat” plan for ERISA purposes. To become a Participant, an Employee must satisfy Section 4.1 and either (a) be a participant under a Qualified Retirement Plan, or (b) for the relevant Plan Year: (i) have an Account from a prior Plan Year (including a hypothetical balance if the Participant would have had one had they accepted a prior offer), or (ii) receive Total Pay (as defined under the RSP, without regard to the Section 401(a)(17) Limitation) in excess of the Section 401(a)(17) Limitation, or (iii) be employed in Band 50 or above as of the Band 50 Determination Date in the prior Plan Year (with exceptions for newly hired or promoted individuals in Band 50 who may participate in open enrollment at the Administrator’s discretion), or (iv) accrue benefits under a Qualified Retirement Plan in excess of the Section 415 Limitation. Under Section 5.1, if a Participant is a participant under the RP (other than a terminated participant), the Company establishes an RP-Related Account, with “Compensation” defined as in the RP, and the Committee may designate additional items; effective with the 2003 performance year (awarded in 2004) and thereafter, restricted stock awards in lieu of cash supplemental Annual Incentive Awards are included. Contribution Credits are credited to the RP-Related Account for each Plan Year as the excess, if any, of (x) the Contribution Credits that would have been credited under the RP if the Plan’s Compensation definition was used, the Section 401(a)(17) Limitation was ignored, and no deferral occurred, over (y) the actual Contribution Credits credited to the Defined Benefit Account under the RP. No credits are made for pay periods ending on or after July 1, 2007. The benefits formula is determined by the Administrator and applied uniformly. Certain Participants, as determined by the Company, may be deemed to have rendered five additional Years of Service; for each such Participant, an additional amount is credited equal to the excess of (x) the total cumulative Contribution Credits that would have been credited had such additional Years of Service been rendered, over (y) the actual cumulative credits, subject to terms and conditions, with such amounts subject to five-year vesting and forfeited if service terminates before five years of actual service due to reasons other than death or disability (as defined in the RP). For Participants with a special agreement who had not accrued five Years of Service as of July 1, 2007, they are entitled to receive the credit for the 2007 Plan Year as if the RP remained in effect through December 31, 2007 and the Participant was active; regardless of such agreements, no credit is available for the 2008 Plan Year or later. Under Section 5.2, if a Participant is in the RSP (other than a terminated participant), the Company establishes an RSP-Related Account. “Compensation” for RSP credits has the meaning of “Total Pay” in the RSP, with the Committee able to designate additional items; effective July 1, 2007, restricted stock awards in lieu of cash Annual Incentive Awards are included, subject to a limitation. For Participants in Band 50 or above, Incentive Pay (including restricted stock awards) in excess of one times Base Salary is excluded; Base Salary and pay band are determined as of January 1 of each Plan Year (or the date of rehire if not employed on January 1, or the rehire date if rehired within the same Plan Year). Incentive Pay subject to this limitation is only those actually paid in the Plan Year. Temporary salary reductions from March 30, 2009 to January 3, 2010 are disregarded in determining Compensation. Contribution Credits are credited to the RSP-Related Account each Plan Year as follows: (i) Company Stock Contribution: an amount equal to (A) one percent of the sum of (1) Compensation calculated without the Section 401(a)(17) Limitation or Section 415 Limitations, plus (2) the portion of Compensation deferred during the Plan Year under a Deferral Plan, minus (B) the amount actually allocated as a Company Stock Contribution under the RSP; the Section 401(a)(17) Limitation is applied pro ratably to each regularly scheduled pay period; no credits are made for pay periods ending on or after July 1, 2007. (ii) Company Profit-Sharing Contribution: an amount equal to the Company Profit-Sharing Contribution percentage utilized for the RSP for that Plan Year.

For each Plan Year, contributions to a Participant’s RSP-Related Account are made in accordance with Section 5.3 as follows: (i) a Company Stock Contribution equal to one percent of the sum of (1) the Participant’s Compensation calculated without the Section 401(a)(17) Limitation or Section 415 Limitations, plus (2) the portion of Compensation deferred during the Plan Year under a Deferral Plan, minus the amount actually allocated as a Company Stock Contribution to the account; this contribution is not credited for any pay period ending on or after July 1, 2007, and the Section 401(a)(17) Limitation is applied pro ratably to each regularly scheduled pay period. (ii) A Company Profit-Sharing Contribution equal to the Company Profit-Sharing Contribution percentage (which includes any Company Discretionary Profit Sharing Contribution or Company Fixed Rate Contribution) times the sum of (1) Compensation without Section 401(a)(17) or Section 415 limitations and (2) deferred Compensation, minus the actual amount allocated as a Company Profit-Sharing Contribution (as applicable); at the time of a Supplemental Distribution, benefits credited under this section are restricted to the Participant’s vested portion, and any non-vested portion is forfeited. (iii) A Company Matching Contribution: (A) effective from Compensation paid on or after January 1, 2017, each eligible Participant receives a Matching Contribution equal to the Participant’s salary reduction amount (from Base Salary, Incentive Pay, or a combination) under a Deferral Election, up to a maximum of six percent of Compensation not counted under the RSP due to exceeding the Section 401(a)(17) Limitation or being deferred under a Deferral Plan; Compensation for this purpose excludes amounts paid prior to the Participant’s Entry Date; (B) separately, a Matching Contribution is provided equal to the Qualified Matching Contribution that would have been made but was not due to Section 415 limitations; (C) vesting of Matching Contributions follows the vesting rules under the RSP. (iv) A Company Conversion Contribution: (A) equal to the Company Conversion Contribution percentage times the sum of (1) Compensation without Section 401(a)(17) or Section 415 limitations and (2) deferred Compensation, minus the actual amount allocated as a Company Conversion Contribution; at a Supplemental Distribution, only the vested portion is credited and non-vested portions are forfeited; no Company Conversion Contributions are made after December 31, 2017 for employees in Band 50 and above, or after December 31, 2018 for employees below Band 50; (B) no contributions were made for the pay period commencing March 30, 2009 through January 3, 2010, except for Participants who were Retirement Eligible as of December 31, 2009; upon resumption after January 3, 2010, contributions resumed at the same level as immediately prior to March 30, 2009; the Company retains the right to modify, amend, or terminate the Plan at any time. (v) Transition Contributions for Former GE Capital Employees: equal to the Transition Contribution percentage times the sum of (1) Compensation without Section 401(a)(17) or Section 415 limitations and (2) deferred Compensation, minus the actual amount allocated as a Transition Contribution; if a Participant is eligible for both Company Conversion Contributions and Transition Contributions, the greater amount is credited; at a Supplemental Distribution, only the vested portion is credited and non-vested portions are forfeited; the right to Transition Contributions expires at the same time as under the RSP; no Transition Contributions are made after March 31, 2011. (vi) No Disability Contributions are provided under the RSP. (c) For certain Participants, as determined by the Company in its sole discretion, five additional Years of Service are deemed to have been rendered starting January 1, 2008; for each such Participant, an additional amount equal to 80 percent (or a lower percentage specified in a special agreement) of the Participant’s annual base salary (as of hire date), before any deferrals under Section 401(k), Section 125, or a Deferral Plan, is credited to the RSP-Related Account; amounts are calculated using procedures determined by the Administrator and consistently applied to similarly situated Participants; unless otherwise agreed, such amounts are subject to five-year vesting and are forfeited if service terminates for any reason other than death or disability before five years of actual service; amounts are credited to the RSP-Related Account established under Section 5.3. Section 5.3 outlines the timing and manner of crediting: (a) credits are made at times and in ways determined by the Administrator, generally similar to Qualified Retirement Plans; (i) amounts related to Section 415 Limitations are estimated at Separation from Service based on assumptions, assuming benefits would begin at Separation or the earliest possible date, and credited immediately before payment; (ii) amounts under Section 5.2(c) are determined as of and credited on the one-year anniversary of the later of the date of the special agreement or the first day of employment; procedures are applied consistently to similarly situated Participants. (b) Company Stock Contributions are initially credited to a subaccount relating to the Stock Fund, with the amount determined by the Administrator in a manner reasonably consistent with similar determinations under the Stock Fund. (c) Other contributions (profit-sharing, matching, conversion, transition, and special agreement credits) are credited to the RSP-Related Account with subaccounts selected by the Administrator, representing available investment funds; (i) amounts directed to the Stock Fund cannot exceed Plan or Administrator-established limits, and excess amounts are redirected per Article 7; (ii) no subaccount coincides with a self-directed brokerage account available under the RSP. (d) The Administrator may establish additional book reserve accounts at its discretion, with procedures for reflecting increases, decreases, interest, dividends, gains, and losses determined by the Administrator. Section 5.4 governs Supplemental Benefits Payment Elections: (a) existing Participants (excluding those in pay status on December 31, 2004) may make Supplemental Elections as follows: (i) Participants without prior initial elections may make such an election on or before the Administrator’s set date, not later than December 31, 2005; (ii) Participants with prior initial elections but without prior modifications may change their election on or before December 31, 2005 to any permissible payment form under Section 5.4(b) and Section 409A, regardless of whether it extends or shortens payment periods; such distributions that accelerate payments do not reduce otherwise payable amounts; any such election made on or before December 31, 2005 constitutes a modification under the one-time limitation in Section 5.4(d), and no further modifications are permitted; (iii) Employees who first become Participants after December 31, 2005 may make initial elections in accordance with Administrator rules compliant with Section 409A; for employees who first become Participants on or after January 1, 2012 or who first become entitled to Supplemental Benefits due to Compensation paid in the fourth quarter of 2011 (with clarification that individuals enrolled in enrollment processes prior to the fourth quarter of 2011 are not covered), the initial election is not effective for Company contributions calculated based on Compensation paid prior to the end of the first calendar year beginning on or after the date of first Compensation, or in the case of a new Participant in Band 50 or above with a 30-day election period expiring no later than December 31 of their first calendar year as a Band 50 Employee, or for a new Participant not in Band 50 who is not permitted to file an election during open enrollment for the following calendar year; for a Participant first paid Compensation in the fourth quarter of a calendar year or with a 30-day election period expiring after December 31 of their first calendar year as a Band 50 Employee and not enrolled in open enrollment, the initial election is not effective for Company contributions based on Compensation paid prior to the end of the second calendar year beginning on or after the date of first Compensation; for purposes of determining which Supplemental Benefits are subject to the Automatic New Participant Supplemental Election, a Participant with Compensation for which Supplemental Benefits could be calculated is considered to have such benefits calculated, regardless of whether they actually qualify or meet the requirements for receiving Company Matching Contributions or the Company’s decision not to make contributions; instead, for Company contributions not covered by the Participant’s election, the Company is deemed to have made an Automatic New Participant election.

A Participant who is not permitted to participate in open enrollment under Article 6 for the following calendar year has an initial Supplemental Election that is not effective with respect to Company contributions calculated based on Compensation paid prior to the end of the second calendar year beginning on or after the date the Participant is first paid Compensation with respect to which Company contributions are calculated, or in which the Participant is otherwise described in this paragraph. For the avoidance of doubt, a Participant with Compensation for which Supplemental Benefits could be calculated is considered to have such benefits calculated for purposes of determining which Supplemental Benefits are subject to the Automatic New Participant Supplemental Election, regardless of whether the Participant actually qualifies for such benefits to be credited to their Account. A Participant’s failure to satisfy service requirements or make required contributions, or the Company’s decision not to make contributions, does not affect the duration of the Automatic New Participant Supplemental Election. With respect to Company contributions not covered by a Participant’s Supplemental Election, the Company is deemed to have made an Automatic New Participant Supplemental Election for the Participant (or their beneficiary in the event of death) to receive Supplemental Benefits attributable to such contributions in a single lump sum as of January 1 or July 1 that is at least six months following the earliest of their Separation from Service or the date of Disability or death, as applicable (or as soon as administratively feasible thereafter, but no later than 90 days). Company contributions calculated with respect to Compensation paid later than the time periods set forth in Section 5.4(a)(iii)(A) are subject to a Participant’s initial Supplemental Election. For an Employee who was a former Participant and again becomes a Participant after rehiring following Separation from Service, the election rules in this Section apply to Company Matching Contributions, Company Conversion Contributions, and Company Profit-Sharing Contributions made after the rehire date as if the rehire date (or, if later, the resumption of eligibility to participate) were the date of initial participation eligibility. Participants who have previously made both a Supplemental Election and a modification to such Election are subject to the rules in Section 5.4(d) prohibiting any further changes to their Supplemental Elections. However, any Participant who was not in pay status on January 1, 2005 and who previously modified an initial Supplemental Election to accelerate the payment period from the Plan shall not have any reduction in the amounts otherwise payable (notwithstanding Section V(D)(1)(b)(ii) of the Prior SRP Plan). A Participant may elect to receive Supplemental Benefits not covered by the Automatic New Participant Supplemental Election in a single lump-sum payment or in annual installments over five, ten, or fifteen consecutive calendar years. Except as provided in Section 5.4(d), a Participant may not modify their initial Supplemental Election as described. Such subsequent Supplemental Election applies to all Supplemental Benefits under the Plan and the Prior SRP Plan not covered by the Automatic New Participant Supplemental Election (except for benefits that were in pay status on December 31, 2004). A Participant’s reemployment after Separation from Service does not affect benefits attributable to periods prior to Separation from Service, and they are subject to a new Automatic New Participant Supplemental Election and initial Supplemental Election with respect to post-reemployment benefits. If a Participant fails to make a valid, timely Supplemental Election in accordance with Section 5.4(a) and the rules and procedures adopted by the Administrator, they are deemed to have made an initial Supplemental Election to receive their Supplemental Benefits not covered by the Automatic New Participant Supplemental Election in a single lump sum as of January 1 or July 1 that is at least six months following the earliest of their Separation from Service or the date of Disability or death, as applicable (or as soon as administratively feasible thereafter, but no later than 90 days). A Participant who has not previously modified an initial Supplemental Election may make a one-time modification to elect a different form of payment for Supplemental Benefits not covered by the Automatic New Participant Supplemental Election. To be effective, such a modification must be filed in writing as prescribed by the Administrator and must comply with Section 409A, including a minimum additional deferral period of five years and the requirement that the subsequent Supplemental Election not be effective until 12 months after it is made. A Participant may not change the payment method of their Supplemental Benefits after Separation from Service. Notwithstanding this, with respect to an Employee who was a former Participant and again becomes a Participant after rehiring following Separation from Service, a one-time modification under Section 5.4(d) is permitted with respect to the initial Supplemental Election made following the rehire date, regardless of whether the Participant had also made such a modification for benefits earned prior to Separation from Service. By way of clarification, the Automatic New Participant Supplemental Election cannot be modified. Employees eligible to participate in the Plan for a Plan Year with respect to Deferral Benefits will be notified by Amex of their eligibility. If Amex erroneously notifies an individual of eligibility and such individual does not meet the requirements of Section 4.2 or has been excluded by the Administrator pursuant to Section 4.1, the erroneous notification does not cause eligibility, and any Deferral Election made by such ineligible individual is null and void and of no effect to the extent permissible under Section 409A. An eligible Employee for a Plan Year who was a Participant in the prior Plan Year as of the Band 50 Determination Date, or who is employed in Band 50 or above as of that date in the prior Plan Year, or who otherwise becomes employed in Band 50 or above or first becomes eligible while in Band 50 or above prior to the end of the prior Plan Year and is authorized by the Administrator to participate in enrollment, becomes a Participant in the Plan with respect to Deferral Benefits for such Plan Year by making a Deferral Election in accordance with Section 6.5. Such an Employee’s Deferral Benefits Eligibility Date for the Plan Year is January 1. Special rules apply to the extent permitted by Section 6.3: (a) An Employee not already a Participant who first becomes employed in Band 50 or above (or, in the case of an employee in Band 50 or above but not eligible for a Qualified Retirement Plan, as of the date they become eligible for such a plan) is considered eligible as of that date and may file an election within 30 days of that date; their Deferral Benefits Eligibility Date is the first payroll period beginning after the expiration of the 30-day period. The Administrator may establish procedures for coordination of special enrollment and open enrollment opportunities for Employees who would otherwise become eligible for Band 50 or above special enrollment at the end of the Plan Year, and/or may impose limits on the availability of special enrollment in appropriate circumstances. (b) An Employee not already a Participant and not employed in Band 50 or above: (i) who first satisfies the requirements for participation during one of the first three quarters of the Plan Year by exceeding the Section 401(a)(17) Limitation becomes eligible to participate in Deferral Benefits effective January 1 of the following Plan Year, which is their Deferral Benefits Eligibility Date, and may participate in the Plan’s open enrollment period; (ii) who first satisfies the requirements during the final calendar quarter of the Plan Year by exceeding the Section 401(a)(17) Limitation becomes eligible as of the first pay period beginning after the first day of the second month of the first calendar quarter of the following Plan Year (the first day of such pay period being the Deferral Benefits Eligibility Date), and may make an election in advance of such date and in accordance with Section 6.3 by the deadline established by the Administrator. (iii) An Employee does not have a special enrollment right merely because they exceed the Section 415 limit under a Qualified Retirement Plan. (iv) The date an Employee exceeds the Section 401(a)(17) Limit is determined based on Compensation for the Plan Year, regardless of whether some portion of that Compensation is excluded from Supplemental Benefits calculations because the Participant had not yet completed the service requirement for Company contributions. (c) Mid-year elections are not allowed unless the Employee also satisfies all requirements of Section 6.3 and must be filed by the deadline established by the Administrator. All Deferral Elections become irrevocable as of the day before the Deferral Benefits Eligibility Date, or such earlier date as established by the Administrator. To the extent permissible under Section 409A and Section 6.2, Employees who become eligible to participate in the Plan during a Plan Year with respect to Deferral Benefits and who have not previously been eligible to participate in an elective account-balance deferred compensation arrangement (as defined for purposes of Section 409A) of Amex or its subsidiaries may be offered the opportunity to participate in the Plan for the Plan Year in accordance with Section 6.2. In the case of an Employee who had previously been eligible to participate in an elective account-balance deferred compensation arrangement (as defined for purposes of Section 409A) of Amex or its subsidiaries (regardless of whether they chose to do so), that Employee may be treated as newly eligible to participate and entitled to mid-year enrollment to the extent permitted by Section 6.2 if: (a) the Employee had received payment of all amounts under the Plan’s Deferral Account and any other elective account-balance plan and, as of the date of the last payment, was not eligible to continue participation in the Plan’s Deferral Benefits or any other elective account-balance plan, disregarding any right to delay payment; or (b) the Employee had ceased to be eligible to participate in Deferral Benefits under the Plan and all other elective account-balance plans and had not been eligible to participate in Deferral Benefits under the Plan or any other elective account-balance plan at any time during the 24-month period ending on the date the Employee again became eligible (disregarding for purposes of determining eligibility the right to accrue earnings on amounts in the Plan or other elective account-balance plan), regardless of whether the Employee has received payments of amounts previously deferred. Eligible Compensation includes: (i) an eligible Employee for a Plan Year may elect to defer a specified amount from one or more of the following items: (A) the Employee’s Base Salary to be paid during that Plan Year; and (B) the Employee’s Incentive Pay to be paid in the second Plan Year to commence after the election is made (excluding any amounts that would otherwise be Incentive Pay but which are earned prior to the start of the Plan Year following the Plan Year in which the Deferral Election is filed). Notwithstanding Section 6.4(a)(i), an Employee who becomes eligible to participate in the Plan with respect to Deferral Benefits during a Plan Year who is offered the opportunity by Amex to participate as described in Section 6.3 may only elect to defer a specified amount from one or more of the following items: (A) the Employee’s Base Salary for the Plan Year of the Deferral Election which is paid for payroll periods beginning on and after the Employee’s Deferral Benefits Eligibility Date; and (B) a portion of the Employee’s Incentive Pay to be paid in the following Plan Year, calculated by multiplying the amount of each Incentive Pay payment made in the following Plan Year by a percentage, such percentage to be determined by dividing the number of days remaining in the calendar year as of the Employee’s Deferral Benefits Eligibility Date by 365 or, in the case of an Employee hired during the performance period, by the total number of days in the performance period measured from the date of hire. The Administrator shall impose the following limits on Deferral Benefits: (i) the amount that may be deferred from (A) Base Salary to be paid in the following Plan Year and (B) Incentive Pay to be paid in the second following Plan Year is limited to 100 percent of the Participant’s Base Salary rate in effect as of December 31 of the Plan Year during which the Deferral Election is filed (or, for an Employee who becomes eligible during a Plan Year, 100 percent of the Employee’s Base Salary rate in effect as of the date they become eligible to participate: (1) if eligible by being hired into or promoted to Band 50 or above (or transferred to eligible status while in Band 50), or (2) if eligible by exceeding the Section 401(a)(17) Limitation, then as of the last day of the calendar quarter preceding the date they become eligible). The Administrator calculates this limit by (X) subtracting the percentage of Base Salary elected to be deferred from 100 percent, (Y) multiplying the Base Salary rate by the percentage obtained under clause (X), and (Z) limiting the Incentive Pay Deferral Benefits for the second following (or, in the case of mid-year enrollment, the following) Plan Year to the dollar amount obtained under clause (Y). A Participant’s actual Base Salary Deferral Benefits will vary based on actual Base Salary paid, but shall not affect this maximum limit on Incentive Pay in the second following (or in the case of mid-year enrollment, the following) Plan Year. (ii) All Deferral Elections are limited to the amount of any payment otherwise payable in cash, net of applicable withholdings. (iii) The Administrator may, in its discretion, impose further limits on the amount or percentage that can be deferred from Base Salary and/or Incentive Pay for a given Plan Year, with such limits imposed no later than the day before the Deferral Election takes effect. Unless and until the Administrator decides otherwise, the maximum percentage of Incentive Pay that may be elected is 85 percent. The Administrator may specify that Deferral Elections must be made as a percentage of Base Salary and Incentive Pay, as a dollar amount of Base Salary and Incentive Pay, or in some other reasonable fashion. The Administrator may permit the use of multiple methods of calculating Deferral Elections or require use of a single method. The Administrator may permit Employees to specify that a Deferral Election shall apply only to the extent that the Employee is paid amounts in excess of the Section 401(a)(17) Limitation. An eligible Employee for a Plan Year who wants to participate in the Plan with respect to Deferral Benefits for a Plan Year must make an irrevocable Deferral Election for the Plan Year on or before December 15 of the preceding Plan Year, or if December 15 is on a weekend, the following Monday, or as of such other deadline as the Administrator may establish (but in all events prior to the beginning of such Plan Year); provided, however, that an Employee permitted under Section 6.2 to make a mid-year Deferral Election for the Plan Year in which they become eligible may make a Deferral Election by the deadline established under that Section (or by such earlier deadline as may be established by the Administrator). A Deferral Election for a Plan Year shall be made in the manner and by the deadlines prescribed by the Administrator. In his or her Deferral Election for a Plan Year, the Employee shall specify: (i) the items of his or her compensation eligible for deferral under Section 6.4(a) that the Employee wishes to defer for the Plan Year and the amount of each such item to be deferred, provided that the amount of all items to be deferred combined does not exceed the maximum limits set forth in Section 6.4(b).

An Employee must make an irrevocable Deferral Election for a Plan Year on or before December 15 of the preceding Plan Year, or if December 15 falls on a weekend, then the following Monday, or such other deadline as the Administrator may establish, but in all cases prior to the beginning of the Plan Year; however, an Employee permitted under Section 6.2 to make a mid-year Deferral Election for the Plan Year in which they become eligible may do so by the deadline established under that Section (or by an earlier deadline set by the Administrator). A Deferral Election must be made in the manner and by the deadlines prescribed by the Administrator. The Employee must specify, in their election, (i) the items of compensation eligible for deferral under Section 6.4(a) that they wish to defer for the Plan Year and the amount of each such item, provided that the total deferred amount complies with Section 6.4(b) and any administrative limits; and (ii) for Employees in Band 50 or above as of the Band 50 Determination Date in the prior Plan Year (or a non-Participant who first becomes an eligible Band 50 Employee after that date and is permitted by the Administrator to participate in open enrollment for the following Plan Year due to such hire or promotion into Band 50): (A) the time when Deferral Benefits for the Plan Year shall be paid, which must be either (A) at the Participant’s Separation from Service or (B) a specified date at least five years after the last day of the Plan Year; and (B) the form of payment, which must be either (A) a lump sum or (B) five, ten, or 15 substantially equal annual installments. If an Employee’s Deferral Election under Section 6.5(a) and (b) does not specify both a valid time of payment and a valid form of payment, they are deemed to have elected a lump-sum payment on January 1 or July 1 that is at least six months after their Separation from Service (or as soon as administratively feasible, but no later than 90 days). An Employee not in Band 50 or above as of the Band 50 Determination Date for the prior Plan Year may not file a special election regarding time and form of payment for Deferral Benefits; instead, the Supplemental Election made pursuant to Section 5.4 will apply. However, if a new Participant is hired into or promoted to Band 50 (or transfers to eligible status while in Band 50 or above) after that date, the Administrator may permit such Employee to participate in open enrollment for the following Plan Year as a Band 50 or above Employee. For each Plan Year, the Base Salary portion of a Participant’s Deferral Election is withheld from each regularly scheduled Base Salary payroll, and the Incentive Pay portion is withheld at the time Incentive Pay is or would otherwise be paid. The Administrator shall establish and maintain a Deferral Account for each Participant’s Deferral Benefits, crediting deferred amounts at times and in manners determined by the Administrator, and may divide the Deferral Account into subaccounts for tracking earnings and losses as per Article 7. For each Participant, the RP-Related Account established under Section 5.1 shall be increased by the Imputed Earnings Credit not less frequently than annually, under procedures and at times determined by the Administrator and consistently applied for similarly situated Participants, at the same interest rate and computed in a similar manner as Imputed Earnings Credits under the RP. A Participant’s RSP-Related Account shall be credited with earnings under the Hypothetical Investment Method set forth below. For Plan Year 2011 and later, a Participant’s Deferral Benefits for that Plan Year shall be credited with earnings under the Hypothetical Investment Method; for 2010 Incentive Pay paid in 2011 and deferred, it will be considered 2010 Deferral Benefits. For Executive Officers, Deferral Benefits for Plan Years prior to 2011 shall be credited with earnings under the Hypothetical Investment Method effective for all earnings credited in any Plan Year beginning on or after January 1, 2011, and under the Interest Method for earnings credited in 2010 and prior Plan Years; however, earnings credited in 2010 (not paid out by October 27, 2010) will not exceed the AFR if Amex’s ROE is below the ROE Target Range, and for Executive Officers who received payment in the 2010 Plan Year prior to October 27, 2010, earnings on amounts paid prior to that date were calculated under the Interest Method without AFR limitation. For Non-Executive Officers, Deferral Benefits for Plan Years prior to 2011 shall be credited under the Interest Method through December 31, 2011; if a Participant becomes an Executive Officer during 2011, earnings for 2011 credited to Deferral Benefits for prior Plan Years shall not exceed the AFR (except to the extent earnings in excess of the AFR have been paid out prior to becoming an Executive Officer); for 2012 and subsequent years, the Hypothetical Investment Method applies. For Retirees, Deferral Benefits for Plan Years prior to 2011 shall be credited under the Interest Method through December 31, 2012, and under the Hypothetical Investment Method effective January 1, 2013. Credits to a Participant’s RSP-Related and Deferral Account (to the extent subject to the Hypothetical Investment Method) shall be made to subaccounts as directed by the Participant using the subaccounts described in Section 5.3, provided that for Deferral Benefits attributable to Plan Years prior to 2011, the Participant may elect to invest in an investment option that credits earnings at the AFR instead of in the Stock Fund or RSP-based options, and no Participant may transfer amounts to the Stock Fund if such transfer would result in the aggregate Company Stock holdings exceeding ten percent of (i) the total value of their Deferral Account or (ii) the total value of their RSP-Related Account at the time of transfer, nor may a Participant direct more than ten percent of new contributions to the RSP-Related or Deferral Account to the Stock Fund subaccount. If more than one subaccount is available, a Participant must designate, on a form or other medium acceptable to the Administrator, in one-percent increments, the amounts to be credited to each subaccount, and may amend such designation consistent with the frequency of investment changes offered under RSP rules, subject to any additional rules established by the Administrator. If a Participant has directed a transfer to the Stock Fund and such a transfer would result in aggregate Company Stock holdings exceeding ten percent of the total value of the Account or new contributions to the Stock Fund subaccount exceeding ten percent of new contributions to the Account, then such Participant is deemed to have selected the default subaccount designated by the Administrator (which is the subaccount representing the default fund under the RSP, unless the Administrator directs otherwise). If a Participant elects to invest in the Stock Fund subaccount, subject to Section 7.4(d) and Section 7.6, the performance of the book reserve subaccount established under Section 5.3 or 6.6 shall reflect the performance of the Stock Fund, including dividends, gains, losses, or other changes in value. A Participant may transfer credits among the Stock Fund and other investment options in a manner similar to RSP transfer rules, subject to Administrator-established rules, but no transfer to the Stock Fund may violate a limit established by the Plan or Administrator. If a Participant does not elect (or is not permitted) to invest in the Stock Fund, the performance of each book reserve subaccount shall reflect the performance of the investment fund the Participant elects, or, in the case of the AFR option, as indicated by the AFR. Credits to such subaccounts may be transferred to any other subaccount under Plan rules similar to RSP transfer rules, subject to applicable terms and times, and if a Participant fails to designate one or more subaccounts, they are deemed to have selected the default subaccount designated by the Administrator (the default fund under the RSP, unless otherwise directed). The Administrator may, in its sole discretion, provide that one or more investment funds available under the RSP, including any self-directed brokerage account, shall not be available for designation under the Plan. Subaccounts shall be valued using reasonable rules and procedures adopted by the Administrator, with an effort to value them as if amounts were invested at similar times and in manners, subject to administrative convenience and market fluctuation factors used in the RSP. Under the Interest Method, a Participant’s Deferral Account for a Plan Year is credited with interest equivalents each calendar year at the Schedule Rate in effect for that year, subject to any Plan limitations. Earnings in such Deferral Account vest as follows: (i) the principal is 100 percent vested at all times; (ii) until January 1, 2011, earnings credited at the Minimum Schedule Rate are 100 percent vested as they are accrued, and any earnings at the applicable Schedule Rate in excess of the Minimum Schedule Rate vest upon the Participant becoming Retirement Eligible, upon earlier death or Disability, and thereafter as they are accrued; effective December 31, 2010, all earnings under the Interest Method for Deferral Benefits not yet paid out are fully vested. Special restrictions in Section 7.6 apply to Insiders and during all periods they are Insiders, including any period after cessation of Insider status during which they are required to report transactions under Rule 16a-2(b) or its successor. A “Change in Control” occurs if (a) a Person becomes the beneficial owner of 25% or more of either the outstanding common shares of Amex or the combined voting power of its outstanding voting securities, excluding acquisitions directly from Amex, by a Subsidiary, by an employee benefit plan, by an underwriter temporarily holding securities, by a Person reporting on Schedule 13-G who later reports on Schedule 13D, or by a corporation in a reorganization, merger, or consolidation if the conditions in clauses (i), (ii), and (iii) of Section 9.1(c) are satisfied, with an exception that if a Person’s ownership increases due to Amex’s share reduction and then further increases, a Change in Control occurs; (b) the Incumbent Board ceases to constitute at least a majority of the Board, excluding individuals elected or nominated by a majority of the Incumbent Board and excluding those whose appointment results from an actual or threatened election contest or solicitation; (c) a Business Combination occurs unless, following the transaction, (i) the outstanding shares and voting power immediately prior to the transaction continue to represent more than 50% of the outstanding shares and voting power of the resulting entity, (ii) no Person (excluding Amex, its employee benefit plans, subsidiaries, or persons who beneficially owned 25% or more prior to the transaction) owns 25% or more of the resulting entity’s shares or voting power, and (iii) at least a majority of the board of directors of the resulting entity were members of the Incumbent Board at the time of the initial agreement; (d) all or substantially all of Amex’s assets are sold, leased, exchanged, or disposed of unless the transaction results in a corporation where (i) more than 50% of the shares or voting power are beneficially owned by the same individuals and entities as before, in substantially the same proportions, (ii) no Person (excluding Amex, its employee benefit plans, or persons who beneficially owned 25% or more prior to the transaction) owns 25% or more of the shares or voting power, and (iii) at least a majority of the board of directors of the resulting corporation were members of the Incumbent Board at the time of the initial agreement; or (e) shareholders of Amex approve a complete liquidation or dissolution of Amex. Upon a Change in Control, the entire value of each Participant’s Account is maintained in a Rabbi Trust established by Amex, and the Company transfers funds to fund the full value of each Participant’s Account, to the extent permitted by Section 409A. Under Article 10, Claims Procedures: (a) A claimant who believes they are being denied Benefits or has a claim involving the Plan may file a written request with the Administrator, setting forth their claim. A cause of action is considered to have accrued when the claimant knew, or in the exercise of reasonable diligence should have known, that a Plan party had clearly repudiated the claim or legal position at issue, regardless of whether a claim was filed. The Administrator shall be the Plan’s agent for service of process. Section 10.2 Claim Decision: (a) Except as otherwise provided in Section 10.2(b), the Administrator shall reply to any claim within 90 days of receipt, unless it extends the period by an additional 90 days for reasonable cause and notifies the claimant in advance of the reasons and expected decision date. If the claim is denied in whole or in part, the reply shall include a written explanation in understandable language setting forth: (i) the specific reason or reasons for denial; (ii) the specific reference to relevant Plan provisions on which the denial is based; (iii) a description of any additional material or information necessary to perfect the claim and why it is needed; (iv) appropriate information on steps to take if the claimant wishes to submit it for review, including access to and copies of relevant documents; (v) time limits for requesting a review under Section 10.3 and under Section 10.4; and (vi) the claimant’s right to bring an action under Section 502 of ERISA (subject to Section 10.5) if the claim is denied on review. (b) If the claim requires a determination of whether a Participant is disabled to be made by the Administrator (and not by another party), the Administrator will respond within a reasonable period and in any case within 45 days, with up to two 30-day extensions if circumstances beyond the Plan’s control require it, and shall provide advance notice of the reasons for the extension, expected decision date, standards for entitlement, unresolved issues, and additional information needed. If additional information is required to resolve the claim, the claimant shall be afforded at least 45 days to provide it (during which time the notice and decision periods are tolled). (c) In the event of a claim requiring a determination of the Participant’s disabled status, the Administrator’s written notice of denial shall provide, in addition to the items in Section 10.2(a): (i) a discussion of the decision, including an explanation of the basis for disagreeing with or not following the views of health care professionals treating the claimant, vocational professionals who evaluated the claimant, medical or vocational experts whose advice was obtained on behalf of the Plan, and the Social Security Administration’s determination of disability presented by the claimant; (ii) a copy of any internal rule, guideline, protocol, or similar criterion relied upon, or a statement that no such criteria exist; and (iii) if a medical necessity or experimental treatment exclusion or limit was imposed, an explanation of the scientific or clinical judgment (applying Plan terms to the claimant’s medical circumstances) or a statement that such explanation will be provided free of charge upon request. Section 10.3 Request for Review: (a) Except as otherwise provided in Section 10.3(b), within 60 days of receiving the written explanation, the claimant may request in writing that the Administrator review its determination. The claimant or their duly authorized representative may, but need not, review relevant documents and submit issues and comments in writing. Reasonable access to and copies of relevant documents, records, and information will be provided free of charge upon request, subject to attorney-client, attorney work-product, and other applicable privilege rules unless required by ERISA. American Water, a publicly-traded water and wastewater utility company founded in 1886 and originally incorporated in Delaware in 1936, is the largest and most geographically diverse in the United States by operating revenues and population served. The company employs approximately 7,000 professionals and provides drinking water, wastewater, and related services to over 15 million people across 46 states. Its primary business consists of regulated utilities operating in more than 1,700 communities across 16 states, serving 3.5 million active customers, with services subject to regulation by state public utility commissions (PUCs) and other regulatory bodies. The company also operates market-based businesses, which are not individually reportable under U.S. GAAP and are collectively referred to as “Market-Based Businesses.” The Regulated Businesses generated operating revenues of $3,255 million in 2020, $3,094 million in 2019, and $2,984 million in 2018, accounting for 86%, 86%, and 87% of total operating revenues, respectively. The geographic breakdown of operating revenues and customers for 2020 shows that the top seven states by revenue—New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Missouri, Illinois, California, Indiana, and West Virginia—accounted for 87.7% and 85.5% of total Regulated Businesses revenues and customers, respectively. The remaining operations, including utility activities in Georgia, Hawaii, Iowa, Kentucky, Maryland, Michigan, New York, Tennessee, and Virginia, are categorized as “Other.” The company’s customer base includes residential, commercial, fire service, industrial, public authority, and other utility customers, with residential customers making up a substantial portion. Most regulated water customers are metered, allowing for monthly billing based on usage, while wastewater customers are billed either at a flat rate or based on water consumption. The company’s Regulated Businesses served 3,244,000 water and 252,000 wastewater customers as of December 31, 2020, representing approximately 15 million people. Customer growth occurs through acquisitions, population growth in authorized areas, and sales to other utilities. The company plans to invest between $22 billion and $25 billion over the next decade for capital improvements, including pipe replacement and upgrades to aging treatment facilities, with a target pipe renewal cycle reduced from 250 years in 2009 to an expected 110-year cycle by 2025, enabling the replacement of nearly 2,200 miles of mains and collection pipes between 2021 and 2025. Capital investment in treatment plants, storage tanks, and other above-ground facilities is also expected to increase from 2021 to 2025. The company has completed resiliency projects, including a $15 million emergency power system at the Raritan Millstone Water Treatment Plant in New Jersey and $23 million and $27 million improvements in Muncie and Richmond, Indiana, to retire facilities in 100-year floodplains. Operations are regulated by PUCs, which oversee rates, capital expenditures, operating costs, and other financial and operational matters, with regulatory policies varying by state and subject to change. The company uses various regulatory practices to mitigate regulatory lag, including infrastructure replacement surcharges, future test years, hybrid test years, utility plant recovery mechanisms, expense mechanisms, revenue stability mechanisms, consolidated tariffs, and deferred accounting. These practices are used to improve cost recovery and service reliability. The company’s growth strategy includes acquiring water and wastewater systems in geographic proximity to its existing operations to leverage existing management and achieve operational efficiencies, with a focus on expanding wastewater services where water services already exist. The company intends to grow its regulated footprint by acquiring systems in current markets and, where appropriate, entering new domestic markets after evaluating business and regulatory conditions to ensure a viable return on investment and continued service quality. Increasing regulatory pressures, infrastructure needs, financial challenges, and industry legislation may prompt municipalities to sell their water and wastewater assets. In 2017, New Jersey enacted the Water Quality Accountability Act (the “WQAA”), which sets operational standards for all water utilities in the state, including municipal and investor-owned utilities with more than 500 service connections, covering areas such as cybersecurity, asset management, water quality reporting, remediation of violation notices, and hydrant and valve maintenance. The WQAA requires the most senior water manager—either the executive director of a municipal utility authority or the mayor or chief executive officer of a municipally owned public water system—to certify that the system meets the requirements. To strengthen accountability, the New Jersey Senate held three hearings on the WQAA in 2020, and the New Jersey Assembly has heard legislation to strengthen the WQAA in one committee, with referral to the Assembly Appropriations Committee pending. The Company’s regulated subsidiaries in California, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Maryland, Missouri, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Virginia have access to fair market value legislation for private sector investment in public sector water and wastewater systems. The Company supports full optionality for municipalities, including state legislation that enables the consolidation of the fragmented water and wastewater industries through third-party fair market valuations of purchased property. Fair market value assessment is an alternative to the traditional depreciated original cost method, allowing the Company to offer municipalities a purchase price reflective of the assets’ fair market value while providing the Company with increased opportunity to recover the purchase price over the life of the purchased assets, subject to PUC approval. In 2020, Indiana passed legislation creating an appraisal process to establish fair value for non-municipal utilities and establishing a presumption that a purchase price not exceeding the appraised value is reasonable. The legislation also requires that all new municipal water and wastewater systems be subject to the jurisdiction of the utility regulatory commission for ten years. Separate legislation authorizes recovery for above ground infrastructure without a full rate case for service enhancements completed for health, safety, or environmental concerns and removes relocations completed for road construction from distribution system improvement charge recovery caps. Consolidated tariffs use a unified rate structure for systems owned and operated by a single utility, which may or may not be physically interconnected, moderating the impact of periodic fluctuations in local costs and promoting more universal water infrastructure investment across a state. This structure makes it easier to incorporate new systems, supports economies of scale even for small systems, and prioritizes capital needs statewide. The Company believes consolidated tariffs deliver cost-effective, high-quality services to more customers. Twelve of the Company’s regulated jurisdictions currently have some form of consolidated tariff pricing, including California, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Maryland, Missouri, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Virginia, and West Virginia. The level of water treatment varies based on source quality and customer stipulations, with surface water generally requiring significant treatment and groundwater often requiring only chemical treatment. The Company’s ability to meet existing and future water demands depends on an adequate water supply. Drought, governmental restrictions, overuse, protection of threatened species or habitats, contamination, or other factors may limit the availability of ground and surface water. The Company employs various measures to secure adequate water supply in the short and long term. The geographic diversity of its service areas may mitigate some economic effects of weather extremes, as in any given summer, some areas may experience drier than average weather reducing available water, while others may experience wetter than average weather. The Company evaluates water quality, quantity, growth needs, alternate sources, and transmission and distribution capacity to provide service. Water supply is seasonal and weather conditions significantly affect supply. To ensure adequate supply, the Company uses long-term planning and maintains contingency plans to minimize the impact of climate variability and weather fluctuations. For most surface or groundwater sources, the Company uses models to determine safe yields under different rainfall and drought conditions. Surface and groundwater levels are routinely monitored to predict and mitigate supply capacity deficits through demand management and additional supply development. An example of long-term planning is the Monterey Peninsula Water Supply Project (the “Water Supply Project”) in California, which includes construction of a desalination plant owned by the Company’s California subsidiary and wells supplying water to the desalination plant. The project also includes the California subsidiary’s purchase of water from a groundwater replenishment project (the “GWR Project”) between Monterey One Water and the MPWMD. The Water Supply Project is intended, among other things, to fulfill obligations to eliminate unauthorized diversions from the Carmel River as required under orders from the California State Water Resources Control Board (the “SWRCB”). Wastewater services involve collecting wastewater from customers’ premises through sewer lines, transporting it through a sewer network to a treatment facility, treating it to meet regulatory standards before returning it to the environment, and disposing of or recycling the solid waste by-product in accordance with applicable standards and regulations. Customer demand for water service is affected by weather and varies with temperature and rainfall. Demand is generally higher during warmer months due to increased outdoor water use, such as irrigation. As a result, the Company typically expects its operating revenues to peak in the third quarter of each year. Hotter and drier weather generally increases operating revenues, while cooler and wetter weather suppresses demand and can reduce water operating revenues. Three of the Company’s jurisdictions—California, Illinois, and New York—have adopted revenue stability mechanisms that allow the Company to collect state PUC-authorized revenue for a given period not tied to the volume of water sold, thereby reducing the impact of weather variability. The Company’s water and wastewater operations are subject to extensive federal, state, and local regulations related to environmental protection, health and safety, water quality, wastewater treatment, discharge, recycling, and disposal, including the Safe Drinking Water Act, the Reduction of Lead in Drinking Water Act, and the Clean Water Act, with state standards sometimes being more stringent than federal ones. For example, New Jersey established a standard for PFNA in 2018 and set maximum containment levels for PFOA and PFOS, implemented in January 2021. The Company maintains an environmental program focused on compliance and responsible resource use, with capital and operating costs expected to rise as standards become more stringent. The Company estimates $725 million in capital expenditures over the next five years, including $155 million in 2021, for environmental control facilities. The Company believes its operations are materially in compliance and often exceed minimum standards. Operations involve the use, storage, and disposal of hazardous substances such as chlorine, which generates waste requiring proper handling. The Company could incur remedial costs if contamination is discovered, as CERCLA and comparable state laws hold generators, transporters, and current or former owners or operators liable without fault. Facilities are also subject to U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Act requirements and inspections. The Safe Drinking Water Act sets national standards for drinking water quality, including over 90 regulated contaminants and water quality indicators, with a process to evaluate at least five additional compounds every five years. The EPA may require monitoring of unregulated contaminants under the Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule, which the Company participated in during the fourth round concluding in 2020. The EPA has established rules such as the Long-Term 2 Rule, Stage 2 Disinfectants and Disinfection Byproduct Rule, and Ground Water Rule to improve disinfection and reduce exposure to disinfection by-products. In 2016, the revised Total Coliform Rule introduced a “find and fix” process requiring corrective action when bacterial trigger levels are exceeded. The Company is within the EPA’s compliance timeframe for all these standards, including sample collection, data analysis, and treatment enhancements. Recent monitoring under the Long-Term 2 Rule indicates that approximately 30 of the Company’s surface water systems have completed or need to implement additional disinfection mechanisms against Cryptosporidium, primarily through ultraviolet light systems, with an estimated $150 million to $250 million still required for remaining facilities. The EPA is considering regulations for contaminants such as strontium, hexavalent chromium, fluoride, nitrosamines, pharmaceuticals, and volatile organic compounds, but the Company does not expect any such regulations to require implementation in 2021. In 2020, the Company conducted over ten million water quality and turbidity tests at its facilities, including continuous monitoring of turbidity, disinfectant residuals, and chemical treatment adjustments. The Company participates in the Partnership for Safe Water, with 68 of its 79 surface water treatment plants receiving the “Director” award, which recognizes comprehensive self-assessments, action plans, and high-quality water; the Company accounts for about one-third of all such awards nationally. Additionally, 66 plants received the “Five-Year Phase III” award, 61 received the “Ten-Year Phase III” award, 57 received the “Fifteen-Year Phase III” award, and 26 received the “Twenty-Year Phase III” award, recognizing sustained performance. The Lead and Copper Rule (LCR), first published in 1991 and revised in 2000, 2004, and 2007, includes enhanced monitoring, reporting, and public education requirements. In 2011, the Reduction of Lead in Drinking Water Act restricted the use and introduction of lead pipes, plumbing fittings, solder, and flux. Despite these efforts, legacy lead plumbing remains in many communities. The EPA finalized revisions to the LCR on January 15, 2021, designed to better protect public health by reducing lead and copper exposure, with compliance mandated by January 2024. The Company is reviewing the revised rule and will develop an implementation strategy. Capital and operating costs for compliance cannot yet be determined, but such costs are traditionally recoverable through rate-setting. The Company currently estimates less than 5% of service lines in its regulated territories contain lead on either the Company or customer portion. The Company is replacing lead service lines (LSLs) as part of ongoing water main and service line renewal projects. The goal is to replace a significant majority of known LSLs in most service areas by the end of 2030, at a cost estimated between $600 million and $1.2 billion, which the Company believes is attainable where public policy supports it. For future acquisitions, the Company will set LSL removal goals during the acquisition process. Prioritization of LSL replacement depends on planned renewal projects, adjacent projects by municipalities or other utilities, LCR compliance monitoring results, and customer cooperation in replacing the customer-owned portion. In some cases, these factors may result in shorter or longer timeframes. The Company prefers to replace the entire external LSL if lead is found on either the Company or customer portion, as advised by industry organizations including the U.S. National Drinking Water Advisory Council, the Lead Service Line Replacement Collaborative, and the American Water Works Association, and this approach aligns with the Revised LCR. The Lead Service Line Replacement Collaborative is a diverse group of public health, water utility, environmental, and other stakeholders.

The Clean Water Act regulates discharges from drinking water and wastewater treatment facilities into lakes, rivers, streams, and groundwater. The Company’s operations require discharge permits under the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit program established under the Clean Water Act, which must be renewed every five years. EPA and implementing states set maximum discharge limits for wastewater effluents and overflows under NPDES permits; discharges exceeding these limits can result in fines and penalties, and persistent non-compliance may lead to significant fines and compliance costs. The difficulty of obtaining and renewing NPDES permits may impose time and cost burdens on the Company’s operations. Discharge violations occasionally occur at Company facilities, some of which result in fines, but the Company does not expect such violations or fines to have a material impact on its results of operations or financial condition. The Company believes investing in employee health, well-being, and safety is essential to its people and culture goals, enabling employees to generate great ideas, provide quality customer service, and make a difference in customers’ lives. Employee Safety: Safety is a longstanding value and strategy. The Company focuses on both physical and emotional well-being of employees and contractors to ensure they return home in the same or better condition than when they arrived. The Company measures occupational health and safety performance across the organization with the goal of achieving zero injuries or safety incidents. In 2020, employees completed over 100,000 hours of safety training. Through frequent labor-management meetings, the Company encourages open dialogue to enhance job safety. All employees are empowered to support safety by taking time to complete tasks safely and using “Stop Work Authority”—the right to immediately stop work if they believe a task is unsafe—to address hazards with management. This authority is stated on the back of every employee’s identification badge. In 2020, while the number of injuries for the Company’s Days Away Restricted or Transferred (“DART”) rate increased by 5% compared to 2019, the Company achieved its lowest ORIR injury rate in recorded history, with a 16% reduction from 2019. The Company experienced a 2.6% decrease in labor hours in 2020. The 2020 ORIR was 0.99 (63 injuries) and the DART rate was 0.63 (40 injuries), compared to a DART rate of 0.57 in 2019. In 2020, American Water teams led safety indicator activities including pre-job safety briefings and near miss reporting, and achieved internal Certified Safe Worker designations. Near miss reports were part of these activities.

Employees are granted “Stop Work Authority,” the right to immediately halt work if they believe a task is unsafe, and this authority is clearly stated on the back of every employee’s identification badge. During the COVID-19 pandemic, American Water did not lay off any employees and provided temporary medical and emotional health benefits, including paid time off and emergency leave. Additional resources such as enhanced well-being support, workplace flexibility, back-up child/elder care, sitter database discounts, and academic support were offered. As an essential business, the Company focused on the health and safety of employees, contractors, vendors, and others at or visiting worksites, implementing work-from-home guidelines for non-essential employees, safety training, pausing most air, train, or overnight travel, enforcing social distancing, requiring face coverings, and promoting hygiene and hand-washing. Essential employees and locations received appropriate personal protective equipment and cleaning supplies, and additional COVID-19 guidance was provided for employees entering customer homes and businesses. The Company’s utility operations are subject to extensive regulation by state Public Utility Commissions (PUCs) and other regulatory agencies, which significantly affects its business, financial condition, results of operations, and cash flows. These operations provide water and wastewater services through subsidiaries regulated by state PUCs, which authorize rates sufficient to recover prudently incurred operating expenses, including operating and maintenance costs, depreciation, financing costs, and taxes, and provide an opportunity to earn an appropriate rate of return on invested capital. The Company’s ability to implement its business plan depends on rates authorized by state PUCs, which may take time and may not be approved in full or at all. Rate increase applications are subject to lengthy and costly administrative processes, and even if approved, the rates may not cover expenses, recover investments, or provide an appropriate return. PUCs may also impose fines, penalties, or sanctions for non-compliance with regulations, and utilities must obtain numerous permits, approvals, and certificates for operations, acquisitions, dispositions, debt or equity financing, and affiliated transactions. Although the Company believes each utility subsidiary has obtained or sought renewal of necessary permits and approvals, it cannot predict the impact of future regulatory activities. The current COVID-19 pandemic may limit or curtail the ability of PUCs to approve applications, including rate increases or other requests, as PUCs and their staffs seek to reduce, delay, or streamline proceedings. PUCs may also prohibit service termination for non-payment or extend procedural schedules during the pandemic, and the Company cannot predict the range of impacts on its ability to obtain required approvals. Even if rates are approved, the Company may fail to achieve the rate of return on invested capital due to factors such as lower-than-anticipated water usage, increased customer conservation, negative impacts from the pandemic, or higher-than-estimated investments or expenses. The Company’s operations and water quality are subject to extensive and increasingly stringent environmental, water quality, and health and safety laws and regulations, including those related to contaminants of emerging concern. Violations could result in substantial fines, penalties, reputational damage, or, in severe cases, rate reductions or forced asset sales. CERCLA authorizes the EPA to enforce remedial actions and impose joint and several liability on responsible parties without regard to fault. The Company incurs substantial ongoing operating and capital costs to comply with these regulations, which have become more stringent over time. While the Company may seek to recover compliance costs through customer rates, there is no guarantee that state PUCs will approve such rate increases or that such costs will not materially affect financial condition, results of operations, cash flows, and liquidity. The Company may also face liabilities for investigating and cleaning up environmental contamination, including from hazardous chemicals like chlorine or waste disposed of at off-site locations. Discovery of previously unknown conditions or future cleanup obligations could result in significant costs and negatively impact financial performance, especially if such costs are not covered by insurance or if insurance becomes unattainable. Contaminants of emerging concern, such as manufactured nanomaterials, human and veterinary products, perfluorinated compounds, pathogens, and disinfection by-products, are being closely monitored. Government agencies are responsible for setting regulatory standards, and in some states, PUCs may disapprove cost recovery for treatment infrastructure in the absence of a regulatory standard. Given the rapid emergence of these contaminants, the Company may not detect or mitigate all substances in its water systems, which could adversely affect financial condition, operations, and reputation. These contaminants may also lead to future federal or state regulatory initiatives, increasing operational costs. Limitations on water supply availability or restrictions on water use due to government regulation may adversely affect access to water sources, the ability to serve customers, or demand for services. The Company’s ability to meet customer demand depends on adequate water supply, which is typically allocated through legislation, court decisions, or water purchase agreements, as water sources like rivers, lakes, groundwater, and recycled water are held in public trust and not owned by private entities. Changes in allocation rights, passing-flow requirements, or supply issues such as drought, overuse, habitat protection, or contamination may limit water availability. If the Company cannot secure alternative water sources, its business, financial condition, results of operations, and cash flows could be adversely affected. For example, in Monterey County, California, the Company is seeking to augment its water supply to comply with an October 2009 cease and desist order (the “2009 Order”), amended by a July 2016 order (the “2016 Order”), which requires a significant reduction in diversions from the Carmel River, terminating on December 31, 2021 (the “2021 Deadline”). The Company is also required to augment its water supply to comply with the Endangered Species Act. It cannot predict whether the California subsidiary will secure alternative sources of water or meet the 2021 Deadline or other requirements under the 2009 and 2016 Orders. Failure to comply could result in material additional costs or obligations, including fines and penalties, which could adversely affect the Company. Service disruptions from severe weather, climate variability, or natural disasters—such as storms, freezing conditions, hurricanes, earthquakes, droughts, wildfires, floods, pandemics, or solar flares—may disrupt operations or reduce demand, negatively impacting financial performance. Tariffs or cost recovery proceedings may not reimburse the Company for such impacts. Government restrictions on water use, even when supplies are sufficient, may reduce service demand, and seasonal droughts may lead to voluntary or mandatory water use restrictions, rationing, conservation regulations, or leak reduction requirements. While expenses for implementing conservation plans may be recoverable if deemed reasonable and prudent by a PUC, there is no assurance they will be fully recovered. Even after drought restrictions are lifted, reduced water consumption may persist, adversely affecting business and financial performance. Climate variability may increase weather volatility, leading to more frequent and severe droughts, flooding, storms, temperature changes, ocean level rises, water quality degradation, reduced supply, altered usage patterns, service disruptions, higher repair costs, and increased costs to improve facility resiliency. Due to the uncertainty of climate-related weather volatility, the Company cannot predict its potential impact on business, financial condition, results of operations, cash flows, and liquidity. Laws and regulations aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions and requiring additional reporting and monitoring may become more pervasive or stringent, though the exact nature and timing are uncertain. While some or all costs related to climate variability may be recoverable through rates or regulatory mechanisms, there is no assurance that state PUCs will authorize rate increases to cover such expenditures.

Increases in ocean levels, potential degradation of water quality, decreases in available water supply and changes in water usage patterns, increases in service disruptions, higher costs to repair damaged facilities, and increased expenses to mitigate risks from more frequent natural events—such as improving the resiliency and reliability of water and wastewater treatment and conveyance systems—are all potential impacts of climate variability. Due to the uncertainty of weather volatility, the company cannot predict how climate change will affect its business, financial condition, results of operations, cash flows, or liquidity. Laws and regulations aimed at reducing or limiting greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, requiring additional reporting and monitoring, may become more stringent or widespread, though the exact nature and timing of these changes remain uncertain. While some or all of the associated costs could be recovered through rates, infrastructure replacement surcharges, or other regulatory mechanisms, there is no guarantee that state public utility commissions (PUCs) will authorize rate increases to cover these expenses, in full or in part. The current rate-setting process often results in a significant delay, known as “regulatory lag,” between when capital investments are made or operating expenses increase and when those costs are reflected in rates. This lag also occurs between declines in water usage and the ability to adjust the rate per gallon to reflect those changes. The company attempts to reduce regulatory lag through mechanisms such as revenue stability programs in three states that adjust rates periodically to ensure sufficient revenue regardless of sales volume, including recognizing reduced consumption while encouraging efficient water use. Eleven state PUCs allow rate adjustments outside of standard rate cases via surcharges for capital investments like infrastructure replacement, which are periodically adjusted based on project completion or budgeted expenditures and eliminated once included in approved rates. Ten state PUCs permit the use of future test years to reflect current or projected revenues, expenses, and investments more promptly. Other mechanisms allow rate increases for uncontrollable costs such as purchased water, property taxes, power, conservation, chemicals, or other expenditures. Although these mechanisms have reduced regulatory lag in some states, the company continues to seek broader adoption in others, and PUCs may fail to adopt new surcharges or existing mechanisms, or the company may lose eligibility to use them. Even if successful, these efforts may not fully eliminate regulatory lag, which could materially and adversely affect the company’s business, financial condition, results of operations, cash flows, and liquidity. In 2011, the California Public Utilities Commission directed modifications to Cal Am’s tariffs to reflect this moratorium and required Cal Am to seek written guidance from the SWRCB on implementation issues. In 2012, the SWRCB provided an interpretation of how to calculate a baseline for determining increases in water use. In March 2018, the Monterey Peninsula Water Management District (MPWMD) adopted a resolution directing Cal Am to interpret the baseline differently than the SWRCB’s interpretation. In May 2018, Cal Am notified the MPWMD and SWRCB of its intent to seek declaratory relief on the conflicting interpretations. To resolve the issue before judicial action, Cal Am met with both agencies, and the SWRCB agreed to revise its 2012 interpretive letter, subject to a public comment period. Failure to follow either the MPWMD’s resolution or the SWRCB’s interpretation could result in fines or penalties. The 2016 Order allows proponents of alternative water sources to submit revised milestones to the SWRCB if Cal Am acquires more than 1,000 acre-feet per year from a source other than the Water Supply Project. In May 2018, petitioners submitted a request to add parallel milestones for 2019, 2020, and 2021 based on the proposed expansion of the Pure Water Monterey project, a groundwater replenishment project. Petitioners argued that these milestones would still allow cessation of unauthorized Carmel River diversions by 2021. A feasibility report concluded the expanded project could provide an additional 2,250 acre-feet per year. Cal Am believes the petition is premature, the expanded project is not yet reliable or sufficient to meet the 2009 Order, and that parallel milestones would distract from completing the Water Supply Project. In December 2019, the SWRCB dismissed the petition without prejudice. The 2016 Order includes yearly milestones for the construction of the Water Supply Project’s desalination facilities. Missing a milestone could result in reductions of up to 1,000 acre-feet per year in Carmel River diversions. If the failure is beyond Cal Am’s control, the SWRCB may waive the reduction. On October 21, 2020, Cal Am reported it could not meet the 2020 milestones due to delays by the California Coastal Commission in approving intake well permits and a stay issued by the Monterey Superior Court on physical construction of the desalination plant. Despite this, Cal Am believed customer demand could still be met without additional rationing in the 2020–2021 water year. On November 17, 2020, the SWRCB stated that the milestone reductions were intended to ensure a staggered approach to ending unauthorized diversions and that a 1,000 acre-foot reduction was appropriate regardless of fault. Cal Am continues to work with relevant agencies to obtain necessary approvals for the Water Supply Project.
