Under California’s Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (“SGMA”) enacted in 2015, groundwater basins designated by the state as critically overdrafted must be managed by a groundwater sustainability agency (“GSA”) by 2020 in accordance with an approved groundwater sustainability plan (“GSP”) designed to achieve sustainability by 2040. Under the SGMA, GSAs have broad powers to achieve sustainability including, but not limited to, regulating groundwater extraction by imposing fees on groundwater extractions and controlling groundwater extractions by regulating, limiting or suspending extractions from wells. The 400-acre CEMEX site overlies a small portion of the 180/400 Subbasin of the Salinas Valley Groundwater Basin; the 84,000-acre 180/400 Subbasin has been designated by the state as critically overdrafted, mainly due to seawater intrusion into the subbasin. In late 2016, the Salinas Valley Basin Groundwater Sustainability Agency (the “SVBGSA”) was formed as a joint powers authority to become the GSA for the Salinas Valley Groundwater Basin and prepare a GSP. In April 2018, the City filed a notice to become the GSA for the CEMEX site, creating an overlap with the SVBGSA’s filing for the 180/400 Subbasin. The Company’s adjusted regulated operation and maintenance (O&M) efficiency ratio is a non-GAAP measure defined as the adjusted operation and maintenance expenses from the Regulated Businesses divided by the adjusted operating revenues from the Regulated Businesses, where both expenses and revenues are adjusted to exclude purchased water expenses. The operation and maintenance expenses also exclude the allocable portion of non-operation and maintenance support services, such as depreciation and general taxes, which are categorized separately in consolidated financial statements. Additionally, the impact of certain Freedom Industries chemical spill settlement activities recognized in 2018 and 2019 is excluded from operation and maintenance expenses, as these items are not reflective of management’s ability to improve the efficiency of the Regulated Businesses. The Company uses this ratio to evaluate operating performance and believes it is useful to investors because it directly measures improvements in efficiency, though it is derived from consolidated financial information and not presented in GAAP financial statements. This measure is supplemental to, and should not be considered a substitute for, GAAP disclosures. The adjusted O&M efficiency ratio is not a GAAP accounting measure, is not based on a standard or objective industry method, may not be comparable to other companies’ measures, and should not be used in place of GAAP information. Under ASC 606, a performance obligation is a promise to transfer a distinct good or service, or a series of distinct goods and services, to a customer, and revenue is recognized when performance obligations are satisfied and the customer obtains control. The transaction price is allocated to each distinct performance obligation, and revenue is recognized when, or as, the performance obligation is satisfied. The Company’s revenue from regulated businesses primarily comes from water and wastewater services, which constitute a single performance obligation, as the delivery of these services is not separately identifiable, and revenue is recognized over time as services are provided. There are generally no significant financing components or variable consideration, and revenues include billed amounts and unbilled amounts based on estimated usage from the latest meter reading to the end of the accounting period. Revenue is also recognized when it is probable that future recovery of previously incurred costs or future refunds will occur through the ratemaking process. For market-based businesses, the Company provides fixed-fee services such as home warranty and maintenance, with most contracts having a one-year term and each service being a separate performance obligation satisfied over time as benefits are received. Revenues are recognized ratably over time, and customer advances are deferred until performance obligations are satisfied. The Company also has long-term fixed-fee contracts to operate and maintain water and wastewater systems for U.S. government military installations and municipal facilities, with revenue recognized ratably over the contract term as benefits are simultaneously received and consumed. Capital improvements under these contracts, initiated through separate amendments, are treated as separate performance obligations with revenue recognized over time based on performance completed at the end of each reporting period. Losses on contracts are recognized when they first become probable and estimable. Revenues in excess of billings on construction contracts are recorded as unbilled revenues, and billings in excess of revenues are recorded as other current liabilities until recognition criteria are met. Regarding the Alternative Water Supply in Lieu of Carmel River Diversions—Monterey Peninsula Water Supply Project, under a 2009 order (the “2009 Order”) of the State Water Resources Control Board (the “SWRCB”), the Company’s California subsidiary (Cal Am) is required to significantly reduce yearly diversions from the Carmel River according to a set schedule. In 2016, the SWRCB issued a 2016 Order approving a compliance deadline of December 31, 2021 (the “2021 Deadline”). Cal Am is developing the Monterey Peninsula Water Supply Project, which includes construction of a desalination plant owned by Cal Am and wells to supply water to the desalination plant, as well as Cal Am’s purchase of water from a groundwater replenishment project (the “GWR Project”) between Monterey One Water and the Monterey Peninsula Water Management District (the “MPWMD”). The project is intended to fulfill obligations under the 2009 Order and the 2016 Order. Cal Am’s progress on the Water Supply Project is subject to administrative review by the California Public Utilities Commission (the “CPUC”) and other government agencies, obtaining necessary permits, and intervention from other parties. In September 2016, the CPUC unanimously approved a final decision authorizing Cal Am to enter into a water purchase agreement for the GWR Project, construct a pipeline and pump station facilities, and recover up to the incurred $50 million in associated costs plus AFUDC, subject to meeting certain criteria.

Cal Am is developing the Monterey Peninsula Water Supply Project (the “Water Supply Project”), which includes constructing a desalination plant to be owned by Cal Am and wells to supply water to the plant. The project also involves Cal Am purchasing water from the groundwater replenishment project (the “GWR Project”) between Monterey One Water and the Monterey Peninsula Water Management District (the “MPWMD”). The Water Supply Project is intended to fulfill Cal Am’s obligations under the 2009 Order and the 2016 Order. Cal Am’s progress on the project is subject to administrative review by the California Public Utilities Commission (the “CPUC”) and other government agencies, obtaining necessary permits, and potential intervention from other parties. In September 2016, the CPUC unanimously approved a final decision authorizing Cal Am to enter into a water purchase agreement for the GWR Project, construct a pipeline and pump station, and recover up to $50 million in associated costs plus AFUDC, subject to meeting certain criteria. In September 2018, the CPUC unanimously approved another final decision determining that the Water Supply Project meets the CPUC’s requirements for a certificate of public convenience and necessity, that the decision should not be delayed, and that an additional procedural phase was unnecessary to consider alternative projects. The CPUC concluded that the Water Supply Project is the best project to address estimated future water demands in Monterey and adopted Cal Am’s cost estimates for the project, totaling $279 million plus AFUDC at a rate representative of Cal Am’s actual financing costs. The 2018 decision specifies procedures for recovering all prudently incurred costs upon project completion, subject to cost caps, operation and maintenance costs, financing, ratemaking, and contingency frameworks. The reasonableness of the project costs will be reviewed in the first general rate case filed by Cal Am after it becomes operational. As of December 31, 2020, Cal Am had incurred $154 million in aggregate costs related to the Water Supply Project, including $36 million in AFUDC. While Cal Am believes its expenditures to date have been prudent and necessary to comply with the 2009 Order, the 2016 Order, and the CPUC’s 2016 and 2018 final decisions, it cannot currently predict its ability to recover all costs and expenses, and there is no assurance that it will recover all such costs and expenses beyond the $50 million in construction costs previously approved by the CPUC in 2016. In June 2018, Cal Am submitted a coastal development permit application to the City of Marina (the “City”) for project components within the City’s coastal zone. Members of the City’s Planning Commission and City councilpersons have publicly opposed the project. In May 2019, the City issued a notice of final local action denying Cal Am’s coastal development permit application. Cal Am appealed this decision to the California Coastal Commission (the “Coastal Commission”), as permitted under the City’s code and the California Coastal Act, and simultaneously submitted an application to the Coastal Commission for components within its original jurisdiction. In October 2019, Coastal Commission staff issued a report recommending denial of Cal Am’s application, largely based on a memorandum from the general manager of the MPWMD that contradicted findings in the CPUC’s 2018 decision. In November 2019, discussions between Coastal Commission and CPUC staff occurred regarding the staff recommendation, during which the CPUC raised questions about the Coastal Commission’s findings on water supply and demand, groundwater impacts, and the viability of a project the Coastal Commission believes may be an alternative. On August 25, 2020, Coastal Commission staff released a report again recommending denial of Cal Am’s application, concluding that the Water Supply Project would have a negligible impact on groundwater resources but would impact other coastal resources such as environmentally sensitive habitat areas and wetlands, and that a feasible alternative project exists to avoid those impacts. The report also noted disproportionate impacts on communities of concern. On September 16, 2020, Cal Am withdrew its original jurisdiction application to allow additional time to address environmental justice concerns, which did not affect its appeal of the City’s denial, which remains pending before the Coastal Commission. Cal Am refiled the original jurisdiction application on November 6, 2020. On December 3, 2020, the Coastal Commission sent Cal Am a notice of incomplete application, identifying additional information needed to consider the application complete. Cal Am is preparing a response. Cal Am continues to work constructively with all appropriate agencies to provide necessary information for required approvals, but there can be no assurance that the Water Supply Project in its current configuration will be completed on a timely basis, if ever. Due to delays in the approval schedule, Cal Am currently does not believe it will be able to fully comply with the diversion reduction requirements and other remaining requirements under the 2009 Order and the 2016 Order, including the 2021 Deadline. While the Company cannot currently predict the likelihood or result of any adverse outcome, further attempts to comply with the 2009 Order, the 2016 Order, or the 2021 Deadline may result in material additional costs and obligations to Cal Am, including fines and penalties for noncompliance.

Best Buy Co., Inc. was incorporated in Minnesota in 1966 and operates in the United States, Canada, and Mexico, striving to enrich consumers' lives through technology by solving technology problems and addressing key human needs in areas such as entertainment, productivity, communication, food preparation, security, and health and wellness. The company has two reportable segments: Domestic and International. The Domestic segment includes operations across all U.S. states, districts, and territories under brands such as Best Buy, bestbuy.com, Best Buy Direct, Best Buy Express, Best Buy Mobile, Geek Squad, GreatCall, Magnolia, and Pacific Kitchen and Home. The International segment includes operations in Canada and Mexico under the brands Best Buy, Best Buy Express, Best Buy Mobile, Geek Squad, and the domain names bestbuy.ca and bestbuy.com.mx. On March 1, 2018, Best Buy announced its intent to close all 257 of its remaining Best Buy Mobile stand-alone stores in the U.S., which were fully closed during the second quarter of fiscal 2019. On October 1, 2018, the company acquired all outstanding shares of GreatCall, Inc., a leading connected health services provider for aging consumers offering easy-to-use mobile products and connected devices. The Domestic and International segments operate a multi-channel platform enabling customers to engage with the company online, in stores, or in their homes. The Domestic segment centrally manages merchandise development, pricing, procurement, supply chain, online and mobile operations, marketing, and labor deployment, with support functions like human resources and finance managed from corporate headquarters. Field operations support retail, services, and in-home teams from corporate and regional locations, and store procedures for inventory, asset protection, transactions, customer relations, sales, staff training, and merchandise display are largely standardized with flexibility for local market conditions. The International segment operates similarly to the Domestic segment. Revenue is generated through six categories: Computing and Mobile Phones, Consumer Electronics, Appliances, Entertainment, Services, and Other. Key components include computing and peripherals, e-readers, mobile phones (including carrier commissions), networking, tablets, wearables, digital imaging, health and fitness, home theater, portable audio, smart home, major and small appliances, drones, gaming hardware and software, movies, music, toys, virtual reality, consultation, delivery, design, installation, memberships, protection plans, repair, set-up, technical support, and GreatCall offerings, as well as beverages, snacks, sundries, baby products, luggage, and sporting goods in the International segment. Customers purchasing online can choose to pick up items at U.S. Best Buy stores or have them delivered from distribution centers or retail stores, with most merchandise shipped directly from manufacturers to distribution centers, and some shipped directly to stores to meet release dates. The Canada and Mexico distribution models mirror the Domestic model. In fiscal 2019, the company’s 20 largest suppliers accounted for approximately 64% of merchandise purchased, with five suppliers—Apple, Samsung, Hewlett-Packard, Sony, and LG—accounting for about 51% of total purchases. The company does not have long-term written contracts with vendors and instead manages inventory through continuous monitoring of consumer demand, adjustment of inventory receipt levels and pricing, vendor agreements for markdown reimbursements and return privileges, and a global sourcing operation that designs, develops, tests, and contracts the manufacture of exclusive brand products. As of the end of fiscal 2019, Best Buy had 1,187 large-format and 51 small-format stores across its Domestic and International segments, with all U.S. and large-format Canadian stores capable of shipping from store locations and allowing online orders to be picked up in any store. Beginning in 2013, the company opened vendor store-within-a-store concepts to strengthen vendor partnerships and improve the customer experience. For fiscal 2020 and beyond, Best Buy plans to optimize store space, renegotiate leases, and selectively open or close locations. The company owns or has rights to use valuable intellectual property, including trademarks and service marks such as Best Buy, Best Buy Express, Best Buy Mobile, Dynex, Geek Squad, GreatCall, Insignia, Jitterbug, Lively, Magnolia, Modal, My Best Buy, Pacific Sales, Pacific Kitchen and Home, Platinum, Rocketfish, 5Star, and its Yellow Tag logo, and holds domestic and international trademark and service mark registrations as well as patents for many of its inventions. The company’s business is seasonal, with a significant portion of revenue and earnings generated in the fiscal fourth quarter, which includes the major holiday shopping season in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico. Operations are funded through available cash, cash equivalents, short-term investments, operating cash flows, and revolving credit facilities, with working capital needs increasing in the months leading up to the holiday season due to inventory purchases. Competitors include multi-channel retailers, e-commerce businesses, technology service providers, traditional retailers, vendors, and mobile network carriers. Best Buy believes its ability to serve customers online, in stores, and in their homes, and to connect technology solutions with customer needs, provides key competitive advantages. Some competitors have lower operating costs and focus on price, but a June 2018 Supreme Court decision in South Dakota v. Wayfair allowed states to require online-only retailers to collect and remit sales taxes, eroding the price advantage of some competitors. Best Buy monitors competitor pricing and maintains price-matching policies to match prices offered by certain retail stores and online operators, supported by efficient operations and global vendor partnerships. Key competitive advantages include dedicated and knowledgeable employees, integrated online, retail, and in-home assets, a broad and curated product assortment, strong vendor partnerships, service offerings that solve real customer needs, unique store formats for showcasing technology, and a robust supply chain. The company is committed to values-driven leadership and sustainable development, expanding employee benefits to include enhanced mental health coverage, backup childcare, caregiver leave, and paid time off for part-time employees, and reinforcing its commitment to diversity and inclusion by signing the CEO Action for Diversity & Inclusion Pledge and the Parity Pledge.

Best Buy offers competitive pricing to consumers, matching or undercutting prices from certain retail stores and online operators. To maintain this, the company focuses on efficient operations and leverages economies of scale through global vendor partnerships. Key elements of its competitive advantage include dedicated and knowledgeable employees, integrated online, retail, and in-home services, a broad and curated product selection, strong vendor relationships, service offerings that address real customer needs, unique store formats for showcasing technology, and a robust supply chain. The company is committed to values-driven leadership and sustainable development, applying corporate responsibility to all stakeholders, including customers, employees, vendors, shareholders, communities, and the environment. Employee benefits have been expanded to include enhanced mental health coverage, backup childcare, caregiver leave, and paid time off for part-time workers. Best Buy has signed the CEO Action for Diversity & Inclusion Pledge and the Parity Pledge to reinforce its commitment to diversity and inclusion. The company has achieved a significant reduction in carbon emissions, reaching a 60% decrease by 2020 (based on a 2009 baseline) through operational improvements and renewable energy sourcing. It also promotes sustainability by offering ENERGY STAR® certified products to help customers save on utility bills and collected over 180 million pounds of consumer electronics and appliances for recycling in fiscal 2019. At the end of fiscal 2019, Best Buy employed nearly 125,000 full-time, part-time, and seasonal employees across the U.S., Canada, and Mexico, offering a range of company-paid benefits that are competitive locally and in aggregate within the industry. Key risks include strong competition from multi-channel retailers, e-commerce businesses, technology service providers, traditional retailers, vendors, and mobile network carriers, which directly affect revenue and profitability due to price transparency and real-time price comparisons. The retail sector is shifting toward online and mobile-driven sales, with customers demanding faster, guaranteed delivery times and low or free shipping, putting pressure on Best Buy’s delivery capabilities and potentially impacting margins. The company’s strategy to expand into new products, services, and technologies introduces financial, regulatory, and operational risks, including limited experience in new markets, potential service disruptions, and exposure to privacy and information security regulations such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). Acquiring GreatCall in fiscal 2019, which provides emergency concierge and monitoring services, exposes the company to liability risks related to service failures, data security, and system interruptions. Offering a wide range of services—such as installation, repair, technical support, and health and safety monitoring—increases risks including higher labor costs, service errors, warranty failures, expanded liability due to employee access to customer devices, third-party involvement in installations, and non-compliance with laws and regulations. Best Buy sources products from a wide range of domestic and international vendors; in fiscal 2019, its 20 largest suppliers accounted for approximately 64% of merchandise purchased (70% in fiscal 2018), with five suppliers—Apple, Samsung, Hewlett-Packard, Sony, and LG—accounting for about 51% of total purchases (56% in fiscal 2018). The company generally does not have long-term contracts with vendors and depends on securing favorable terms for pricing, promotions, payment terms, product allocations, promotional experiences, and returns. Vendors may leverage their financial strength, brand power, or retail presence to disadvantage Best Buy, especially when purchases represent a small portion of their revenue or when competition is low. The company also relies on a small number of mobile carriers to offer mobile devices with carrier connections; changes in carrier contracts, upgrade terms, fees, or service levels could reduce new customer contracts and impact revenue. Employee retention and recruitment are critical, as turnover in retail, service, and field positions can impair operations and growth. Market increases in compensation, especially for field employees, could negatively affect profitability. Other risks include evolving financial, labor, healthcare, and corporate governance regulations, restrictive trade policies, higher tariffs, tax law changes, and litigation trends involving consumers, shareholders, and labor. Regulatory scrutiny in the retail sector increases compliance costs and risks of fines. Defending against lawsuits is costly and diverts management attention. Macroeconomic factors such as GDP growth, consumer confidence, inflation, interest rates, employment, oil prices, and foreign exchange rates influence consumer spending, brand choices, device upgrades, and demand for services. Failure to manage costs effectively—despite fixed or long-term cost elements—could harm profitability and limit funding for growth initiatives. The company relies heavily on its information technology systems for core operations, including demand forecasting, purchasing, supply chain, point-of-sale, service fulfillment, staffing, financial management, and data security. These systems are vulnerable to outages, cyberattacks, viruses, denial-of-service attacks, natural disasters, and human error, and any failure could disrupt operations, increase costs, and result in lost revenue. Our business is heavily reliant on information technology systems to manage key operations, including demand forecasting, purchasing, supply chain management, point-of-sale processing, services fulfillment, staff planning, financial management, reporting, forecasting, and the safeguarding of sensitive data. These systems, along with those of our technology vendors and partners, are vulnerable to failures from power outages, computer or telecommunications failures, viruses, worms, malicious software, denial-of-service attacks, security breaches, catastrophic events like fires, tornadoes, earthquakes, or hurricanes, and employee errors. Any failure or interruption could significantly disrupt operations, increase costs, reduce revenues, and threaten our ability to remain in business. We also operate complex platforms for our websites and mobile applications; if we fail to secure them or maintain and upgrade our hardware, software, network, and infrastructure, disruptions may occur due to unforeseen traffic, malicious attacks, technical issues, or events beyond our control—such as natural disasters or data loss—leading to missed customer orders, lost revenue, and reputational harm. Breaches of customer, employee, vendor, or company data—whether from cyber-attacks, control lapses, or employee misconduct—could result in substantial costs, litigation, and reputational damage. We collect and store sensitive customer data, including payment card information, and share confidential data with third parties; vulnerabilities in products we sell or service, such as on customer-owned devices, may lead to data compromises. Increasing costs for information security, compliance, fraud, and insurance, along with new regulations like the General Data Protection Regulation and CCPA, require additional resources and increase breach risks. Any data compromise could raise protection costs and legal exposure. We may enter into new ventures, partnerships, or acquisitions, which carry significant risks, including failure to integrate operations, retain key personnel, forecast performance, generate synergies, or maintain financial controls, and could impair liquidity, profitability, or divert management attention. The industry is rapidly evolving due to technological innovation, product life cycle changes, and shifting consumer preferences, and failure to adapt could result in offering outdated products, excess inventory, supply shortages, delayed responses to trends, or brand damage. Our promotional financing and credit card programs—used by approximately 25% of fiscal 2019 revenue—generate profit-sharing income and are subject to transaction volume, financing terms, bad debt rates, interest rates, regulatory changes, and competition; adverse changes could reduce customer access to financing and lower our earnings. Our supply chain, critical due to trends like ship-from-store and fast delivery, depends on vendors delivering products on time and in the right quantities, and risks include delivery interruptions, third-party failures, system disruptions, capacity limits, transportation sector consolidation, labor strikes, product damage, and rising transportation costs. Inefficient supply chain operations or disruptions could harm revenue and profitability, especially in small parcel deliveries where few carriers meet our needs. Catastrophic events such as natural disasters, diseases, fires, or terrorism could disrupt operations, damage property, disable supply chains, and affect IT systems, leading to lost revenue and profitability. Declines in brand perception—due to poor service, pricing, delivery failures, or negative public comments—can reduce revenues, customer loyalty, gift card sales, employee retention, and vendor relationships. Product safety and quality failures may lead to legal risks, regulatory enforcement, and product recalls, especially if replacement products are unavailable, negatively impacting revenue and profitability. Changes in labor laws—such as unionization, independent contractor regulations, or minimum wage and leave requirements—could increase payroll costs and affect service delivery; even though as of February 2, 2019, no U.S. operations had unionized employees, future organizing could increase costs and impact operations. Poor management of our real estate portfolio—such as failing to secure suitable store locations or misjudging store layouts, demand, or lease terms—could impair competitiveness and profitability, with consequences like store closures, costly remodels, or excessive lease expenses. Exiting leased properties may incur significant costs due to lease terms, market conditions, or lack of sub-lease tenants, and we remain liable for taxes, insurance, and common area maintenance on vacant properties. Sub-lease defaults also expose us to liability. Constraints in capital markets or tighter vendor credit terms could reduce our liquidity, forcing operational curtailments or limiting business opportunities. Our primary liquidity sources are operating cash flow, cash reserves, investments, credit facilities, debt arrangements, and trade payables; reduced vendor payment terms or tighter credit limits could strain liquidity. If we fail to secure sufficient financing, our borrowing costs and access to capital could increase, and our ability to meet obligations may be threatened. Downgrades in our credit ratings could reduce market access, raise borrowing costs, and negatively affect vendor and lease terms, as ratings are subject to change due to external factors like new methodologies. We rely on third-party vendors for IT, web hosting, HR, customer loyalty, financing, gift cards, warranty, delivery, support, transportation, and insurance; any material disruption in these relationships or services could impact revenues, costs, and operations, especially during peak periods. Our exclusive brand products—such as Dynex, Insignia, Modal, Platinum, and Rocketfish—are manufactured in southeast Asia, exposing us to risks including greater warranty liability, limited recourse to manufacturers in foreign jurisdictions, and potential regulatory or product liability claims, including recalls, which could materially affect our operating results.

Sales of the company’s exclusive brand products—Dynex, Insignia, Modal, Platinum, and Rocketfish—represent a significant part of its revenue and profitability. These products are primarily manufactured by contract manufacturers located in southeast Asia, which introduces several risks that could materially affect operating results. These risks include greater consumer responsibility for warranty claims due to product defects, limited recourse to manufacturers in foreign jurisdictions, potential regulatory compliance and product liability claims—some of which may require recalls—disruptions in manufacturing or logistics from inconsistent order patterns, inability to form long-term relationships with manufacturers, or unforeseen natural disasters, difficulty in finding manufacturers that meet internal quality and safety standards, increased risk of inventory obsolescence due to the absence of return-to-vendor rights, exposure to changing labor and environmental laws in foreign countries, potential intellectual property infringement claims or failure to pay royalties, disruptions from trade disputes or excessive tariffs that may prevent timely sourcing of alternatives, inability to secure or protect patents and intellectual property rights, and increased costs and reputational harm from regulations requiring disclosure of the origin of “conflict minerals” in the supply chain. Maintaining consistent quality, availability, and competitive pricing of these products is essential for customer loyalty, revenue generation, and profitability; failure to do so could significantly reduce demand and profits. The company is also exposed to risks related to vendors sourcing products outside the U.S., including political or economic instability, trade restrictions, tariffs, quality or safety issues, work stoppages, port delays, foreign currency fluctuations, transportation constraints, inflation, civil unrest, natural disasters, pandemics, and vendor underinvestment in facilities or changes in pricing or promotional policies. These factors could have a material adverse impact on financial results. The company manages economic and transaction exposure using foreign currency derivative instruments and interest rate swaps, with the objective of reducing volatility in net earnings, cash flows, and net asset value related to foreign exchange rates and interest rates, without holding derivatives for trading or speculative purposes. All derivative instruments are recorded at fair value on the Consolidated Balance Sheets, and hedge effectiveness is evaluated prospectively or retrospectively when hedge accounting is applied. Hedging relationships are formally documented at inception, including risk management objectives and strategies. Derivatives not designated as hedges are also used. For net investment hedges, foreign exchange forward contracts are used to hedge Canadian dollar exchange rate fluctuations on a portion of the net investment in Canadian operations, with terms up to 12 months. Changes in the fair value of these derivatives are recognized in other comprehensive income (OCI) to offset changes in the translated value of the net investment, with gains and losses excluded from net earnings only under specific circumstances such as complete or substantially complete liquidation. Interest rate swaps, specifically "receive fixed-rate, pay variable-rate" swaps, were used to mitigate interest rate fluctuations on the 2018 Notes prior to maturity and are currently outstanding on the 2021 and 2028 Notes. These swaps are considered perfect hedges because the critical terms and notional amounts match those of the fixed-rate debt being hedged and are accounted for as fair value hedges using the shortcut method, where changes in the derivative’s fair value are offset by adjustments to the carrying value of the debt, resulting in no impact on net earnings. Derivatives not designated as hedges are used to manage foreign currency fluctuations relative to recognized receivables and payables in non-functional currencies, with terms up to 12 months, and gains and losses are recorded directly in net earnings. Best Buy Co., Inc. was incorporated in Minnesota in 1966 and operates in the United States and Canada, driven by its purpose to enrich lives through technology and its vision to personalize and humanize technology solutions for every stage of life. The company operates through two reportable segments: Domestic and International. The Domestic segment includes all U.S. states, districts, and territories, as well as Best Buy Health, and encompasses brand names such as Best Buy, Best Buy Ads, Best Buy Business, Best Buy Health, CST, Current Health, Geek Squad, Lively, Magnolia, Pacific Kitchen and Home, TechLiquidators, and Yardbird, along with domain names bestbuy.com, currenthealth.com, lively.com, techliquidators.com, and yardbird.com. All of Best Buy’s former stores in Mexico were closed by the end of the first quarter of fiscal 2022, and the International segment consists of all operations in Canada under the brands Best Buy, Best Buy Mobile, and Geek Squad, and the domain bestbuy.ca. In fiscal 2022, the company acquired all outstanding shares of Current Health Ltd. and Two Peaks, LLC d/b/a Yardbird Furniture. Both segments operate an omnichannel platform enabling customers to shop online, visit stores, or have services delivered to their homes. Key business functions such as merchandise development, pricing, procurement, supply chain, marketing, and labor deployment are centrally managed, while support functions like human resources, finance, IT, and real estate are based at corporate headquarters. Field operations support retail, services, and in-home teams from corporate and regional locations. Store operations follow standardized procedures with flexibility for local market adjustments. The Best Buy Health business has a dedicated leadership and operations team that manages daily operations with support from enterprise capabilities. Revenue is generated through six categories: Computing and Mobile Phones, Consumer Electronics, Appliances, Entertainment, Services, and Other. Online customers can choose to pick up products at a Best Buy store, at an alternative location, or have them delivered directly to their homes, with a ship-from-store capability improving availability and delivery times. Most merchandise is shipped directly from manufacturers to distribution centers. In fiscal 2023, the company’s 20 largest suppliers accounted for approximately 79% of merchandise purchased, with Apple, Samsung, HP, LG, and Sony representing about 57% of total purchases. The company does not have long-term written contracts with vendors and manages inventory through continuous monitoring of demand, adjusting receipt levels and pricing, and agreements on markdown reimbursements and return privileges. A global sourcing operation designs, develops, tests, and contracts the manufacture of exclusive brand products. As of the end of fiscal 2023, Best Buy operated 1,138 stores across its Domestic and International segments, which are central to its omnichannel strategy and competitive advantage. The company also offers vendor store-within-a-store concepts to strengthen vendor partnerships and enhance the customer experience, and continuously evaluates store space, leases, and locations. Best Buy owns or has rights to use valuable intellectual property, including trademarks and service marks such as Best Buy, Geek Squad, Lively, Magnolia, Pacific Kitchen and Home, and others, and holds patents for many of its inventions. The company is committed to environmental sustainability, aiming to advance the circular economy, reduce waste, promote sustainable products, and transition to renewable energy, having invested in five solar fields by the end of fiscal 2023 to support its carbon reduction goals. The business is seasonal, with a significant portion of revenue and earnings generated in the fiscal fourth quarter, which includes the holiday shopping season. Operations are funded through available cash, cash equivalents, operating cash flows, and revolving credit facilities used for working capital, general corporate purposes, investments, and growth. Working capital needs increase before the holiday season due to inventory purchases. Competitors include multi-channel retailers, e-commerce businesses, technology service providers, traditional retailers, vendors, and mobile network carriers. Best Buy’s competitive advantages include its ability to serve customers online, in stores, and at home, integrated technology solutions, broad product assortment, strong vendor partnerships, service offerings tailored to customer needs, unique store formats, and efficient supply chain operations. The company monitors competitor pricing and offers price-matching policies to maintain competitiveness. The Nominating, Corporate Governance and Public Policy Committee of the Board of Directors oversees the effectiveness and risks of the company’s environmental, social, and governance strategy, including environmental goals, social responsibility programs, and public policy initiatives. As of March 15, 2023, the company had 218,045,737 shares of common stock, $0.10 par value per share, issued and outstanding. The aggregate market value of the voting and non-voting common equity held by non-affiliates as of July 29, 2022, was approximately $13.4 billion, based on a share price of $76.99, as reported on the New York Stock Exchange-Composite Index. All of the company’s directors and executive officers are considered affiliates for this calculation. The report is filed pursuant to Section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 for the fiscal year ended January 28, 2023, and includes portions of the Definitive Proxy Statement for the 2023 Regular Meeting of Shareholders, which will be filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission within 120 days after the fiscal year-end. The document includes forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties, with a description of key factors outlined in Item 1A, Risk Factors.

Our competitive advantage is built on a broad and curated product assortment, strong vendor partnerships, service and support offerings that address real customer needs, our unique ability to showcase technology in distinct store formats, and a robust supply chain. We are committed to enriching lives through technology while positively impacting the environment, communities, and stakeholders, including customers, employees, vendors, and shareholders. The Nominating, Corporate Governance and Public Policy Committee of the Board oversees our environmental, social, and governance strategy, including environmental goals, social responsibility programs, and public policy initiatives. We aim to advance the circular economy by conserving natural resources, reducing waste, offering sustainable products, and transitioning to renewable energy. As of the end of fiscal 2023, we have invested in five solar fields to support our carbon reduction goals. We target a 75% reduction in carbon emissions by 2030 (over a 2009 baseline) and carbon neutrality by 2040, achieved through energy efficiency, renewable energy deployment, fleet electrification, and emission neutralization. We also aim to reduce water consumption by 15% by 2025 (over a 2019 baseline) and achieve zero-waste certification at additional distribution centers. We expect our ENERGY STAR® products to help customers reduce carbon emissions by 20% by 2030 (over a 2017 baseline), saving them at least $5 billion in utility costs. We support the circular economy through repair and trade-in services and an electronics and appliance recycling program, having collected more than 2.7 billion pounds of such materials since 2009, including over 183 million pounds in fiscal 2023. In social matters, we uphold human rights and responsible sourcing through alignment with the United Nations Guiding Principles and our Responsible Sourcing Program, participating in the Responsible Business Alliance with brands like Apple, Intel, Microsoft, and Samsung, and adhering to a shared Supplier Code of Conduct and audit methodology. The Best Buy Foundation supports 52 Best Buy Teen Tech Center® locations and aims to reach 100 by 2025, offering teens access to cutting-edge technology, post-secondary guidance, mentors, social and emotional support, and paid internships. At the end of fiscal 2023, we employed more than 90,000 employees in the U.S. and Canada, with approximately 58% full-time, 32% part-time, and 10% seasonal/occasional. We set diversity goals for fiscal 2025 and achieved 37% of new salaried corporate positions and 25% of new salaried field positions with Black, Indigenous and People of Color (BIPOC) employees, meeting our one-in-three target. We are committed to spending at least $1.2 billion with BIPOC and diverse businesses by 2025 and investing up to $10 million with Brown Venture Group, a firm focused on Black, Latino, and Indigenous technology startups. We also plan to spend $44 million by 2025 to expand college preparation and career opportunities for BIPOC students, including scholarships for Historically Black Colleges and Universities and increased funding for Best Buy Teen Tech Center youth. The Compensation and Human Resources Committee oversees human capital policies, while the Nominating, Corporate Governance and Public Policy Committee includes diversity considerations in Board candidate selection. In fiscal 2023, each U.S. employee spent an average of at least 44 hours on training and development, with enhancements including expanded leadership development, an AI-driven workforce planning program, LinkedIn Learning for full-time employees, and a new onboarding training program. Employee benefits include caregiver support for disabilities and neurodivergence via Joshin, caregiver support through Wellthy for emergency housing, healthcare, substance abuse, and eldercare, pay continuation and caregiver pay, 10 weeks of maternity leave at 100% pay, Included Health for LGBTQ+ needs, access to virtual physical and mental health visits, emergency assistance through the HOPE Fund (up to $2,500), mental health awareness and training, and tuition assistance with expanded partnerships for degree attainment at no out-of-pocket cost. The Compensation and Human Resources Committee reviews employee wellness, engagement, benefit compliance, leadership succession, wage, retention, and hiring programs. Key external risks include macroeconomic pressures such as geopolitical climate, inflation, consumer confidence, and oil prices, which can affect consumer spending, brand choices, device upgrades, and service demand. Geopolitical issues, such as the conflict in Ukraine, may impact fuel prices, inflation, global supply chains, and raw material costs, particularly for nickel, aluminum, and copper, due to Russia’s role as a major producer. Disruptions in supply chains or manufacturing in regions like Taiwan or China, due to tensions between Taiwan and China or other trade or political factors, could affect semiconductor and television panel production. Catastrophic events, including pandemics like COVID-19, natural disasters, extreme weather, or terrorism, can disrupt operations, supply chains, distribution networks, and IT systems, with effects amplified when occurring simultaneously. The COVID-19 pandemic has specifically impacted customer store visits, supply chain disruptions, fluctuating consumer spending, operational changes like contactless pick-up, safety standards, channel shifts to online shopping, and our ability to finance operations. The emergence of new, more transmissible SARS-COV-2 variants could worsen these risks. Three of our largest sales states—California, Texas, and Florida—are prone to natural disasters and extreme weather conditions.

The COVID-19 pandemic has introduced and may continue to introduce significant risks to the business, operations, and financial condition, including (i) reduced customer visits and spending at stores, (ii) supply chain disruptions, (iii) fluctuating consumer spending influenced by government stimulus, (iv) operational changes such as the rollout of contactless and curbside pick-up, (v) safety standards imposed by state and federal agencies, (vi) shifts in customer channels—such as increased online shopping—potentially affecting profitability, and (vii) challenges in financing operations. The emergence of new, more transmissible, virulent, or immune-evading SARS-COV-2 variants could worsen these risks. Three of the largest states by total sales—California, Texas, and Florida—have experienced and may continue to experience natural disasters and extreme weather, which could cause physical damage or closures of stores, distribution centers, or other facilities. External social activism, tension, and violence related to social justice and inequality, and the company’s response to such events, may negatively affect employees, customers, properties, and communities, potentially damaging the brand and reputation if the response is perceived as inappropriate or inadequate. Such events could lead to operational interruptions, property or inventory losses, and adverse effects on revenue and profitability. Many products sold are vulnerable to technological advancements, product life cycle changes, and shifting consumer preferences. The industry is highly dynamic, driven by rapid innovation, including new product categories, rapid category maturation, cannibalization, changing price points, and frequent product replacement or upgrades. This pace of change is difficult to predict and manage; failure to respond effectively could result in offering unwanted products, excess inventory requiring discounting, inability to secure products due to high demand, delays in adapting merchandising, marketing, or supply chain capabilities, and brand damage. The company faces strong competition from multi-channel retailers, e-commerce businesses, technology service providers, traditional retailers, vendors, and mobile network carriers, with price transparency and real-time price comparison increasing competitive pressure. Online and mobile-driven sales, including in-store or curbside pickup, are growing, and customers increasingly demand faster, guaranteed delivery and low or free shipping. The company’s higher cost structure due to its focus on superior customer service and a full range of services may pressure margins, especially as delivery costs and times become more competitive. Failure to attract, retain, and engage qualified employees—particularly in key roles—could harm operations and profitability. High turnover in the retail sector, especially during the pandemic, and market pressures to increase wages and benefits could negatively impact profitability. The company’s strategy to expand into health, new products, services, and technologies introduces business, financial, and regulatory risks, including limited experience in new markets, regulatory challenges, and potential claims from service disruptions or failures. These initiatives increase complexity in management, operations, systems, and financial controls, and pilot programs may not scale as expected, limiting growth. Healthcare-related products and services require regulatory approvals, with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (“FDA”) regulating product safety, quality, and supplier materials; non-compliance could lead to recalls, production stoppages, fines, or legal claims. The digitalization of Best Buy Health, including handling personal and medical data, increases compliance risks under laws such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) and the UK’s General Data Protection Regulation (“GDPR”), exposing the company to data privacy, security, and business interruption risks. Offering a full range of services—such as consultation, delivery, installation, memberships, repair, technical support, and caregiving—introduces risks including declining service attachment due to online purchasing trends, rising labor costs, margin pressure from the Best Buy Totaltech membership (which includes incremental benefits and costs), pressure on traditional labor models, use of third parties that fail to meet labor or independent contractor standards, errors in service fulfillment, unpredictable warranty failures, increased liability from employees using company vehicles or being present in customer homes, expanded liability in managed services, access to customer devices and data, third-party involvement in construction, weather and safety-related disruptions, and non-compliance with new laws. The company relies on a wide range of domestic and international vendors, with the 20 largest suppliers accounting for approximately 79% of merchandise purchased in fiscal 2023, and five suppliers—Apple, Samsung, HP, LG, and Sony—accounting for about 57% of total purchases. Most vendor relationships lack long-term contracts, and the company depends on favorable terms for pricing, promotional funding, payment terms, product allocations, store experiences, and returns. Vendors may leverage their financial strength, brand power, or retail presence to our disadvantage, especially when purchases represent a small portion of their revenue or when competition is low. Mobile carriers, which are limited in number, also impact the business; changes in their contract structures, fee plans, or service levels could reduce new device sales and harm revenue. Declines in demand could occur if brand perception or recognition is damaged through poor service, uncompetitive pricing, missed delivery promises, or negative public remarks, with social media amplifying customer feedback and reputational harm. Third-party fraud using the brand could also harm perception. Strategic ventures, alliances, or acquisitions carry risks such as unanticipated business risks, failure to retain key employees, financial forecasting uncertainty, integration challenges, control deficiencies, failure to achieve cost synergies, environmental changes, disputes with partners, and adverse impacts on vendor or partner relationships; failure could impair liquidity, profitability, and require goodwill or asset impairments, while diverting resources and management focus. Poor management of the real estate portfolio—such as failing to secure suitable store locations or adjusting to changing consumer behavior—could impair competitiveness and profitability. Most properties are under multi-year leases, and key evaluation factors include customer behavior, store format, product mix, local competition, demographics, lease terms, and occupancy costs. Failure to properly assess these factors or negotiate terms could result in store closures with ongoing lease obligations, significant remodeling costs, operating locations that no longer meet business needs, or excessive lease expenses. Exiting leased locations involves variable financial impacts based on lease terms, market conditions, property demand, landlord relationships, and sub-lease availability, with ongoing responsibilities for taxes, insurance, and common area maintenance on vacant properties. When sub-leasing, the company remains liable as the master lessee in case of sub-tenant default. Operational risks include interruptions to store and supply chain operations, such as delivery failures, third-party underperformance, system disruptions, capacity limits, global supply chain issues, inventory loss from theft or damage, employee or customer safety risks from burglary or robbery, transportation or distribution sector consolidation or failures, labor strikes or shortages, pandemics (including COVID-19), and rising transportation costs.

Vendor allowances are received from certain merchandise vendors through various programs to offset inventory invoice costs and promote sales. Allowances based on purchases are initially deferred and recorded as a reduction of merchandise inventory, then recognized as a reduction to cost of sales when the associated inventory is sold. Allowances based on sales volumes are calculated using an agreed-upon amount per unit sold and are recognized as a reduction to cost of sales when the inventory is sold. Other promotional allowances, such as advertising and placement, not tied to purchase or sales volume, are recognized as a reduction to cost of sales ratably over the corresponding performance period. Funds that represent a reimbursement of specific, incremental, and identifiable costs incurred to sell a vendor’s products are recorded as an offset to the related expense when incurred.

Regarding Vendor Allowances, the Company receives allowances from certain merchandise vendors to offset inventory invoice costs and promote sales. Allowances based on purchases are initially deferred and recorded as a reduction of merchandise inventory, then recognized as a reduction to cost of sales when inventory is sold. Allowances based on sales volume are calculated per unit sold and also recognized as a reduction to cost of sales upon sale. Reimbursements of specific, incremental, and identifiable costs incurred to sell vendor products are recorded as an offset to the related expense when incurred. Due to the significance of vendor allowances to the financial statements and the volume and diversity of vendor agreements, auditing these allowances was complex and subjective, requiring substantial effort to verify that allowances were recorded in accordance with vendor terms and that deferred allowances were complete and accurate. Audit procedures included testing controls over the recording of vendor allowances, selecting a sample of allowances recorded as a reduction to cost of sales, recalculating amounts using vendor agreement terms, confirming agreements directly with vendors when possible, and evaluating whether amounts should be deferred as a reduction to inventory. When vendor confirmations were not received, alternative procedures such as reviewing contractual agreements, testing settlement of arrangements, and discussing terms with Company buyers were performed. The amount of deferred vendor allowances was tested by developing an expectation and comparing it to management’s recorded amounts. The Company uses a discounted cash flow model to estimate fair value, requiring management to make subjective estimates and assumptions about revenue growth rates and the weighted average cost of capital rate. Changes in these assumptions could significantly impact fair value or the potential goodwill impairment charge. As of the measurement date, the fair value of the Best Buy Health reporting unit exceeded its carrying value, so no impairment was recognized. Due to the significant judgments made by management in estimating fair value, audit procedures to assess the reasonableness of revenue growth rate and weighted average cost of capital rate assumptions required high auditor judgment and extensive effort, including involvement of fair value specialists. Audit procedures included testing controls over management’s goodwill impairment evaluation, comparing actual results to historical forecasts, evaluating revenue forecasts for new products and services against historical growth rates, internal communications, customer contracts, and business strategy documents, inquiring of operating and sales management about consistency with long-range plans, and with the assistance of fair value specialists, testing the source of the weighted average cost of capital rate, verifying mathematical accuracy, comparing the rate to market data, and developing independent estimates to assess reasonableness. We use foreign exchange forward contracts to hedge against fluctuations in the Canadian dollar exchange rate affecting a portion of our net investment in Canadian operations, with contract terms up to 12 months. For net investment hedges, changes in the fair value of the derivatives are recognized as a component of foreign currency translation within other comprehensive income to offset changes in the translated value of the net investment being hedged, until the investment is sold or liquidated. We limit the recognition of amounts previously recorded in other comprehensive income in net earnings only in circumstances such as complete or substantially complete liquidation of the net investment. Gains and losses related to the amount excluded from the assessment of hedge effectiveness are reported in net earnings. We utilize “receive fixed-rate, pay variable-rate” interest rate swaps to mitigate interest rate fluctuations on our $500 million principal amount of notes due October 1, 2028 (“2028 Notes”). These interest rate swap contracts are considered perfect hedges because the critical terms and notional amounts match those of the fixed-rate debt being hedged, and are accounted for as fair value hedges using the shortcut method. Under this method, changes in the fair value of the derivatives are offset by an equal change in the carrying value of the debt, resulting in no impact on the Consolidated Statements of Earnings from the fair value of the derivatives. Foreign currency forward contracts are also used to manage the impact of foreign currency exchange rate fluctuations on recognized receivable and payable balances denominated in non-functional currencies, with terms generally up to 12 months; these contracts are not designated as hedging instruments and gains and losses are recorded directly to the Consolidated Statements of Earnings. Fair value is defined as the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants in the principal or most advantageous market on the measurement date. Fair value is measured using a three-tier valuation hierarchy: Level 1 includes unadjusted quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities at the measurement date; Level 2 includes significant other observable inputs, such as quoted prices for similar or similar assets in active or non-active markets, or inputs derived from or corroborated by observable market data; Level 3 includes significant unobservable inputs that cannot be corroborated by observable market data and reflect significant management judgment. When inputs from different levels are used, the fair value measurement is based on the lowest level input that is significant to the overall fair value measurement. Fair value remeasurements are based on significant unobservable inputs (Level 3). Fixed asset fair values are primarily derived using a discounted cash flow (“DCF”) model to estimate the present value of expected net cash flows, with key inputs including forecasts of net cash generated from investment operations and an appropriate discount rate. Assets and liabilities measured at fair value on a nonrecurring basis, such as tangible fixed assets, goodwill, and other intangible assets, are remeasured when fair value is below carrying value on the Consolidated Balance Sheets. Carrying values are not adjusted periodically except when impairment occurs, and when impairment is determined, the carrying value is reduced to fair value, with the difference recorded in SG&A and Restructuring charges on the Consolidated Statements of Earnings for non-restructuring and restructuring charges, respectively. Revenue is recognized when control of promised goods or services is transferred to customers, in an amount reflecting the transaction price expected to be received. Revenue associated with unsatisfied performance obligations is deferred until the obligation is satisfied, i.e., when control of a product is transferred to the customer or a service is completed. Product revenue is recognized when the customer takes physical control, either in our stores or at their home. Delivery fees charged to customers are part of the transaction price and are recognized when delivery is completed. In most cases, we are the principal in product contracts because we control the physical products prior to transfer, and revenue is recognized on a gross basis. For certain sales, such as activation-based software licenses and third-party stored-value cards, we act as a sales agent providing access to content and recognize commission revenue net of amounts due to third parties who fulfill the performance obligation, with control passing upon providing access to the content. Warranty obligations for exclusive brand products are assurance-type warranties guaranteeing product functionality and are not considered distinct performance obligations. For services when we are the principal, revenue is recognized upon completion of services, when the customer can direct use and obtain benefits, with payment typically at point of sale or upon completion. Service contracts are primarily with retail customers and merchandise vendors (for factory warranty repairs). For technical support membership contracts (e.g., Best Buy Totaltech), we fulfill the support services and contracts range from one month to one year, typically containing multiple performance obligations. Payment is due at the start of the contract period. We have determined there is no significant financing component. For performance obligations provided over time, revenue is recognized on a usage basis using an input method based on historical utilization patterns, which reflects when customers use the services. Judgment is involved in (1) determining the level at which a portfolio approach is applied, (2) measuring the relative standalone selling price of performance obligations within bundled contracts using either a standalone price or cost-plus margin approach, and (3) assessing the pattern of delivery across multiple customer portfolios, including estimating current and future usage. When insufficient historical data is available, revenue is generally recognized ratably over the contract term. When we are the agent, we sell hardware protection plans on behalf of third-party underwriters, with terms from one month to five years and payment due at point of sale. In some cases, we are eligible for profit-sharing payments based on the underwriter’s portfolio performance, which are recorded as revenue once the uncertainty of the portfolio period (calendar-year based) is no longer constrained using the expected value method, typically during the fiscal fourth quarter, with payments made in the subsequent fiscal year. Square, Inc. is a company headquartered at 1455 Market Street, Suite 600, San Francisco, CA 94103, with a telephone number of (415) 375-3176. The company was incorporated in Delaware and has the IRS Employer Identification Number 80-0429876.
