Square’s Class A Common Stock trades on the New York Stock Exchange under the symbol SQ. As of June 30, 2020, the aggregate market value of the voting and non-voting common equity held by non-affiliates was approximately $38.7 billion, based on the closing price of the Class A common stock on that date. Shares held by executive officers, directors, and holders of 5% or more of the outstanding Class A or Class B common stock have been excluded from this calculation as such individuals may be deemed affiliates. As of February 18, 2021, the number of outstanding shares of Class A common stock was 389,826,763 and the number of outstanding shares of Class B common stock was 64,787,897. The registrant is a well-known seasoned issuer and has filed all required reports under Section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 during the preceding 12 months and has been subject to such filing requirements for the past 90 days. Square has submitted electronically every Interactive Data File required under Rule 405 of Regulation S-T. The company is classified as a large accelerated filer. It has filed a report on and attestation to its management’s assessment of the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting under Section 404(b) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. Portions of the registrant’s Definitive Proxy Statement relating to the Annual Meeting of Stockholders are incorporated by reference into Part III of this Form 10-K and will be filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission within 120 days after the end of the fiscal year ended December 31, 2020. Square began in February 2009 to enable businesses to accept card payments, and has since expanded to offer over 30 distinct products and services to sellers, including software, hardware, and financial services. The company also operates Cash App, which provides financial services to individuals to help them manage their money. Effective June 30, 2020, Square reported its results under two reportable segments: Seller and Cash App, reflecting the two ecosystems and how management and the chief operating decision maker review business performance. The Seller Ecosystem offers a cohesive commerce platform that helps sellers start, run, and grow their businesses through integrated software, hardware, and financial services, differentiating itself from a fragmented industry that traditionally requires sellers to use multiple vendors and inefficient tools. In the year ended December 31, 2020, Square processed $103.7 billion in Seller Gross Payment Volume (GPV), generated by more than 2 billion card payments from 405 million payment cards, and had over 210 million buyer profiles and approximately 295 million items listed by sellers on its platform. The Cash App Ecosystem provides financial products and services to individuals, including the ability to store, send, receive, spend, and invest money, with the goal of making money more relatable, instantly available, and universally accessible. In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, Square made targeted investments in both ecosystems. For sellers, it eliminated fees for software products in March and April 2020, introduced temporary subscription pauses, prioritized omnichannel product launches to support online and contactless commerce, including curbside pickup and delivery, and provided free marketing campaigns to help sellers promote their businesses. As a participant in the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP), Square Capital facilitated approximately $857 million in PPP loans, excluding cancelled loans, providing financial support to over 80,000 small businesses as of December 31, 2020. For Cash App customers, the company published educational materials on the CARES Act stimulus programs, expanded direct deposit access to allow customers to receive government funds into their Cash App accounts, and adapted Boost rewards to support pandemic-relevant merchants and categories such as grocery stores. Square’s sellers include a diverse range of businesses across industries such as services, food-related, and retail, and vary in size from sole proprietors to multi-location businesses, spanning the United States, Canada, Japan, Australia, and the United Kingdom. The company serves larger sellers—defined as those generating more than $125,000 in annualized GPV—and GPV from these larger sellers represented 60% of Seller GPV in the fourth quarter of 2020, up from 56% in the fourth quarter of 2019 and 52% in the fourth quarter of 2018. For the years ended December 31, 2020, 2019, and 2018, no single customer accounted for more than 5% of Square’s GPV or total net revenue. The Seller Ecosystem includes software products such as Square Point of Sale, Square Appointments, Square for Retail, and Square for Restaurants, all of which are designed to be self-serve and intuitive, with automatic updates and upgrades. Square Point of Sale is available on iOS and Android and is pre-installed on Square Register and Square Terminal hardware. Square Appointments supports booking, retail sales, invoicing, and payments, includes a free online booking site, and integrates with Square Assistant, an AI-powered messaging tool that helps reduce no-shows. Square for Retail includes barcode scanning, advanced inventory management, support for tens of thousands of items, cost of goods sold reporting, purchase orders, and vendor management. Square for Restaurants includes table, order, and course management, kitchen display systems, and revenue and cost reporting, enabling managers and owners to make informed decisions. All point of sale products have a free tier without a subscription fee, monetized only through transaction fees, while premium tiers of Square Appointments, Square for Retail, and Square for Restaurants are monetized through subscription fees in addition to transaction fees. The company’s online products are part of its broader software suite.

Square Point of Sale is a general-purpose point-of-sale software available on iOS and Android, pre-installed on Square Register and Square Terminal hardware devices. Square Appointments is an integrated solution supporting booking, retail sales, invoicing, and payments, accessible on iOS, Android, and via a web browser, with a free online booking site allowing buyers to schedule appointments, select time, service, and staff. It integrates with Square Assistant, an AI-powered automated messaging tool that responds professionally to buyers, saving seller time and reducing no-shows. Square for Retail is designed for the retail industry, offering barcode scanning, advanced inventory management, support for tens of thousands of items, cost of goods sold reporting, purchase orders, and vendor management. Square for Restaurants is tailored for the food and beverage sector, including table, order, and course management, as well as back-of-house features like a kitchen display system and revenue and cost reporting, enabling managers and owners to make informed decisions. Square’s online products enable sellers to sell via social media and build websites, supporting omnichannel experiences such as buy online, pickup in store (or curbside), and buy online, return in store. All online products offer a free tier without a subscription, monetized solely through transaction fees on payments; premium tiers include additional functionality charged via software fees in addition to transaction fees. Square Online helps sellers across various verticals reach customers through easy website and online store creation, Instagram and Facebook sales, mobile-responsive app-like ordering, QR code ordering for streamlined in-store operations, and fulfillment options including pickup, seller-managed delivery, and partner delivery platforms. Orders, items, inventory, and customer data remain synchronized across online and in-person sales. Square Online Checkout allows sellers to create a checkout link with just a name and price for goods or services without needing a full website. Square Invoices provides a customizable digital invoicing solution with secure online payment acceptance, eliminating the need to print and mail statements or wait for checks; it supports upcoming, recurring, or previously delivered goods and services, such as catering, contractor work, lessons, and retail orders, and allows sending estimates and collecting partial payments. Square Virtual Terminal lets sellers use a computer as a card terminal to take payments, set up recurring billing, record sales, and send digital receipts, including for checks and bank transfers. Business and customer relationship management products streamline operations by integrating with other Square tools, eliminating time-consuming and error-prone data copying and syncing; these are monetized via software fees except for Square Contracts, Feedback, and Dashboard, which are not directly monetized. Square Team Management enables staff scheduling, real-time performance and sales analytics, and employee payments via Square Payroll, with role-based access control; the Square Team App allows team members to clock in/out, view and adjust schedules, see timecards and hours worked, and view estimated pay, and team members paid via Square Payroll can view their pay stubs in the app. Square Contracts helps sellers create custom or template-based digital contracts with e-signature support for service agreements and liability waivers, usable independently or added to Square Invoices or Square Appointments. Square Loyalty, Marketing, Gift Cards, and Feedback help sellers engage customers in-store and online through integrated omnichannel loyalty, marketing, and feedback, with a closed-loop system enabling performance and return on investment assessment. Square Dashboard provides real-time data and insights on orders, items, inventory, customers, employees, payments, marketing, and loyalty performance, accessible via web or the iOS app, enabling timely business decisions. Square offers a developer platform with APIs and SDKs to allow external developers to integrate with its ecosystem. Payment APIs support in-person, online, and mobile payments; the Square Reader SDK enables integration of Square hardware with custom POS systems to build unique checkout experiences like self-ordering kiosks powered by Square’s managed payments; online payments APIs allow integration into e-commerce websites or stores; the In-App Payments SDK enables developers to build consumer mobile apps using Square for payments, primarily monetized through transaction fees. Commerce APIs include over 30 APIs enabling developers to create and manage orders, subscriptions, product catalogs, inventory, customer profiles, employees, loyalty programs, and gift cards, and to build integrations with existing business systems such as accounting, CRM, employee management, and ERP software. Square’s hardware is custom-designed to process all major card types, including magnetic stripe, EMV chip, and NFC, supporting cards from Visa, MasterCard, American Express, Discover, JCB, Interac Flash (in Canada), e-Money (in Japan), and eftpos (in Australia), and can be paired with accessories like cash drawers, receipt printers, and barcode scanners. The hardware portfolio includes a magstripe reader that connects to iOS or Android devices via headphone jack or lightning connector, a contactless and chip reader supporting Apple Pay, Google Pay, and other mobile wallets, the Square Stand that turns an iPad into a payment terminal with integrated magstripe reader, power, and wireless or USB connectivity to a contactless/chip reader, Square Register—an all-in-one device with two screens (seller and customer displays) and a built-in card reader accepting tap, dip, and swipe payments, and Square Terminal, a portable all-in-one payments device and receipt printer with battery lasting all day, accepting tap, dip, and swipe payments. Square acts as both the merchant of record and payment service provider (PSP), managing transaction settlements and risk loss for sellers, leveraging risk assessment models and transaction-level data to onboard new sellers efficiently and inform product development. Square has negotiated direct contracts with acquiring processors and card networks, and indirectly with issuing banks, securing favorable pricing not available to individual sellers. Financial Services include Managed Payments, Business Banking, and Payroll. Managed Payments offers next-day settlements, payment dispute management, data security, and PCI compliance, with onboarding in minutes and transaction fees charged transparently; Risk Manager provides insight into online payment fraud patterns and allows sellers to set custom rules and alerts, using machine learning to identify and adapt to fraud patterns; Instant Transfer enables sellers to receive funds instantly or later the same day, improving cash flow management; Square Card is a free business prepaid debit card that allows sellers to spend proceeds immediately from their Square stored balance, with Square earning interchange fees when purchases are made; Square Capital provides loans to qualified sellers through a partnership with an industrial bank, using a seller’s Square transaction data for underwriting and collections, with loan terms straightforward, repayment automatic via a fixed percentage of card transactions, loans sized under 20% of expected annual GPV, and average repayment in under nine months; since its public launch in May 2014, Square Capital has facilitated over 1.2 million loans and advances totaling more than $8.1 billion, including approximately $857 million in Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loans to over 80,000 sellers in 2020; Square Payroll enables sellers to hire, onboard employees, pay wages and associated taxes, and offer benefits like 401(k) accounts, with competitive differentiation through integration with POS, Team Management, and Cash App. In 2021, Square plans to open an industrial loan corporation, Square Financial Services (SFS), as a wholly owned subsidiary to engage in lending activities related to Square Capital, subject to regulatory approval. Cash App builds an ecosystem to help individuals manage money by making it more accessible, instant, and relatable, primarily serving customers in the U.S. with certain services in Europe (UK and Spain). Customers can store funds via peer-to-peer transfers or bank account deposits, with enhanced onboarding, and use these funds to send money, spend via Cash Card, withdraw at ATMs, invest in stocks or ETFs, buy or sell bitcoin, or transfer to a bank account (instantly for a fee or free in 1–3 days); as of December 31, 2020, Cash App held approximately $2.0 billion in stored balances. Cross-border payments between the U.S. and UK were launched in Q1 2020 with real-time exchange rates and no fees. The Cash Card is a debit card linked directly to a Cash App balance, available for free, usable anywhere that accepts cards, with customers able to select new or promotional designs for a fee; the Cash Boost program offers instant discounts at specific businesses or business types (e.g., 10% off on DoorDash or grocery stores), selected and funded by Square or partners, with Square-funded costs recognized as revenue reductions. Customers can invest in U.S. stocks, ETFs, or bitcoin using funds in their Cash App balance or a linked debit card, with fractional purchases starting at $1, and revenue recognized when bitcoin is purchased and transferred. In Q4 2020, Square acquired Credit Karma Tax, adding a free, mobile-first tax filing product to the Cash App ecosystem. Sales and marketing efforts focus on seller ecosystem growth through brand affinity, direct marketing, public relations, direct sales, and partnerships, with a Net Promoter Score averaging nearly 65 over the past four quarters—double the banking industry average—indicating strong seller recommendations and efficient customer acquisition. Our business operations face numerous risks and uncertainties, both within and outside our control, which could harm our actual results. Our participation in government relief programs, such as the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) established under the CARES Act in March 2020 and extended until March 31, 2021 with an additional $284 billion allocation, exposes us to new risks. Square Capital, as a PPP participant, provides small businesses with two-year or five-year loans at a 1% fixed interest rate, up to 2.5 times (or 3.5 times for restaurants) their monthly payroll expenses, with loan forgiveness tied to specific spending requirements, including at least 60% for payroll. As of December 31, 2020, Square Capital had facilitated approximately $857 million in PPP loans, excluding cancelled loans, and has retained some loans while selling 100% participation rights to third-party investors; it also borrowed from the Federal Reserve secured by its PPP loan portfolio. These activities expose Square Capital to risks related to documentation, verification, forgiveness, and servicing, including potential losses if borrowers fail to meet requirements or if the SBA declines to honor guarantees. Additionally, Cash App has facilitated economic impact payments and unemployment benefits by providing account and routing numbers and accepting deposits from state-issued prepaid cards, which introduces risks of fraud, data breaches, and technical issues. We also depend on retail partners to sell hardware and acquire customers, and our ability to maintain such partnerships is critical. Harm to our brand can arise from service failures, data misuse, fraud, compliance issues, litigation, or negative publicity. Regarding ownership of common stock, the company has a dual-class structure with Class B common stock having ten votes per share and Class A having one vote per share. When Class B shares represent less than 5% of the combined voting power, the outstanding shares of Class B automatically convert to Class A shares. Transfers of Class B shares generally result in conversion to Class A shares, with limited exceptions. For example, if Class B holders retain shares constituting as little as 10% of all outstanding Class A and Class B shares combined, they will continue to control a majority of the combined voting power. Square began in February 2009 to enable businesses to accept card payments, expanding to offer a cohesive ecosystem of software, hardware, and financial services for sellers, including transaction, subscription, and service fees. The Seller ecosystem includes over 30 products and services, with revenue recognized upon sale of loans or over time as sellers pay down balances. Sellers can accept payments in person via swipe, dip, or tap, or online via Square Invoices, Square Virtual Terminal, or their website, and access hardware such as magstripe readers, contactless and chip readers, Square Stand, Square Register, Square Terminal, and third-party peripherals. Square Card allows sellers to spend stored balances, deposit funds, and access business loans through Square Capital, which are repaid via a percentage of collections. Revenue from Square Capital is recognized when loans are sold to investors or as sellers pay down balances. Square serves millions of sellers across diverse industries and sizes, including services, food-related, and retail, and spans the U.S., Canada, Japan, Australia, and the U.K. The Cash App ecosystem provides individuals with tools to store, send, receive, spend, and invest money, including P2P payments, Cash Card transactions, and bitcoin and equity investments. In the fourth quarter of 2020, Square acquired Credit Karma Tax, adding a free, mobile-first tax filing product. Effective June 30, 2020, Square restructured into two reportable segments: Seller and Cash App. In April 2020, Square was licensed to participate in the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) administered by the SBA under the CARES Act, facilitating $857 million in PPP loans for the year ended December 31, 2020, of which $399.0 million were sold to investors. As of December 31, 2020, approximately $46.4 million in PPP loans held for sale were forgiven by the SBA. In February 2021, Square began participating in the second round of PPP, accepting applications from existing customers who received loans in spring 2020, with loans guaranteed by the U.S. government and eligible for forgiveness. On June 2, 2020, Square entered into a Paycheck Protection Program Liquidity Facility (First PPPLF Agreement) with the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco to secure up to $500.0 million in credit, with borrowings accruing 0.35% interest and collateralized by PPP loans. As of December 31, 2020, $464.1 million in PPPLF advances were outstanding, collateralized by $464.1 million in PPP loans held for sale. On January 29, 2021, Square entered into a second PPPLF Agreement (Second PPPLF Agreement), together with the First PPPLF Agreement, to secure up to $1.0 billion in credit, collateralized by loans from the second round of PPP. On March 5, 2020, Square issued $1.0 billion in convertible senior notes maturing on March 1, 2025, bearing 0.1250% interest payable semi-annually. On November 13, 2020, Square issued $1.150 billion in convertible senior notes: $575 million maturing on May 1, 2026, with a 0.0% coupon, and $575 million maturing on November 1, 2027, with a 0.25% coupon, payable semi-annually starting May 1, 2021. The notes mature unless earlier converted or repurchased. The net proceeds from the 2025, 2026, and 2027 notes are intended for general corporate purposes, including capital expenditures, investments, working capital, and potential acquisitions. By March 2020, the World Health Organization declared the COVID-19 pandemic a global pandemic, leading to business closures and social distancing orders, which caused a significant decline in sales for many Square customers in the first half of 2020. In the second half, modest improvements occurred due to higher-priced card-not-present transactions, new seller onboarding, and government assistance programs increasing consumer spending. Seller GPV trends varied by region and depended on local reopening timelines. Cash App engagement increased due to customer adoption and deposits of stimulus funds and unemployment benefits. In response to the pandemic, Square refunded software subscription fees in March and April 2020 and introduced options for sellers to pause and resume subscriptions. The company continues to monitor the global spread of COVID-19, with growth trends varying by region, product, and vertical. Safety remains a priority for employees, customers, and communities. As of December 31, 2020, goodwill and long-lived assets were not impaired. Revenue includes transaction fees based on a percentage of transaction amounts, custom pricing for larger sellers, and fees for Cash App peer-to-peer transactions. Subscription and services-based revenue includes Cash App Instant Deposit, Cash Card, Instant Transfers, website hosting, domain registration, Gift Cards, Square Appointments, Customer Engagement, Employee Management, Payroll, Square Card, and other products. Prior to 2020, Caviar revenue was included, which was sold in the fourth quarter of 2019. Instant Deposit enables instant bank deposits, and Cash Card allows use of stored funds via a Visa prepaid card. Square Capital facilitates loans to sellers and customers through bank partners, with loans purchased from banks and sold to investors for an upfront fee, with Square retaining servicing fees. In April 2020, Square Capital was licensed for PPP participation, with loans guaranteed by the U.S. government and eligible for forgiveness. Hardware revenue comes from sales of contactless and chip readers, Square Stand, Square Register, Square Terminal, and third-party peripherals like cash drawers, receipt printers, and barcode scanners. Bitcoin revenue is recognized when customers purchase and receive bitcoin, with revenue recorded on a gross basis and costs as cost of revenue. Square is the principal in bitcoin sales due to control before delivery, responsibility for delivery, exposure to market price fluctuations, and pricing discretion. Bitcoin revenue fluctuates with customer demand and market price. Transaction-based costs include interchange, assessment, processing, and bank settlement fees. Subscription and services-based costs include Cash App and Instant Transfer expenses, and prior to 2019, Caviar costs. Hardware costs include product costs such as manufacturing, personnel, royalties, packaging, and fulfillment. Hardware is sold to grow transaction-based revenue, and positive gross margins are not the primary goal. Bitcoin costs are the amounts paid to purchase bitcoin for customer access. Amortization of acquired technology is not material. Operating expenses include product development, sales and marketing, general and administrative expenses, transaction and loan losses, and amortization of acquired customer assets. Product development is the largest component, primarily consisting of personnel-related expenses such as salaries, commissions, bonuses, benefits, and share-based compensation. Sales and marketing expenses include Cash App peer-to-peer and Cash Card issuance costs, paid advertising, and personnel-related expenses. Operating expenses also include allocated overhead for facilities, human resources, and IT.

The primary goal of the hardware business is not to generate positive gross margins from hardware sales, but rather to grow transaction-based revenue. Bitcoin cost of revenue consists of amounts paid to purchase bitcoin, which fluctuates with the market price of bitcoin, and these purchases are made to facilitate customers’ access to bitcoin. Amortization of acquired technology, which includes costs related to technologies acquired through acquisitions, was not material to the financial statements. Operating expenses include product development, sales and marketing, general and administrative expenses, transaction and loan losses, and amortization of acquired customer assets. Product development expenses, the largest component of operating expenses, consist primarily of engineering, data science, and design personnel costs, third-party data center maintenance fees, hardware development and tooling costs, and software license, consulting, legal, and other directly related fees. These expenses also include depreciation of product-related infrastructure such as data center equipment, internally developed software, and computer equipment. The company focuses on adding new features and apps and enhancing product functionality and ease of use, with returns on these investments depending on successfully addressing current and emerging customer needs. Sales and marketing expenses are divided into two components: traditional advertising costs such as direct sales, account management, local and product marketing, retail and e-commerce, partnerships, and communications personnel; and non-revenue-generating marketing costs including Cash App peer-to-peer processing costs, transaction losses, card issuance costs, customer referral bonuses, and promotional giveaways. General and administrative expenses primarily include costs for customer support, finance, legal, risk operations, human resources, and administrative personnel, as well as professional services like legal, tax, and accounting fees. Transaction losses arise from chargebacks due to fraud or uncollectibility, including unauthorized credit card use, disputes over goods or services, and losses from peer-to-peer payments via credit card, Cash for Business, and Cash Card. These losses are estimated based on prior chargeback history and current data, with additions to reserves reflected in current operating results and realized losses offsetting the reserve. Loan losses are recorded when the amortized cost of retained loans exceeds their fair value, determined using industry-standard models like discounted cash flow, and charges are reversed only if fair value increases without causing amortized cost to exceed fair value. Amortization of acquired customer assets, including customer, restaurant, courier, subscriber, and partner relationships, was not material. The gain on sale of the asset group in 2019 represents the excess of consideration received from the disposal of the Caviar business over the carrying value of net assets sold. Interest and other income and expense, net, primarily includes gains or losses from marking to market of equity investments, interest expense on long-term debt, interest income on marketable debt securities, and foreign currency-related gains and losses. The provision for income taxes includes federal, state, local, and foreign taxes, with the effective tax rate fluctuating due to changes in income and losses by jurisdiction, acquisitions, valuation allowances, permanent accounting differences, one-time items, and tax contingencies. Revenue for the year ended December 31, 2020, increased by $4.8 billion, or 101%, compared to 2019, with bitcoin revenue increasing by $4.1 billion, or 785%, representing 85% of the total revenue increase. Excluding bitcoin revenue, total net revenue increased by $729.0 million, or 17%. Transaction-based revenue increased by $213.9 million, or 7%, driven by growth in payment volume from existing and new sellers in January and February 2020, offset by a significant decline in March through mid-April 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic, followed by recovery in mid-April as shelter-in-place measures eased, sellers adapted to contactless commerce, and consumer spending rose. Growth in higher-priced card-not-present transactions and the November 2019 card-present price change, along with Cash App GPV including Cash for Business and peer-to-peer payments, contributed to the overall increase. Subscription and services-based revenue increased by $507.9 million, or 49%, with the sale of Caviar on October 31, 2019, removing its contribution. Excluding Caviar, this revenue grew by $653.9 million, or 74%, driven by Cash App, Square Card, and Instant Transfers, partially offset by lower Square Capital loan volumes. Cash App subscription and services-based revenue comes primarily from transaction fees on Cash App Instant Deposit and Cash Card, with a small portion from interest on customer funds. Software subscription fees were temporarily suspended and refunded in March and April 2020, then resumed in May 2020. Square Capital suspended facilitating loans to sellers, except for PPP loans, in March 2020, resuming in July 2020, with loan volumes remaining below 2019 levels and uncertainty about future recovery. Hardware revenue increased by $7.1 million, or 8%, due to higher sales in international markets and contactless hardware sales from promotions in the second and third quarters. Bitcoin revenue increased by $4.1 billion, or 785%, due to higher bitcoin market prices, growth in active bitcoin customers, and increased volume per customer. The amount of bitcoin revenue recognized varies with customer demand and market price. While bitcoin accounted for 48% of total revenue in 2020 and 85% of the revenue increase, gross margin from bitcoin was only 3.5% of total gross margin. Cost of revenue increased by $3.9 billion, or 140%, with bitcoin costs rising by $4.0 billion, or 780%, representing 101% of the total increase. Excluding bitcoin costs, total cost of revenue decreased by $25.9 million, or 1%. Transaction-based costs decreased by $26.1 million, or 1%, due to growth in debit card transactions and higher average transaction sizes reducing the average cost per transaction, partially offset by increased GPV. Subscription and services-based costs decreased by $11.6 million, or 5%, primarily due to the Caviar sale, which accounted for 45% of those costs in 2019. Excluding Caviar, these costs increased by $92.7 million, or 71%, driven by higher Cash Card and Instant Deposit costs. Hardware costs increased by $7.5 million, or 6%, due to the same factors as hardware revenue. Bitcoin costs consist of the total amounts paid to purchase bitcoin, which fluctuate with bitcoin revenue. Product development expenses increased by $211.2 million, or 31%, due to a $155.4 million increase in personnel costs, including $78.7 million in share-based compensation, and a $23.5 million increase in software and data center operating costs due to higher capacity needs and cloud service expansion. Sales and marketing expenses increased by $484.8 million, or 78%, primarily due to a $355.6 million increase in Cash App marketing costs, including higher processing costs, transaction losses, card issuance costs, and customer incentives not directly tied to revenue-generating transactions.

Sales and marketing expenses for the year ended December 31, 2020, increased by $484.8 million, or 78%, compared to the year ended December 31, 2019, primarily due to a $355.6 million increase in Cash App marketing costs related to higher processing costs and transaction losses from increased activity in the peer-to-peer service, higher card issuance costs, and customer incentives not directly tied to revenue-generating transactions, as well as a $52.5 million increase in advertising costs; a $29.6 million increase in advertising costs for Seller Ecosystem services from expanded online and television campaigns; and a $28.3 million increase in sales and marketing personnel costs to support growth initiatives, including $9.9 million in share-based compensation. General and administrative expenses for the year ended December 31, 2020, increased by $143.0 million, or 33%, compared to the prior year, mainly due to a $58.7 million increase in personnel costs from hiring in customer support, finance, and legal to support business growth, including $10.8 million in share-based compensation, and additional costs from new leases, software and subscription fees, local business taxes, third-party legal and professional fees, and administrative expenses, as well as the impact of statutory reserves. Transaction and loan losses increased by $50.7 million, or 40%, due to a $44.8 million rise in transaction losses from Cash App business growth and increased provisions for Seller business losses due to the COVID-19 pandemic’s impact on seller activity, and a $6.0 million increase in loan losses from provisions related to the pandemic and aging of the Square Capital loan portfolio, offset by lower loan volumes after suspending new loan offers in March 2020 and resuming them at reduced volumes in July 2020. The report dated February 23, 2021, issued by Ernst & Young LLP, expresses an unqualified opinion on the consolidated financial statements of Square, Inc. as of December 31, 2020, and for the year then ended. The financial statements are the responsibility of Square’s management, and the audit was conducted in accordance with the standards of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB), which require the auditor to plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance that the financial statements are free of material misstatement, whether due to error or fraud. The audit included evaluating the accounting principles used, significant estimates made by management, and the overall presentation of the financial statements, as well as assessing the risks of material misstatement and performing procedures to respond to those risks. The report also includes a section on critical audit matters, which are matters that were both material to the financial statements and involved especially challenging, subjective, or complex judgments. The first critical audit matter is the accrued transaction losses, where the Company established a reserve of $70.6 million at December 31, 2020, based on available data, historical trends, and qualitative adjustments for uncertainty in the economic environment. The audit involved testing controls over the process for determining the reserve, including the completeness and accuracy of loss rate data, management’s evaluation of new or contradictory information, and the appropriateness of qualitative adjustments. The second critical audit matter is the accounting for the Convertible Senior Notes, which were issued in March 2020 and November 2020 totaling $2.15 billion, due in 2025, 2026, and 2027. These notes permit the Company to pay or deliver cash, shares of common stock, or a combination thereof upon conversion. The audit addressed the significant judgment required in determining the fair value of the liability component and the balance sheet classification of the components, including evaluating the Company’s use of similar debt instruments without convertible features and assessing key assumptions such as credit risk, equity volatility, dividend yield, and the market risk-free rate. The audit also involved a valuation specialist to evaluate the methodology and assumptions used. Additionally, the report includes an opinion on internal control over financial reporting, stating that Square maintained effective internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2020, based on the COSO criteria. Revenue is recognized when control of the promised goods or services is transferred to customers, in an amount that reflects the consideration the Company expects to be entitled to in exchange for those goods or services. Transaction-based revenue: The Company charges its sellers a transaction fee for managed payments solutions that is generally calculated as a percentage of the total transaction amount processed. The Company collects the transaction amount from the seller's customer's bank, net of acquiring interchange and assessment fees, processing fees, and bank settlement fees paid to third-party payment processors and financial institutions. The Company retains its fees and remits the net amount to the sellers. The Company acts as the merchant of record for its sellers and works directly with payment card networks and banks so that its sellers do not need to manage the complex systems, rules, and requirements of the payments industry. The Company satisfies its performance obligations and therefore recognizes the transaction fees as revenue upon authorization of a transaction by the seller's customer's bank. The Company applies the optional exemption allowed under ASC 606 not to disclose consideration attributable to performance obligations for future transaction processing since the term of the contract with a seller is not defined and any future consideration on the contract would be dependent on the value and volume of transactions processed in the future, which are not determinable. Revenue is recognized net of refunds, which arise from reversals of transactions initiated by sellers. The transaction fees collected from sellers are recognized as revenue on a gross basis as the Company is the principal in the delivery of the managed payments solutions to the sellers. The Company has concluded it is the principal because as the merchant of record, it controls the services before delivery to the seller, it is primarily responsible for the delivery of the services to its sellers, and it has discretion in setting prices charged to sellers. The Company also has the unilateral ability to accept or reject a transaction based on criteria established by the Company. As the merchant of record, Square is liable for the costs of processing the transactions for its sellers, and records such costs within cost of revenue. Subscription and services-based revenue: Subscription and services-based revenue is primarily comprised of revenue the Company generates from Instant Deposit and Cash Card, Square Capital, website hosting and domain name registration services, and various other software as a service (SaaS) products. Instant Deposit is a functionality within the Cash App and the Company's managed payments solution that enables customers, including individuals and sellers, to instantly deposit funds into their bank accounts. The Company charges a per transaction fee which is recognized as revenue when customers instantly deposit funds to their bank account. The Company also offers Cash App customers the ability to use funds stored in the Cash App via a Visa prepaid card (Cash Card), for which the Company charges a per transaction fee that is recorded as revenue. Square Capital facilitates a loan that is offered through a partnership with an industrial bank that is either repaid through withholding a percentage of the collections of the seller's receivables processed by the Company or a specified monthly amount. The Company generally facilitates loans to its sellers through a pre-qualification process that includes an analysis of the aggregated data of the seller’s business which includes, but is not limited to, the seller’s historical processing volumes, transaction count, chargebacks, growth, and length of time as a Square customer. The Company also facilitates loans to the customers of certain sellers as well as to the sellers of its partners who do not process payments through the Company. The loans are generally originated by a bank partner, from whom the Company purchases the loans obtaining all rights, title, and interest. The loans have no stated coupon rate but the seller is charged a one-time origination fee by the bank partner based upon their risk rating, which is derived primarily from processing activity. It is the Company’s intent to sell all of its rights, title, and interest of these loans to third-party investors for an upfront fee when the loans are sold. The Company records the net amounts paid to the bank as the cost of the loans purchased and subsequently records a gain on sale of the loans to the third-party investors as revenue upon transfer of title. The Company is retained by the third-party investors to service the loans and earns a servicing fee for facilitating the repayment of these receivables through its managed payments solutions. The Company records servicing revenue as servicing is delivered. For the loans which are not immediately sold to third-party investors, the Company recognizes a portion of the expected seller repayments over the cost of the loans as revenue in proportion to the loan principal reduction. The Company offers customers website hosting services for a fee that is generally billed at inception. The Company also acts as a reseller of domain names registration services for a registrar for a fee, which is also generally billed at inception. The Company considers that it satisfies its performance obligations over time and as such recognizes revenue ratably over the term of the relevant arrangements, which vary from one month to twenty four months for website hosting, and one year to ten years for domain name registration. SaaS represents software products and solutions that provide customers with access to various technologies for a fee which is recognized as revenue ratably as the service is provided. The Company's contracts with customers are generally for a term of one month and renew automatically each month. The Company invoices its customers monthly. The Company considers that it satisfies its performance obligations over time each month as it provides the SaaS services to customers and hence recognizes revenue ratably over the month. Subscription and services revenue also included revenue generated from Caviar, a food ordering platform that facilitated food delivery services that was sold by the Company on October 31, 2019. The performance obligations were the delivery of food orders from restaurants to customers and the provision of catered meals to corporate customers. For delivery of food orders, the Company charged fees to restaurants, as sellers, and also charged delivery and service fees to individuals. For provision of catered meals the Company charged corporate customers a fee. All fees were billed upon delivery of food orders or catered meals, when the Company considers that it has satisfied its performance obligations. Revenue was recognized upon delivery of the food orders or catered meals, net of refunds. Refunds were estimated based on historical experience. Hardware revenue: The Company generates revenue through the sale of hardware through e-commerce and through its retail distribution channels. The Company satisfies its performance obligation upon delivery of hardware to its customers who include end user customers, distributors, and retailers. The Company allows for customer returns which are accounted for as variable consideration. The Company estimates these amounts based on historical experience and reduces revenue recognized. The Company invoices end user customers upon delivery of the products to customers, and payments from such customers are due upon invoicing. Distributors and retailers have payment terms that range from 30 to 90 days after delivery. The Company offers hardware installment sales to customers with terms ranging from three to twenty four months. The Company allocates a portion of the consideration received from these arrangements to a financing component when it determines that a significant financing component exists. The financing component is subsequently recognized as financing revenue separate from hardware revenue, within subscription and services-based revenue, over the terms of the arrangement with the customer. Pursuant to practical expedients afforded under ASC 606, the Company does not recognize a financing component for hardware installment sales that have a term of one year or less. Bitcoin revenue: The Company offers its Cash App customers the ability to purchase bitcoin, a cryptocurrency denominated asset, from the Company. The Company satisfies its performance obligation and records revenue when bitcoin is transferred to the customer's account. The Company purchases bitcoin from private broker dealers or from Cash App customers and applies a small margin before selling it to its customers. The sale amounts received from customers are recorded as revenue on a gross basis and the associated bitcoin cost as cost of revenues, as the Company is the principal in the bitcoin sale transaction. The Company has concluded it is the principal because it controls the bitcoin before delivery to the customers, it is primarily responsible for the delivery of the bitcoin to the customers, it is exposed to risks arising from fluctuations of the market price of bitcoin before delivery to customers, and has discretion in setting prices charged to customers. Arrangements with Multiple Performance Obligations: The Company's contracts with customers generally do not include multiple performance obligations with differing patterns of revenue recognition, except for domain name registration offered with website hosting services. The Company offers its customers the option to buy website hosting bundled with domain name registration, and infrequently the Company has offered its hardware customers free managed payments solutions with the purchase of its hardware as part of a marketing promotion. For such arrangements, the Company allocates revenue to each performance obligation based on its relative standalone selling price. The Company determines standalone selling prices based on the prices charged to customers since the Company's products and services are normally sold on a stand-alone basis. The fair value of stock options and ESPP shares granted to employees is estimated using the Black-Scholes-Merton option valuation model. This model requires assumptions and judgments regarding the expected term (calculated as the weighted average of the vesting term and the contractual term to maturity), expected volatility of the Company’s stock, expected risk-free interest rate, and expected dividends. Expected volatility is based on a weighted average of the historical volatilities of the Company’s common stock and similar entities, but in May 2020, the Company began using its own historical stock price data, eliminating the need for a peer group. The expected risk-free rate is based on the U.S. Treasury yield curve in effect at the time of grant for periods matching the expected life of the option. Share-based compensation expense is recorded on a straight-line basis over the requisite service period, and forfeitures are accounted for as they occur. The Company reports income taxes under the asset and liability approach, recognizing deferred tax assets and liabilities for future tax consequences of temporary differences between financial statement carrying amounts and tax bases, as well as net operating loss and tax credit carryforwards. A valuation allowance reduces deferred tax assets to the amount more likely than not to be realized, based on historical information, tax planning strategies, expected reversal of temporary differences, and financial projections. The Company assesses the realizability of deferred tax assets at each period; if it is more likely than not that the assets will not be realized, a valuation allowance is established. The Company holds marketable and non-marketable equity investments without significant influence or controlling interest. Marketable equity investments are measured using quoted prices in active markets, with changes recorded in other expense (income), net. Non-marketable equity investments lack readily determinable fair values and are measured using the measurement alternative—cost, less impairment, adjusted for observable price changes from orderly transactions for identical or similar investments of the same issuer—also recorded in other expense (income), net. Valuations for non-marketable investments use significant unobservable inputs and require management judgment due to the absence of market prices and lack of liquidity. Carrying value is not adjusted without observable transactions or identified impairment indicators. The Company assesses impairment of non-marketable equity investments quarterly, evaluating severity and duration of impairment, qualitative and quantitative factors such as financial metrics, market acceptance, competitive conditions, general market trends, and cash usage rates. The Company uses valuation techniques that prioritize observable inputs. Fair value is determined based on market participant assumptions in the principal or most advantageous market. The Company leases office space and equipment under non-cancellable finance and operating leases with various expiration dates. On January 1, 2019, the Company adopted Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) 842, Leases, and elected the optional transition method, which requires recognizing the cumulative effect of adoption on the date of adoption without changing prior period balances. The Company elected not to reassess whether expired or existing contracts contain leases, the lease classification for such leases, or initial direct costs for existing leases. It also applied the short-term lease measurement and recognition exemption where applicable. Operating lease right-of-use assets and operating lease liabilities are recognized at the present value of future lease payments, generally for the base noncancellable lease term, at the lease commencement date. The interest rate used is the Company's incremental borrowing rate, as the interest rate implicit in most leases is not readily determinable. The incremental borrowing rate approximates the rate the Company would pay to borrow on a collateralized basis with similar terms and payments as the lease, in the economic environment where the leased asset is located. Operating lease right-of-use assets include prepaid lease payments and lease incentives. Lease agreements generally contain lease and non-lease components; non-lease components, such as maintenance and utilities, are combined with lease payments and accounted for as a single lease component. Fixed non-lease components are included in the determination of right-of-use assets and operating lease liabilities. The Company records amortization of the right-of-use asset and accretion of the lease liability as a component of rent expense in the consolidated statement of operations. Accounting for finance leases remained substantially unchanged. Upon adoption of ASC 842, the Company recognized $112.0 million of operating right-of-use lease assets and $135.6 million of operating lease liabilities on its consolidated balance sheet. Additionally, the Company derecognized $149.0 million related to the build-to-suit asset and liability because it was no longer deemed the owner of the related asset under construction under the new standard. When lease agreements provide allowances for leasehold improvements, the Company assesses whether it is the owner of the leasehold improvements for accounting purposes. If it is the owner, the improvements are capitalized and depreciated on a straight-line basis over the lesser of the lease term or the estimated useful life. If not, payments for leasehold improvements are accounted for as part of lease payments. The Outside Director Compensation Policy was adopted on November 4, 2015, became effective as of November 18, 2015, and was last amended on October 21, 2020. The policy provides that each Outside Director will receive an annual cash retainer of $40,000, with additional cash retainers for committee chairpersons and members: $20,000 for chair of the Audit and Risk Committee, $15,000 for chair of the Compensation Committee, $10,000 for chair of the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee, $15,000 for chair of the Capital Compliance and Governance Committee, $10,000 for member of the Audit and Risk Committee, $5,000 for member of the Compensation Committee, $2,500 for member of the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee, and $5,000 for member of the Capital Compliance and Governance Committee. All cash compensation is paid quarterly in arrears on a prorated basis on the last day of each fiscal quarter. An Outside Director who serves as chair of a committee is not paid additional compensation for serving as a member of that committee. No Outside Director receives per-meeting attendance fees. Outside Directors may receive equity awards under the Company’s 2015 Equity Incentive Plan or any other Company equity plan in place at the time of grant, including discretionary awards not covered by this policy, provided such awards do not exceed any limitations in the Plan. Each Outside Director may elect to convert all of their cash compensation into a Retainer Award of Restricted Stock Units, with the number of units equal to the aggregate cash compensation divided by the closing price per share on the Retainer Accrual Date (or the last trading day of the quarter if the Retainer Accrual Date falls on a non-trading day), rounded down to the next whole share. The Retainer Award is fully vested on the grant date. Such election must be submitted in writing to the Company’s General Counsel at least 10 business days before a Retainer Accrual Date and is only permitted during periods when the Company is not in a quarterly or special blackout period. Once properly submitted, the election is effective for the applicable period.

An Outside Director must make a timely Retainer Award Election on the first business day following the immediately preceding Retainer Accrual Date to which it applies, and upon such election, the director will automatically receive a Retainer Award of Restricted Stock Units equal to the aggregate amount of cash compensation otherwise payable under Section 1 on that Retainer Accrual Date, divided by the closing price per Share as of the Retainer Accrual Date (or the last trading day of the quarter if the Retainer Accrual Date falls on a non-trading day), rounded down to the next whole Share. The Retainer Award will be fully vested on the grant date. To submit a Retainer Award Election, the director must provide written notice to the Company’s General Counsel at least 10 business days before the Retainer Accrual Date, subject to any conditions set by the Board or Compensation Committee, and such an election is only permitted during periods when the Company is not in a quarterly or special blackout period. Once submitted, the election remains in effect for the next Retainer Accrual Date and continues for subsequent dates unless revoked. A revocation must also be submitted in writing to the General Counsel at least 10 business days before a Retainer Accrual Date, subject to the same conditions and blackout period restrictions, and the director must not be aware of any material non-public information. Revoked elections remain in effect for the next Retainer Accrual Date and continue for subsequent dates until a new election is made. An Outside Director may revoke a Retainer Award Election at any time before the grant of the award if receiving it or issuing Shares thereunder would reasonably be expected to violate or result in a penalty, fee, or filing under Applicable Law; in such case, the rules in the last sentence of the prior paragraph apply. All grants of Awards to Outside Directors under Section 2(b) are automatic and nondiscretionary, with no discretion to select directors or determine the number of Shares. Upon initial appointment to the Board (except by appointment on the date of an Annual Meeting following the Effective Date), an Outside Director automatically receives an Initial Award of Restricted Stock Units with a grant date fair value of $250,000 multiplied by a fraction where the numerator is (x) 12 minus (y) the number of months between the date of the last Annual Meeting and the date of appointment, and the denominator is 12. This Initial Award fully vests on the earlier of the first anniversary of the grant date or the next Annual Meeting, subject to the director continuing as a Service Provider through the vesting date. On each Annual Meeting following the Effective Date, each Outside Director automatically receives an Annual Award of Restricted Stock Units with a grant date fair value of $250,000, which fully vests on the earlier of the first anniversary of the grant date or the next Annual Meeting, subject to continued service. The Lead Independent Director also receives an additional Lead Independent Director Annual Award with a grant date fair value of $70,000, which fully vests on the earlier of the first anniversary of the grant date or the next Annual Meeting, subject to continued service as Lead Independent Director. In the event of a Change in Control, all Outside Director Awards granted under this Policy will fully vest. All provisions of the Plan not inconsistent with this Policy apply to Awards granted to Outside Directors. The Board may at any time revise the terms of cash compensation under this Policy, including the amount or timing of future payments, revise the terms of Awards, including the number of Shares, or suspend or terminate the Policy. The Boeing Company, along with its subsidiaries, is one of the world’s major aerospace firms and operates in four reportable segments: Commercial Airplanes (BCA), Defense, Space & Security (BDS), Global Services (BGS), and Boeing Capital (BCC). The Commercial Airplanes segment develops, produces, and markets commercial jet aircraft to the global airline industry, offering a family of jetliners including the 737 narrow-body and 767, 777, and 787 wide-body models, with production of the 747 ending in 2022. Development continues on the 777X program and the 737-7 and 737-10 derivatives. The Defense, Space & Security segment produces and modifies manned and unmanned military aircraft, weapons systems, and related products such as strategic defense systems, C4ISR, cyber solutions, satellite systems, and space exploration. The Global Services segment provides a full range of services to commercial and defense customers, including supply chain management, engineering, maintenance, upgrades, spare parts, training, technical documentation, and data analytics. Boeing Capital provides financing to customers to purchase and take delivery of Boeing products, managing financing exposure through equipment leases, sales-type/finance leases, notes, receivables, assets held for sale or re-lease, and investments. Boeing owns numerous patents and licenses intellectual property from third parties, including U.S. government licenses for inventions developed under government contracts, and also relies on unpatented research, engineering skills, trademarks, trade secrets, and other intellectual property. As of December 31, 2022, Boeing’s total workforce was approximately 156,000, with 13% located outside the U.S., and included about 50,000 union members. The company has major collective bargaining agreements with the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (20% of employees, expiring in September 2024 and July 2025), the Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace (10%, expiring in October 2026), and the United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (1%, expiring in April 2027). Boeing is committed to diversity and inclusion, with a workforce composition in the U.S. as of December 2021 of approximately 23% women, 33% U.S. racial and ethnic minorities, and 15% U.S. veterans, and supports over 15,000 participants in 170 global Business Resource Groups. In 2022, Boeing hired approximately 23,000 new employees for critical skills, with a 78% offer acceptance rate and a voluntary resignation rate of about 4%. Employees engage in ongoing feedback through surveys from pre-hire to exit, and the company maintains a multi-level recognition program for performance. In 2022, Boeing employees completed approximately 5.8 million hours of learning, with over 9,000 employees annually using tuition assistance to pursue degrees, certificates, or courses from more than 300 accredited institutions worldwide. Safety, quality, integrity, and sustainability are central to Boeing’s operations, with a commitment to zero workplace injuries and an annual Code of Conduct signed by employees to uphold ethical and compliant work practices. Employees can report concerns related to ethics or safety through multiple channels, and the company addresses such concerns to uphold its values. The commercial jet aircraft market is highly competitive, with strong international competitors such as Airbus and emerging players from China, and Boeing focuses on product improvements, cost reduction, and delivering superior design, safety, efficiency, and value. The Defense, Space & Security segment competes with Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon Technologies, General Dynamics, SpaceX, and non-U.S. companies like BAE Systems and Airbus Group, which are expanding their U.S. presence through partnerships. In the commercial and defense services markets, BGS faces similar competition and intends to grow market share through high customer satisfaction and productivity. Boeing’s businesses are heavily regulated, working with U.S. government agencies such as the U.S. military, NASA, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), and the Department of Homeland Security, as well as equivalent authorities in non-U.S. markets. Government contracts may be terminated at the government’s convenience or for default; in the case of convenience termination, Boeing is entitled to payment for completed work and allowable termination costs, while in default termination, the government pays only for accepted work and may require Boeing to cover the cost difference to reprocure the items. For default, Boeing may also face liability for damages. Commercial aircraft must comply with FAA regulations on production, quality, airworthiness, repair procedures, and operational safety, with new models requiring FAA certification before service; similar requirements exist outside the U.S. under national aviation authorities, coordinated in Europe by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency. Boeing is subject to environmental laws and regulations regarding the discharge, treatment, storage, disposal, and remediation of hazardous substances and wastes, as well as climate change-related laws affecting greenhouse gas emissions, which could increase compliance costs, energy and raw material expenses, and investment in new technologies. Environmental compliance costs are a normal, recurring part of operations and are often allowable under U.S. government contracts. It is reasonably possible that increased environmental compliance costs could materially impact Boeing’s results of operations, financial condition, or cash flows if stricter clean-up standards or new contamination areas are imposed. For further details on environmental contingencies, see Note 13 to the Consolidated Financial Statements. Non-U.S. sales are subject to both U.S. and non-U.S. governmental regulations and procurement policies, including import-export controls and tariffs.

Boeing is highly dependent on the availability of key raw materials, parts, and subassemblies from suppliers and subcontractors, primarily aluminum (sheet, plate, forgings, and extrusions), titanium (sheet, plate, forgings, and extrusions), and composites (including carbon and boron). Although alternative sources exist, qualification can take a year or more. In 2022, due to the Russia-Ukraine war, Boeing suspended purchasing titanium from Russia, which did not disrupt operations because it used inventory on hand and identified alternative sources. Many major components and equipment are procured or subcontracted on a sole-source basis, and the company continues to work with a small number of sole-source suppliers to ensure supply continuity. While the company maintains an extensive qualification and performance surveillance system to manage third-party risks, supplier or subcontractor failures could negatively affect production schedules and program profitability, jeopardizing customer commitments. A significant portion of Boeing’s revenue comes from commercial airlines, which are subject to market volatility. Demand for commercial aircraft is driven by long-term trends in airline passenger and cargo traffic, influenced by economic growth, political stability, airline profitability, aircraft financing, trade policies, government relations, technological advances, fuel prices, terrorism, pandemics, epidemics, and environmental regulations. The airline industry is cyclical and competitive, with significant profit swings, and deterioration in the global economy or financial instability among major customers could reduce new orders, cause delays or cancellations of contracts, or lead to lower revenues, profitability, and cash flows, especially given that the commercial aircraft backlog spans several years. Boeing enters into firm fixed-price aircraft sales contracts with indexed price escalation clauses, which could result in losses if cost overruns occur or if cost increases exceed the escalation rate. Pricing is based on fixed amounts adjusted by formulas derived from labor, commodity, and other price indices, which are outside the company’s control and can fluctuate significantly, impacting revenue and operating margins. A significant portion of revenues comes from a limited number of commercial airlines, and there is no assurance that customers will exercise purchase options, fulfill commitments, or buy additional products or services. Fleet decisions, airline consolidations, or financial difficulties among major customers could reduce revenues and limit profit opportunities. Airlines are facing rising fuel and other costs, and the global economy is experiencing high inflation. Boeing’s Commercial Airplanes business depends on maintaining a healthy production system, ensuring every aircraft meets exacting specifications, achieving production targets, successfully developing and certifying new or derivative aircraft, and meeting stringent performance and reliability standards. The business is highly complex, involving extensive coordination with U.S. and non-U.S. suppliers, skilled labor, and evolving regulatory requirements. The FAA has implemented safety reforms, including the 2018 FAA Reauthorization Act and the 2020 Aircraft Certification, Safety and Accountability Act (ACSAA). Section 116 of ACSAA prohibited the FAA from issuing a type certificate to aircraft after December 27, 2022, unless the aircraft’s flight crew alerting system met certain specifications. The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 amended Section 116, so applications for original or amended type certifications submitted before December 27, 2020—including those for the 737-7 and 737-10—are no longer subject to the crew alerting requirements. Beginning one year after the FAA issues a type certificate for the 737-10, any new 737 MAX aircraft must include certain safety enhancements to receive an original airworthiness certification, which are included in Boeing’s 737-10 certification application and will be evaluated by the FAA. Beginning three years after the issuance of a type certificate for the 737-10, all previously delivered 737 MAX aircraft must be retrofitted with these safety enhancements, and as the holder of the type certificate, Boeing is responsible for any associated retrofit costs. The company has provisioned for these estimated costs and does not expect them to be material. Delays in certification or incorporating safety enhancements could negatively impact future revenues, cash flows, and results of operations. Comparable agencies in other countries may adopt similar regulations, and if the FAA or similar foreign agencies implement more stringent rules, Boeing may incur additional compliance costs. The introduction of new programs or derivatives, such as the 777X, 737-7, and 737-10, involves increased risks related to meeting development, testing, certification, and production schedules. Boeing has experienced production quality issues, including in the supply chain, which contributed to reduced 787 deliveries, including a suspension from May 2021 to August 2022. The company continues inspections and rework on stored 787 aircraft. Some customers have contractual rights to compensation for late deliveries or to reject individual aircraft. Delays on the 737, 777X, and 787 programs have led to, and may continue to lead to, customer rights to terminate orders, receive compensation, or substitute orders with other Boeing aircraft. Boeing must minimize production disruptions, achieve operational stability, and implement productivity improvements to meet customer demand and maintain profitability. The company has announced plans to adjust production rates on several programs. The 787 program is currently producing at low rates and is expected to gradually increase to 5 per month in 2023. 777X production is currently paused and expected to resume in 2023. The 737 program has stabilized at 31 per month due to operational and supply chain challenges, with plans to gradually increase production based on market demand and supply chain capacity. Boeing and its suppliers must successfully adapt to these changing priorities or face adverse impacts on revenues and market share. Boeing is committed to leading the commercial aviation industry by offering airplanes and services that deliver superior design, safety, efficiency, and value to customers worldwide. Its Business Commercial Airplanes (BCA) segment focuses on meeting market demands by improving efficiency and quality to provide a fair return for shareholders. Boeing Defense, Space & Security (BDS) integrates its resources in defense, intelligence, communications, security, space, and services to deliver capability-driven solutions at reduced costs, with a strategy to leverage core businesses to capture key next-generation programs and expand in adjacent and international markets, emphasizing growth and productivity. BGS provides innovative, comprehensive, and cost-competitive product and service solutions for both commercial and defense sectors. Boeing Capital (BCC) facilitates, arranges, structures, and provides selective financing solutions for Boeing customers. Domestic travel continues to recover from the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, with the narrow-body market following this recovery, while the wide-body market remains paced by international travel recovery. Travel demand for airline customers in North and South America, the Middle East, and Europe is strong, and demand for dedicated freighters remains robust due to a strong recovery in global trade. Supply chain disruptions persist due to the lingering impacts of the pandemic, global constraints, and labor instability, along with inflationary pressures, which have reduced productivity and negatively affected financial performance, results of operations, and cash flows. Airline financial performance has been adversely impacted by the pandemic, with the International Air Transport Association (IATA) reporting net losses of $138 billion in 2020, $42 billion in 2021, and forecasting $6.9 billion in losses for 2022, with $9.9 billion in North America profits offset by losses elsewhere; IATA forecasts $4.6 billion in global profits for 2023. Despite a positive long-term outlook driven by economic growth, increased trade, globalization, and improved airline services, the industry remains vulnerable to fuel price spikes, credit shocks, terrorism, natural disasters, conflicts, epidemics, pandemics, and environmental regulations. The long-term global economic growth projection of 2.6% per year supports a forecast of approximately 41,170 new airplanes needed over the next 20 years, with a 3.8% annual growth rate in passenger and cargo traffic. The company assesses the recoverability of deferred tax assets quarterly, using a more-likely-than-not threshold of over 50%, and due to a recent history of financial losses, future projected earnings are not included in the analysis. Instead, systematic and logical methods are used to estimate when deferred tax liabilities and assets will reverse, involving significant management judgment and subjectivity. The company believes its methodologies are reasonable and consistent.

The specific years in which temporary differences lead to taxable or deductible amounts are determined by the timing of the recovery of related assets or the settlement of related liabilities. On a quarterly basis, the company evaluates the likelihood of recovering its deferred tax assets from future taxable income and reduces the carrying amounts of these assets by recording a valuation allowance if, based on available evidence, it is more likely than not (defined as a likelihood exceeding 50%) that all or part of the assets will not be realized. This assessment considers both positive and negative evidence, with a recent history of financial reporting losses serving as a heavily weighted source of objectively verifiable negative evidence. Due to this recent history of losses, the company does not include future projected earnings in its analysis. Instead, it uses systematic and logical methods to estimate when deferred tax liabilities will reverse and generate taxable income and when deferred tax assets will reverse and generate tax deductions. The selection of methodologies and the determination of when temporary differences will result in taxable or deductible amounts involve significant management judgment and are inherently complex and subjective. The company believes its methodologies are reasonable and can be consistently applied in future periods. Deferred tax liabilities are assumed to generate taxable amounts primarily within the next five years, while deferred tax assets related to pension and other postretirement benefits are assumed to generate significant deductible amounts beyond five years. The company’s valuation allowance of $3,162 million at December 31, 2022, primarily relates to pension and other postretirement benefit obligation deferred tax assets, tax credits, and other carryforwards that are expected to reverse beyond the period when deferred tax liabilities are expected to reverse. During 2022, the company increased its valuation allowance by $739 million mainly due to tax credits and other carryforwards generated in 2022 that could not be realized in that year, partially offset by favorable pension remeasurement. Until the company achieves sustained profitability, additional valuation allowances may be required, which would have adverse effects on earnings and/or other comprehensive income.
