The accounting policies include principles of consolidation, use of estimates, operating cycle, revenue and cost recognition, and treatment of long-term contracts, commercial spare parts, service contracts, and concession sharing arrangements. For commercial aircraft contracts, revenue is recognized upon completion and acceptance, with transaction prices allocated based on relative standalone selling prices adjusted by an escalation formula. For long-term contracts, revenue is recognized over time as work progresses, with adjustments for changes in estimated revenues and costs using cumulative catch-up adjustments. Significant adjustments in 2022 included losses on VC-25B, KC-46A Tanker, MQ-25, Commercial Crew, and T-7A Red Hawk programs. Payments under long-term contracts may occur before or after revenue recognition, and unbilled receivables or advances and progress billings are not considered significant financing components. Financial services revenue is recorded in Sales of services on the Consolidated Statements of Operations. See Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements on pages 59–114.

The transfer of control to the customer is determined based on the method that best reflects the type of service performed, and cost of sales is recorded as incurred. Sales concessions to customers are recognized as a reduction of the transaction price and the related revenue from performance obligations; reimbursements from suppliers under concession sharing arrangements are recorded as a reduction in Cost of products. Unbilled receivables (contract assets) arise when revenue is recognized for amounts not yet billable under customer contracts, while advances and progress billings (contract liabilities) occur when payments are received before revenue recognition; these amounts are determined for each contract. Financial services revenue from sales-type/finance leases, operating leases, and loans is recorded in Sales of services. For sales-type leases, selling profit or loss is recognized at lease inception if collection of lease payments is probable; customer financing receivables are recorded at lease inception for sales-type and direct finance leases, calculated as the sum of future minimum lease payments, estimated residual value of leased equipment, and deferred incremental direct costs less unearned income, and income is recognized over the lease term to approximate a level rate of return on net investment. For notes receivable, customer financing receivables are recorded net of unamortized discounts and deferred incremental direct costs, with interest income and discount amortization recognized ratably over the note term. Income recognition for customer financing receivables is suspended if uncollectible, determined when it is probable that amounts due under contractual terms will not be collected; a receivable is considered past due when cash is not received by the due date. Collectability is evaluated at inception and on a recurring basis; if uncollectible, the customer is placed in non-accrual status. For sales-type leases with customers in non-accrual status at inception or after commencement, revenue is deferred until substantially all cash is received or the customer is removed from non-accrual status. For direct finance leases or notes receivable with customers in non-accrual status, contractual interest income is recognized as payments are received, provided there is sufficient collateral and payments exceed past due principal. Residual values, reviewed periodically, represent the estimated amount to be received at lease termination from the disposition of leased equipment; declines deemed other-than-temporary are recognized in the period they occur. Operating lease revenue for aircraft and equipment is recorded on a straight-line basis over the lease term; operating lease assets are recorded at cost and depreciated to estimated residual value using the straight-line method over the projected holding period, with periodic reviews adjusting depreciation for changes in residual value estimates. Assets held for sale are recorded at the lower of carrying value or fair value less costs to sell. Impairment is evaluated for operating lease assets when events or changes indicate expected undiscounted cash flows may be less than carrying value; impairment expense is the excess of carrying value over fair value. Early issue sales consideration paid or credited to airline customers is recognized as a reduction to revenue upon delivery; if the customer does not take delivery, recovery is believed possible; if early issue sales consideration exceeds advances and is not otherwise recoverable, it is written off in the current period. Property, plant, and equipment are recorded at cost, including construction-period interest, less accumulated depreciation, with useful lives of 10 to 40 years for new buildings and land improvements and 4 to 20 years for machinery and equipment; depreciation methods are 150% declining balance for buildings and land improvements and sum-of-the-years’ digits for machinery and equipment. Leases are determined at inception for arrangements where the company is the lessee; operating lease assets are included in Other assets, with liabilities in Accrued liabilities and Other long-term liabilities; finance lease assets (primarily computer equipment) are included in Property, plant and equipment, net, with liabilities in Short-term debt, current portion of long-term debt, and Long-term debt. Operating lease assets represent the right to use an underlying asset for the lease term, and lease liabilities represent the obligation to make lease payments; both are recognized at lease commencement based on the estimated present value of lease payments over the term, using the company’s estimated incremental borrowing rate; variable lease components such as fair market value adjustments, utilities, and maintenance are expensed as incurred and not included in present value calculations. Lease terms include options to extend or terminate, which are included if it is reasonably certain the option will be exercised. Lease expense for operating leases is recognized on a straight-line basis over the lease term. Real property lease agreements with lease and non-lease components are accounted for as a single lease component. Asset retirement obligations are recorded for known obligations where fair value can be reasonably estimated, including asbestos removal, decommissioning, and lease restoration; recorded amounts are not material. Known conditional asset retirement obligations, such as future asbestos remediation or decommissioning with insufficient information on timing or method, are not recorded due to inability to make a reasonable estimate; a liability will be recorded when sufficient information becomes available to make a reasonable estimate. Additionally, undiscovered conditional obligations (e.g., asbestos in buildings not yet identified) are not included in the financial statements. Goodwill and other acquired intangibles with indefinite lives are not amortized but are tested for impairment annually on April 1 and when events or circumstances indicate impairment may exist. Impairment testing begins with a qualitative assessment; if it is more likely than not that the carrying value of net assets exceeds the fair value of related operations, a quantitative test is performed; otherwise, no further testing is required. For operations using a quantitative test, the carrying value of net assets is compared to the estimated fair value of the related operations; if fair value is less than carrying value, impairment is recognized.

A liability is recognized when sufficient information about the timing and method of settlement becomes available to make a reasonable estimate of its fair value. Additionally, there may be conditional asset retirement obligations that have not yet been discovered—such as asbestos in certain buildings—therefore these obligations are not included in the Consolidated Financial Statements. Goodwill and other acquired intangible assets with indefinite lives are not amortized but are tested for impairment annually on April 1 or when an event occurs or circumstances change indicating it is more likely than not that impairment may exist. A qualitative assessment is performed first; if it indicates the carrying value of net assets exceeds the fair value of the related operations, a quantitative test follows. In the quantitative test, the carrying value of net assets is compared to the estimated fair value of the related operations; if fair value is less than carrying value, the shortfall up to the goodwill carrying value represents the impairment. Indefinite-lived intangibles include a brand and trade name and in-process research and development (IPR&D) acquired in business combinations. IPR&D is initially capitalized at fair value with an indefinite life and tested for impairment thereafter. When a project is completed, IPR&D is reclassified to finite-lived acquired intangible assets and amortized on a straight-line basis over its estimated useful life. These intangibles are tested for impairment by comparing carrying values to current projections of discounted cash flows; any excess carrying value over discounted cash flows represents impairment. Finite-lived acquired intangible assets are amortized on a straight-line basis over their estimated useful lives: developed technology (4 to 14 years), product know-how (6 to 30 years), customer base (3 to 17 years), distribution rights (3 to 27 years), and other (1 to 32 years). These assets are evaluated for impairment whenever events or changes in circumstances suggest the carrying amount may not be recoverable. If the carrying value exceeds undiscounted future cash flows, the impairment is the difference between the carrying amount and the fair value. Time deposits are held-to-maturity investments carried at cost. Available-for-sale debt securities include commercial paper, U.S. government agency securities, and corporate debt securities, recorded at fair value with unrealized gains and losses, net of tax, recorded in accumulated other comprehensive income. Realized gains and losses are recognized using the specific identification method. These securities are assessed for impairment quarterly. The equity method is used for investments where significant influence (20% to 50% ownership) is exercised but control is not. The cumulative earnings approach is used for cash flow classification of distributions from equity method investments. Other equity investments are recorded at fair value, with gains and losses in net earnings; those without readily determinable fair value are measured at cost less impairments plus or minus observable price changes and are assessed for impairment quarterly. Investment income and loss are classified on the Consolidated Statements of Operations as operating or non-operating. Operating investments, which are strategically aligned and integrated with operations, include earnings from equity method investments, dividend income from other equity investments, and impairments or gains/losses on disposition, recorded in (Loss)/Income from operating investments, net. Non-operating investments, held for non-strategic purposes, include interest and dividends on marketable securities and impairments or gains/losses on disposition, recorded in Other income, net. All derivative instruments are recognized in the financial statements and measured at fair value regardless of purpose. Derivatives are used primarily to manage market risks. For cash flow hedges, the derivative’s gain or loss is initially reported in comprehensive income and later reclassified into earnings when the hedged forecasted transaction affects earnings. Agreements to purchase and sell aluminum are used to meet long-term strategic sourcing and non-U.S. business needs. These aluminum agreements and other derivative instruments are derivatives for accounting purposes but are not designated as hedges. Changes in their fair value are recorded in earnings immediately. Allowances for credit losses are established for accounts receivable, unbilled receivables, customer financing receivables, and certain other financial assets. These allowances are assessed quarterly, considering customer credit ratings, bankruptcy filings, credit default rates, age of receivables, expected loss rates, and collateral exposures. Collateral exposure is the excess of carrying value over fair value of related collateral. Internal credit ratings are assigned based on publicly available and direct customer information, comparable to major credit rating agencies. Customer financing receivables are collateralized by the related asset; fair value of aircraft collateral is determined using median values from multiple third-party aircraft value publications based on type and age, with judgment applied when aircraft features or use differ significantly. Agreements with certain customers allow the company to look beyond specific collateral in case of default; if proceeds from sale of the underlying asset are insufficient to cover the receivable (a shortfall), the company may sell or retain other customer-owned assets and use proceeds to cover the shortfall. In connection with the sale of new commercial aircraft (Sale Aircraft), trade-in commitments are entered into with certain customers, giving them the right to trade in used aircraft at a specified price. Exposure may arise from (1) adjustments to revenue for the difference between the contractual trade-in price and the fair value of the trade-in aircraft at the date of the agreement, recognized upon delivery of the Sale Aircraft, and/or (2) charges to cost of products for adverse changes in the fair value of trade-in aircraft after the agreement is signed but before purchase. Fair value of trade-in aircraft is determined using model, age, condition, market conditions, and multiple valuation sources, with assessments beginning years before return. Markets include resale (with possible long-term storage costs), leasing (with potential refurbishment costs), or scrap. Valuation varies based on the most likely market. Valuation is updated quarterly based on actual market activities or third-party valuations adjusted for individual attributes and conditions. Warranties are provided with certain product sales, primarily by the BCA segment. Aircraft sales typically include a 3 to 4-year standard warranty covering systems, accessories, equipment, parts, and software, included in the program’s estimate at completion. Occasionally, commitments beyond standard warranties are made to address fleet-wide major issues, resulting in additional accrued warranty expenses. Warranties from the BDS segment relate to military aircraft and weapons systems, with a six-month to two-year warranty period covering similar items, and estimated costs recorded in the period of product delivery. The warranty liability at each balance sheet date reflects the estimated number of months of warranty coverage outstanding times the average of historical monthly payments, plus additional amounts for major warranty issues exceeding normal claims levels. Estimated costs for these additional issues are considered changes to the initial liability estimate. Performance guarantees to commercial aircraft customers, including compensation for failure to meet specified performance targets, are accounted for as warranties. The estimated liability is based on known and anticipated operational characteristics and forecasted customer operation relative to performance targets and anticipated settlements when remedies are not specified. These liabilities are recorded as a reduction of revenue at delivery. Agreements require certain suppliers to compensate the company for amounts paid to customers when supplied equipment fails to meet performance targets. Claims against suppliers are included in Inventories and recorded as a reduction in Cost of products at delivery. These performance warranties and supplier claims are included in the programs’ estimate at completion. Supplier penalties are accrued when an event makes it probable that a penalty will be incurred and the amount is reasonably estimable. At the inception of a guarantee, a liability is recorded in Accrued liabilities for the fair value of the guarantee. For credit guarantees, the liability equals the present value of expected loss, calculated by multiplying the creditor’s default rate by the guarantee amount reduced by expected recovery, if applicable. A liability for expected contingent loss is recognized at inception and adjusted each quarter. The independent registered public accounting firm opined that the financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, the financial position and results of operations of The Boeing Company as of December 31, 2022 and 2021, and for the three years ended December 31, 2022, in accordance with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles. The audit also included an unqualified opinion on internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2022. Critical audit matters included cost estimates for fixed-price development contracts such as KC-46A Tanker, Commercial Crew, VC-25B Presidential Aircraft, T-7A Redhawk, and MQ-25, which involved estimating future costs and margins with significant variability due to supply chain disruptions, labor shortages, and inflation, requiring extensive audit effort and specialized judgment. The audit procedures included evaluating management’s methods, assumptions, and ranges of outcomes, inquiring of project managers and engineers, observing project sites, testing data accuracy, and performing retrospective reviews. Another critical audit matter was program accounting estimates for the 777X program, involving estimating sales and costs for the initial program quantity and unsold units, with uncertainty due to market demand and certification challenges, including potential delays and increased costs. Audit procedures included inquiring of sales and pricing personnel, comparing management’s demand estimates to external sources, evaluating historical performance, and assessing assumptions and internal controls. A third critical audit matter was program accounting revenue estimates for the 787 program, where production quality issues and supply chain disruptions increased risk to forecasted revenue due to difficulty in assessing customer consideration for delivery delays.

Production quality issues and supply chain disruptions in the 787 program have increased the risk associated with forecasted revenue estimates, primarily due to difficulties in assessing the value of consideration expected to be provided to customers as a result of delivery delays. The Company uses program accounting to calculate cost of sales and margins for each commercial airplane sold, which requires estimating the revenue expected to be earned upon delivery of aircraft included in the program’s accounting quantity. Although the 787 program resumed deliveries in 2022, the forecasted delivery schedule and the value of consideration for delivery delays remain key factors affecting estimated revenue. Estimation uncertainty arises for aircraft that have reached or are expected to reach a delivery delay period, which grants customers a contractual termination right, and changes to the delivery schedule could result in additional consideration to customers, potentially leading to lower margins or material reach-forward losses. Auditing the estimated revenues for the 787 program involved extensive audit effort, a high degree of auditor judgment, and required professionals with specialized industry experience. The audit procedures included inquiring of management, including operational and supply chain leadership, about assumptions related to supply chain disruption impacts on the delivery schedule and rework completion timelines; evaluating the appropriateness and consistency of management’s methods for developing delivery schedule assumptions, including the impact of production quality issues and supply chain disruptions; inquiring of sales and pricing personnel about the status of current customer contracts and estimated customer consideration; evaluating the consistency of management’s methods and the appropriateness of significant assumptions used in developing revenue estimates for aircraft with or expected to have delivery delays; and testing the effectiveness of internal controls over the review of significant judgments, assumptions, key data, and mathematical extrapolation used in developing key estimates. Deloitte & Touche LLP, the Company’s auditor since at least 1934 (though an earlier year cannot be reliably determined), has issued an unqualified opinion on the consolidated financial statements for the year ended December 31, 2022, and concluded that the Company maintained effective internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2022, based on the Internal Control – Integrated Framework (2013) issued by the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission. The Company’s management evaluated its disclosure controls and procedures as of December 31, 2022, and concluded they were effective to ensure timely recording, processing, summarization, and reporting of required disclosures. Management also concluded that internal control over financial reporting was effective as of December 31, 2022, and this assessment was audited by Deloitte & Touche LLP. There were no changes in internal controls over financial reporting during the fourth quarter of 2022 that materially affected or are reasonably likely to materially affect such controls.

The Boeing Company Executive Supplemental Savings Plan, as amended and restated on December 21, 2022 and effective January 1, 2022, consists of four components: (i) Extra Deferrals, allowing eligible employees to defer payments of their base salaries and eligible incentive compensation awards; (ii) the Restoration Benefit, designed to restore qualified plan benefits from The Boeing Company 401(k) Retirement Plan (formerly known as the Voluntary Investment Plan) to the extent such benefits are limited by Code sections 415 and 401(a)(17); (iii) Executive Benefit, which includes Company Non-Elective Contributions, DC SERP Contributions, and historic Executive SSP+ Company Contributions; and (iv) DCP Accounts, established for participants in the Deferred Compensation Plan for Employees of The Boeing Company, which was frozen as of December 31, 2018 and merged into this Plan effective January 1, 2022. The Plan was originally established on January 1, 1978, and has been amended and restated over time, including on January 1, 2008 to comply with Code section 409A. As of January 1, 2022, the Plan was amended and restated to (A) reflect the merger of the Deferred Compensation Plan with the Plan, (B) eliminate Restoration SSP+ Company Contributions and Executive SSP+ Company Contributions, (C) add new Restoration True-Up Contributions, Incentive Matching Contributions, and Company Non-Elective Contributions, (D) simplify mid-year enrollment provisions in the Participant Deferral component, and (E) make other changes. Effective January 1, 2022, the Plan was further amended to incorporate Amendments 1 and 2 to the December 10, 2021 restatement, reflect the March enrollment window for Cash Incentive Deferrals, and clarify or update certain definitions and administrative aspects. The Plan is a nonqualified deferred compensation plan subject to Code section 409A and is intended to be, in part, an excess benefit plan under ERISA section 3(36) to the extent benefits exceed Code section 415 limits; if not an excess benefit plan, it is intended to be an unfunded plan providing deferred compensation to a select group of management or highly compensated employees under ERISA sections 201(2), 301(a)(3), and 401(a)(1). The Plan defines an "Account" as a recordkeeping account for each Participant, consisting of sub-accounts: (a) the Restoration Account (including Restoration Deferrals, Matching Contributions, True-Up Contributions, and prior Restoration SSP+ Company Contributions), (b) the Extra Deferral Account (including Extra Deferrals, Cash Incentive Deferrals, Incentive Matching Contributions, and Vested Performance Award Deferrals), (c) the Executive Benefit Account (including Company Non-Elective Contributions, DC SERP Contributions, and prior Executive SSP+ Company Contributions), and (d) the DCP Account (including DCP Deferrals and DCP Match prior to January 1, 2019). The "Administrator" is the Employee Benefit Plans Committee of The Boeing Company. An "Affiliate" or "Subsidiary" is a member of a controlled group of corporations (under Code section 1563(a), excluding subsections (a)(4) and (e)(3)(c)), a group of trades or businesses under common control (under Code section 414(c)), or an affiliated service group (under Code sections 414(m) or 414(o)), in which The Boeing Company is a part. An "Authorized Period of Absence" is a leave of absence approved by the Company. "Base Pay" refers to an employee’s base salary from the Company, equivalent to "Compensation" as defined in the Boeing 401(k), but without regard to Code section 401(a)(17) limitations or deferrals under this Plan, and does not include amounts earned under a union collective bargaining agreement without participation in the Plan or payments under incentive compensation or performance awards. "Base Pay Deferrals" are deferrals of Base Pay under Section 3.1(A). "Base Pay Rate" is an employee’s annual Base Pay rate. A "Beneficiary" is the person or persons designated by a Participant to receive distributions upon death, following the Administrator’s rules; if no effective designation exists, the Boeing 401(k) beneficiary designation applies; if no designation exists or the beneficiary does not survive, the Boeing 401(k) default beneficiary rules apply. A Beneficiary may disclaim benefits per Administrator rules, and if disclaimed, the designation is treated as ineffective. "Board of Directors" refers to the board of directors of The Boeing Company. "Boeing 401(k)" is the Boeing Company 401(k) Retirement Plan as amended. "BSS Plan" is the BSS Retirement Plan as amended. "Cash Incentive" refers to amounts awarded under the Boeing Company Elected Officer Annual Incentive Plan or Annual Incentive Plan (formerly the Incentive Compensation Plan for Employees of The Boeing Company and Subsidiaries). Cash Incentives deferred under Article III are deemed paid for purposes of calculating Company Non-Elective Contributions under Article IV. Cash Incentives paid after termination of employment from the Controlled Group remain subject to the Participant’s deferral election under Article III if they have become irrevocable under Section 3.3(c) at termination.

The Plan provides Eligible Employees with two methods to defer Compensation on a pre-tax basis: the Extra Deferral component and the Restoration Deferral component. Only Eligible Employees may participate. Elections for a full Plan Year are generally made during the applicable annual Election Period. For the Extra Deferral component, an individual is an Eligible Employee if they are an Employee paid on a U.S. dollar-based payroll as of the Eligibility Determination Date. An Eligible Employee may elect to defer up to 50% of their Base Pay payable in the Plan Year, 100% of their Cash Incentive earned in the Plan Year (even if payable in a subsequent Plan Year), or 100% of their Vested Performance Awards granted in the Plan Year (which generally covers the next three Plan Years, even if payable later), without regard to Code section 401(a)(17) or 415(c) limitations. These Extra Deferrals are credited to the Participant’s Account on the date Compensation would otherwise be payable or as soon thereafter as administratively feasible. For the Restoration Deferral component, an Eligible Employee may elect a deferral percentage up to the maximum percentage of their Base Pay they can contribute on a pre-tax, after-tax, or Roth basis under the Boeing 401(k). Restoration Deferrals are made from Base Pay only after either (1) Base Pay for the Plan Year reaches the Code section 401(a)(17) limitation as indexed, or (2) the Participant’s annual additions under the Boeing 401(k) reach the Code section 415(c) dollar limitation as indexed. These Restoration Deferrals are also credited to the Account on the date Compensation would otherwise be payable or as soon thereafter as administratively feasible. Mid-year participation is permitted for Newly Eligible Employees, allowing them to elect Extra Deferrals up to 50% of Base Pay earned and payable in each full regular pay period after the end of the Election Period for the remainder of the Plan Year, Restoration Deferrals (if criteria are met), and the form and timing of distribution, as permitted by Section 6.1, during the mid-year Election Period. Mid-year elections cannot be made for Cash Incentive Deferrals or Vested Performance Award Deferrals. In a mid-year Restoration Deferral election, an Eligible Employee may defer up to the maximum percentage of Base Pay they can contribute under the Boeing 401(k) for each full regular pay period after the Election Period, subject to the same 401(a)(17) and 415(c) limitations. A Newly Eligible individual means one who (i) is hired or rehired as an Employee, (ii) was not eligible to participate in the Plan or in a deferred compensation plan aggregated with the Plan under Code section 409A (including The Boeing Company Supplemental Savings Plan), other than the crediting of earnings, within the 24-month period immediately preceding the Eligibility Determination Date (or has taken a full distribution of his or her interest in such plan), and (iii) is paid on a U.S. dollar-based payroll as of the Eligibility Determination Date. A Participant means an Eligible Employee who has elected to defer Compensation or who is eligible to receive a Company Contribution hereunder, or for purposes of Articles V through X, an Employee or former Employee who has amounts credited to his or her Account. Participant Deferrals mean Extra Deferrals and Restoration Deferrals. Performance Awards mean any award designated as such under The Boeing Company’s 2003 Incentive Stock Plan and any successor or other long-term equity incentive plan maintained by The Boeing Company from time to time. The Plan means The Boeing Company Executive Supplemental Savings Plan as herein set forth, together with any amendments adopted from time to time. A Separation from Service means an Employee’s death, retirement, or termination of employment from the Controlled Group within the meaning of Code section 409A. For purposes of determining whether a Separation from Service has occurred, Affiliates and Subsidiaries are defined using the language “at least 80 percent” under Code section 1563(a) instead of the 50 percent default rule in Treasury Regulation section 1.409A-1(h)(3). A Separation from Service is deemed to include a reasonably anticipated permanent reduction in the level of services performed by an Employee to less than 50 percent of the average level of services performed during the immediately preceding 36-month period. Service means the Participant’s years of service with the Controlled Group, determined in the same manner as under the Boeing Service Awards Program procedure, in completed whole years. A Specified Employee means an Employee who is a “specified employee” within the meaning of Code section 409A. Specified Employee status is determined on the last day of the prior Plan Year and takes effect as of April 1 of the Plan Year for a 12-month period. Notwithstanding the foregoing, Specified Employees are determined by including the employees who are reasonably determined to be the 75 top-paid officers of the Controlled Group as of the determination date, rather than the 50 top-paid officers as provided under Code section 416(i)(1)(A), to the extent permitted under Code section 409A. An Unforeseeable Emergency means “unforeseeable emergency” within the meaning of Code section 409A, as determined by the Administrator. The US Executive Payroll means the executive designation of level EL, EV, or ED at the Company (prior to August 15, 2022, the executive designation of level E-1 to E-5 at the Company). The US Executive Payroll was previously called the “E-Series Payroll.” Vested Performance Award Deferrals mean deferrals of Performance Awards under Section 3.1(A).

An Eligible Employee may elect to defer a percentage of their eligible Compensation for a Plan Year (or a portion of a Plan Year in the case of mid-year enrollment) on a pre-tax basis by submitting one or more timely Deferral Elections in accordance with Section 3.3. The types and amounts of Compensation that may be deferred are outlined in Section 3.1 for annual deferrals and Section 3.2 for mid-year deferrals. If an Eligible Employee had an active Restoration Deferral Election under this Plan immediately prior to its amendment and restatement as of January 1, 2019 and does not timely change it for the Plan Year beginning January 1, 2019, such election will be deemed continued on an “evergreen basis” for future Plan Years unless changed in accordance with Section 3.3. Similarly, if an Employee had an election to defer compensation under the DCP immediately prior to that plan’s amendment and restatement as of January 1, 2019 and fails to make a timely Extra Deferral Election or affirmatively indicate they do not wish to make one for the Plan Year beginning January 1, 2019, such Employee will be deemed to have made an Extra Deferral Election identical to the prior DCP election, on an “evergreen basis” unless changed. Deferral Elections must be made in accordance with rules established by the Administrator and may include separate Extra Deferral Elections for Base Pay, Cash Incentive, and Performance Awards, and/or a separate Restoration Deferral Election for Base Pay, as described in Section 3.1 or 3.2. Eligible Employees may make new Deferral Elections each succeeding Plan Year, and such elections will be “evergreen” and carry over from one Plan Year to the next (or from a partial Plan Year to the subsequent Plan Year in the case of mid-year enrollment) unless changed or cancelled per Administrator rules or as otherwise provided. Deferral Elections include an option to elect the form and timing of distribution, as described in Article VI, and any such election with respect to Restoration Deferrals applies to the entire Restoration Account. Deferral Elections must be filed during the applicable Election Period; for a full Plan Year, they become irrevocable no later than the date prescribed under Code section 409A, provided the individual is an Eligible Employee on that date. For example, Restoration Deferral and Base Pay Deferral Elections applying to Base Pay earned in 2023 become irrevocable no later than December 31, 2022, and Cash Incentive Deferral Elections applying to Cash Incentive earned in 2023 become irrevocable no later than March 30, 2023. Mid-year Deferral Elections become irrevocable on the last day of the applicable mid-year Election Period. Once irrevocable, Deferral Elections generally cannot be modified for the Plan Year or the Compensation to which they apply. If an Employee ceases to be an Eligible Employee during the Plan Year (e.g., due to reclassification as other than US Executive Payroll or Separation from Service), any irrevocable Deferral Election in effect as of that date remains in effect for the Plan Year and the Compensation to which it applies. If an Employee ceases to be an Eligible Employee prior to the date any Deferral Election would have become irrevocable, such election is cancelled as of that date. A limited exception exists under Section 3.4 for Unforeseeable Emergency, allowing a Participant to cancel a Deferral Election during a Plan Year if they incur such an emergency, as determined by the Administrator. If a Participant has elected and received a distribution due to an Unforeseeable Emergency under Section 6.1(I), they are deemed to have cancelled their Deferral Election(s) for Base Pay for the remainder of the applicable Plan Year. Participant Deferrals are credited to the Participant’s Account on the date the Compensation would otherwise have been payable, or as soon thereafter as administratively feasible. A Participant who defers Base Pay under a Restoration Deferral Election will be credited with a Restoration Matching Contribution equal to a percentage (based on the matching contribution formula under the Boeing 401(k) for the Plan Year) of their Restoration Deferrals for the Plan Year. These contributions apply only to Base Pay deferrals made under a Restoration Deferral Election and not to those made under an Extra Deferral Election. An Eligible Employee must make a timely Restoration Deferral Election to be eligible for Restoration Matching Contributions, and such contributions are credited to the Account on the same date as the underlying Restoration Deferrals. The Company may make a Restoration True-Up Contribution to the Plan for certain Eligible Employees, equal to the true-up matching contribution calculated under the Boeing 401(k) for the Plan Year (with adjustments if contributions to the Boeing 401(k) were stopped due to Code limits, treating the portion prior to the stop as if it were the full Plan Year) minus any true-up matching contribution actually made to the Boeing 401(k), as determined by the Committee in its sole discretion. No Restoration True-Up Contribution will be made if the Employee terminates employment prior to the last business day of the Plan Year for any reason other than retirement (after attaining age 55 with 10 years of service or age 62 with 1 year of service), disability (as determined by the Social Security Administration), layoff, or death. In no event will the Restoration True-Up Contribution, when added to matching contributions to the Boeing 401(k) and any Restoration Matching Contributions, exceed 100% of the first 10% of eligible compensation contributed or credited to the Boeing 401(k) and this Plan. A Restoration True-Up Contribution is made only if the Employee meets the eligibility requirements for a true-up matching contribution in the Boeing 401(k). An Eligible Employee does not need to make a timely Restoration Deferral Election to receive a Restoration True-Up Contribution for a Plan Year. The Restoration True-Up Contribution is credited to the Participant’s Account on the date true-up matching contributions are made to the Boeing 401(k), or as soon thereafter as administratively feasible. A Participant who makes Cash Incentive Deferrals will be credited with an Incentive Matching Contribution equal to a percentage (based on the matching contribution formula under the Boeing 401(k) for the Plan Year) of their Cash Incentive Deferrals for the Plan Year. An Eligible Employee must make a timely Cash Incentive Deferral Election to be eligible for such Incentive Matching Contributions, and these contributions are credited to the Account on the date the underlying Cash Incentive Deferrals are credited. No Incentive Matching Contribution will be made for any Cash Incentive paid (or that would be paid without the deferral election) after the date the Participant terminates from employment. The Company may make Company Non-Elective Contributions to the Plan for certain Eligible Employees in an amount and subject to terms determined by the Compensation Committee or its delegates. For Plan Years beginning January 1, 2022 and January 1, 2023, the Company Non-Elective Contribution includes 2% of the Eligible Employee’s Base Pay and Cash Incentive paid during the Plan Year, provided that (i) such contribution is not made if the Employee terminates prior to the last business day of the Plan Year for any reason other than retirement (after age 55 with 10 years of service or age 62 with 1 year of service), disability (as determined by the Social Security Administration), layoff, or death, and (ii) Cash Incentive paid after termination of employment is not counted in the calculation. For an Eligible Employee promoted to the US Executive Payroll during a Plan Year, the computation of the Company Non-Elective Contribution takes into account any eligible pay (i) paid prior to the promotion and (ii) that would have been used to compute the special 2% non-elective contribution under the Boeing 401(k) if not for the promotion, as per Administrator rules. An Eligible Employee does not need to make deferrals to receive a Company Non-Elective Contribution for a Plan Year. A Company Non-Elective Contribution is credited to the Eligible Employee’s Account on the date the related non-elective contribution is made to the Boeing 401(k) (if any) or on the date otherwise determined by the Compensation Committee or its delegates, or as soon thereafter as administratively feasible. An Employee is eligible to receive DC SERP Contributions for a Plan Year as long as they satisfy either (i) or (ii): (i) hired on or after January 1, 2009, but before January 1, 2020; on the US Executive Payroll in level EL or EV (level E-1, E-2, or E-3 prior to August 15, 2022) as of December 31, 2019; not an elected officer; and ineligible to accrue benefits under any defined benefit plan maintained by the Controlled Group; or (ii) hired before January 1, 2009; on the US Executive Payroll (in any level E-1 through E-5) as of December 31, 2019; and not an elected officer. For purposes of eligibility, “hired” generally refers to the most recent date of hire or rehire with the Company, except as provided. A return to the Controlled Group from an approved leave of absence without termination is not considered a rehire. A transfer of employment among members of the Controlled Group without interruption is not considered a rehire, and the most recent date of hire or rehire is the date with the Company’s controlled group member from which the Employee transferred. A rehire following a layoff generally will not be treated as a rehire if it occurs within six years of the layoff, except if the Employee commences a retirement benefit during that period and later rehires. An individual who became a “group-acquired employee” after September 30, 2008 and before January 1, 2009 will be deemed to have been hired on or after January 1, 2009 for purposes of eligibility for contributions on and after January 1, 2009. No contribution will be paid prior to January 1, 2009. A “group-acquired employee” is defined as an employee of the Company who became such as an immediate or ultimate result of a merger to which the Company was a party or the acquisition by the Company of all or part of another entity.

The Employee’s most recent date of hire or rehire with a Company’s controlled group member from which the Employee transferred is relevant for determining eligibility. A rehire to the Controlled Group following a termination due to layoff is generally not treated as a rehire if it occurs within six years of the layoff event; however, if a laid-off Employee commences a retirement benefit during this six-year period, they will be treated as a rehire if they later rehire to the Controlled Group. An individual who became a “group-acquired employee” after September 30, 2008 and before January 1, 2009 will be deemed to have been hired on or after January 1, 2009 for purposes of determining eligibility to receive a contribution for periods on and after January 1, 2009, and no contribution will be paid prior to that date. A “group-acquired employee” is defined as an employee of the Company who became such as an immediate or ultimate result of a merger to which the Company was a party or of the acquisition by the Company of all or part of the assets, businesses, or capital stock of another corporation or firm. An Eligible Employee will be a Participant in the DC SERP for the period(s), if any, that the Employee satisfies the eligibility conditions in Section 4.5(A). Each Participant eligible for DC SERP Contributions shall be entitled to contributions as described. For payroll contributions, contributions are credited to the Participant’s Account on the date the Base Pay and Cash Incentive otherwise would be payable, or as soon thereafter as administratively feasible. A Participant hired between January 1, 2009 and December 31, 2019 will receive a DC SERP contribution equal to a Contribution Credit times the sum of the Participant’s Base Pay and Cash Incentive for each applicable pay period. The Contribution Credit is 2% for a Participant at level EV (referred to as level E-2 or E-3 prior to August 15, 2022) and 4% for a Participant at level EL (referred to as level E-1 prior to August 15, 2022). If a Participant changes levels during a pay period, the level as in effect on the last day of the pay period applies. For calculating the contribution, Base Pay and Cash Incentive are counted only if (1) the Participant is on the US Executive Payroll during the applicable pay period or (2) the Cash Incentive is paid after termination of employment from the Controlled Group but on or before the Participant receives their final regular paycheck. A Participant hired before January 1, 2009 will receive a DC SERP contribution equal to a Contribution Credit times the sum of Base Pay and Cash Incentive for each applicable pay period, with Base Pay and Cash Incentive counted only if (1) the Participant is on the US Executive Payroll during the applicable pay period or (2) the Cash Incentive is paid after termination of employment from the Controlled Group but on or before the Participant receives their final regular paycheck. The Contribution Credit equals 5%, plus, if applicable, 0.5% times the Participant’s whole years of Benefit Service (as defined under the PVP and/or BSS Plan, as applicable, and determined as of January 1, 2016), subject to a limitation, with the supplemental percentage credited for a period not to exceed seven years. This seven-year period begins on January 1, 2016 (or January 1 of the year the Participant attains age 55, or the date of promotion to the US Executive Payroll, whichever is latest) and is measured cumulatively over the Participant’s lifetime. A one-time contribution is available to an Employee who satisfies the requirements in Section 4.5(A)(i) (hired between January 1, 2009 and December 31, 2019) and is first promoted to a level of EL or EV (from a position at level ED) during the Plan Year (prior to August 15, 2022, first promoted to a level of E-1 through E-3 from a position at level E-4 or E-5 during the Plan Year). The one-time contribution equals 2% times the sum of (1) the Participant’s Base Pay Rate immediately following the promotion and (2) the Cash Incentive target percentage multiplied by the Base Pay Rate, both as in effect immediately following the promotion, multiplied by the Participant’s whole years of Service as of the date of first promotion to a level of EL or EV (from a position at level ED) (prior to August 15, 2022, to a level of E-1 through E-3 from a position at level E-4 or E-5), with years of Service limited to service earned since the most recent hire date. This amount is credited to the Participant’s Account as of the date of first promotion to a level of EL or EV (referred to as level E-1, E-2, or E-3 prior to August 15, 2022), or as soon thereafter as administratively feasible. A Participant who has received a one-time contribution under this Section upon promotion to a level of EL or EV (referred to as level E-1, E-2, or E-3 prior to August 15, 2022) will be ineligible for any further contributions under this subsection (C)(ii). Article V outlines vesting and forfeiture rules applicable to certain benefits under the Plan. A Participant’s interest in their Extra Deferral Account will be 100% vested at all times. A Participant’s interest in their Restoration Account will be 100% vested at all times. A Participant’s interest in their Executive Benefit Account will be 100% vested at all times, subject to Section 5.5 and Section 5.6. A Participant may forfeit any part or all of their legacy Executive SSP+ Company Contribution Account attributable to Executive SSP+ Company Contributions made on and after January 1, 2017, if any of the following occur while employed by the Controlled Group or within five years after termination: (A) conviction of a felony involving theft, fraud, embezzlement, or other similar unlawful acts against the Controlled Group or its interests, including acts detrimental to or in conflict with the Controlled Group’s interests as determined by the Administrator in its sole discretion; (B) engaging in any activity, whether individually or as an employee, consultant, or otherwise, that the Administrator determines in its sole discretion constitutes competition with any significant aspect of the Controlled Group’s business, including representing, providing services to, or being an employee of or associated in a business capacity with any person or entity in competition with the Controlled Group’s business or taking a position adverse to it, in a manner detrimental, prejudicial, or in conflict with the Controlled Group’s interests; (C) inducing or attempting to induce any of the Controlled Group’s employees, representatives, or consultants to terminate, discontinue, or cease working with or for the Controlled Group, or to breach any contract with the Controlled Group, in order to work with or for the Participant or any third party, without the advance approval of The Boeing Company’s Senior Vice President of Human Resources (or successor position); (D) disparaging or making statements about the Controlled Group, its products, or its employees that could be viewed as negative or critical, except for legally protected communications to government agencies or statements made in the course of sworn testimony in administrative, judicial, or arbitral proceedings; (E) using or disclosing proprietary or confidential information, including trade secrets, of the Controlled Group, except for legally protected communications to government agencies or statements made in the course of sworn testimony in administrative, judicial, or arbitral proceedings. If a Participant has already received or commenced payment of such portion of their Executive SSP+ Company Contribution Account, the Administrator may pursue legal and equitable relief to enforce forfeiture and recover the amount distributed. The forfeiture provisions will continue in effect unless and to the extent modified by a court of competent jurisdiction; if any portion is held unenforceable, the provisions shall be deemed amended to limit their scope to the broadest enforceable scope and shall continue in effect. Additionally, the Administrator will require reimbursement of any Executive SSP+ Company Contribution Account attributable to an incentive award that the Controlled Group seeks to recover under the clawback provision of any plan providing Cash Incentive. For DC SERP vesting, no payments shall be made from a Participant’s DC SERP Account except to the extent the Participant is vested. A Participant hired between January 1, 2009 and December 31, 2019 will vest 100% in their DC SERP Account component(s) covered under subsection (A) on the date they satisfy any of the following: (i) being on the US Executive Payroll at a level of EL or EV (referred to as level E-1, E-2, or E-3 prior to August 15, 2022) for 36 consecutive months, with prior periods of employment on the US Executive Payroll at a level of E-1 through E-3 being counted; (ii) dying while an Employee; or (iii) being laid off from a position at level EL or EV (referred to as level E-1, E-2, or E-3 prior to August 15, 2022) and being eligible for benefits under The Boeing Company Executive Layoff Benefits Plan. A Participant hired before January 1, 2009 will vest 100% in their DC SERP Account component covered under subsection (B) on the date they satisfy any of the following: (i) being on the US Executive Payroll for 36 consecutive months, with prior consecutive months before January 1, 2016 being counted for those on the US Executive Payroll as of January 1, 2016; (ii) being fully vested under the PVP and/or BSS Plan, as applicable, and dying while an Employee before their DC SERP Account commences payment; or (iii) being laid off from an US Executive position and being eligible for benefits under The Boeing Company Executive Layoff Benefits Plan. Special vesting rules apply to a Participant hired between January 1, 2009 and December 31, 2019 who has attained either (i) age 55 with 10 years of Service or (ii) age 62 with one year of Service while employed by the Controlled Group. This Participant will be 100% vested in the portion of their DC SERP Account described in Section 4.5(C)(i) (Payroll Contributions) after being on the US Executive Payroll for 36 consecutive months. For the portion described in Section 4.5(C)(ii) (One-Time Contribution), if any, the Participant will vest ratably at a rate of 1/36 for each consecutive month on the US Executive Payroll at a level of EL or EV (referred to as level E-1, E-2, or E-3 prior to August 15, 2022), starting from the date of first promotion to that level, with this pro rata vesting not precluding acceleration under subsections (A)(ii) (death) or (iii) (layoff). An Authorized Period of Absence from the US Executive Payroll will count as a period on the US Executive Payroll, and an Authorized Period of Absence from a position at level EL or EV (referred to as level E-1, E-2, or E-3 prior to August 15, 2022) will count as a period at these levels. If an Employee ceases to be at the applicable level for any reason other than an Authorized Period of Absence and later returns to that level, these non-consecutive periods will not be aggregated for determining whether the 36-consecutive month requirement has been met. For a Participant transferring employment directly from the Controlled Group to ULA or USA, uninterrupted service at ULA or USA as an executive in a position at a comparable level will be credited toward the 36 consecutive months requirement, provided the transfer is from the US Executive Payroll (or a position at level EL or EV, if applicable) at the Controlled Group to comparable executive status at ULA or USA. ULA and USA service will not be credited toward vesting under this Plan for any period following the Participant’s removal from this executive status. For a participant transferring directly from ULA or USA to the Controlled Group, uninterrupted service at ULA or USA as an executive at a position comparable to the US Executive Payroll (or a position at level EL or EV, if applicable) will be considered for vesting purposes.

For purposes of computing vesting, a Participant who transfers directly from the Controlled Group to ULA or USA will have uninterrupted service at ULA or USA as an executive in a comparable position credited toward the 36 consecutive months requirement, provided the transfer is from the US Executive Payroll (or a position at level EL or EV, referred to as level E-1, E-2, or E-3 prior to August 15, 2022) to comparable executive status at ULA or USA. Service at ULA or USA will not be credited for any period after the Participant’s removal from executive status. Similarly, a Participant transferring directly from ULA or USA to the Controlled Group will have uninterrupted service at ULA or USA as an executive in a comparable position credited toward the 36 consecutive months requirement, provided the transfer is from executive status at ULA or USA to a comparable position at the Controlled Group. Service at ULA or USA will not be credited for any period prior to the Participant’s attainment of executive status at ULA or USA. If a Participant Separates from Service (other than due to an Authorized Period of Absence) or transfers off the US Executive Payroll (or a position at level EL or EV, referred to as level E-1, E-2, or E-3 prior to August 15, 2022) before becoming 100% vested in the payroll contribution portion of their DC SERP Account, they will forfeit all rights to the nonvested portion of the account attributable to the period prior to Separation from Service or transfer. Any benefit that becomes vested during an Authorized Period of Absence that continues after a deemed Separation from Service remains subject to the payment timing rules under Section 6.1. If a Participant stops accruing service toward vesting requirements after becoming partially vested in the one-time contribution portion of the DC SERP Account and later resumes accruing service, the accrued amounts after resumption will not be vested until the Participant satisfies the vesting requirements under subsection (A) or (C) following resumption. Separate vesting requirements apply to each component of a Participant’s DC SERP Account described in Sections 4.4(C)(i)(a), (i)(b), and (ii). A Participant who has accrued more than one component (e.g., due to Separation from Service and subsequent rehire) must satisfy the vesting requirements for each component. If a Participant Separates from Service after becoming 100% vested in a particular DC SERP Account component, they will be fully vested in any additional accruals under the same component following rehire or return, even if they fail to meet the 36 consecutive months requirement after rehire or return. However, they will not be fully vested in amounts accrued under a different component unless the corresponding vesting requirements are satisfied. The Administrator may determine, in its sole discretion, that a Participant forfeits any part or all of their DC SERP Account if: (A) the Participant is convicted of a felony involving theft, fraud, embezzlement, or other similar unlawful acts against the Controlled Group or its interests, including acts detrimental to, prejudicial to, or in conflict with the Controlled Group’s interests as determined by the Administrator; (B) the Participant engages in any activity, directly or indirectly, that the Administrator determines constitutes competition with any significant aspect of Controlled Group business, such as representing, providing services to, or being employed by or associated with a business in competition with the Controlled Group or taking a position adverse to the Controlled Group’s business; (C) the Participant, without advance approval from The Boeing Company’s Senior Vice President of Human Resources (or equivalent), induces or attempts to induce any Controlled Group employee, representative, or consultant to terminate or breach their contract with the Controlled Group to work for the Participant or a third party; (D) the Participant disparages the Controlled Group, its products, or its employees in a manner viewed as negative or critical, except for legally protected communications to government agencies or statements made in sworn testimony in administrative, judicial, or arbitral proceedings; or (E) the Participant uses or discloses proprietary or confidential information, including trade secrets, of the Controlled Group after January 1, 2017, except for legally protected communications to government agencies or statements made in sworn testimony. If a Participant has already received or commenced payment of their DC SERP Account, the Administrator may pursue legal or equitable relief to enforce forfeiture and recover the benefit. These forfeiture provisions continue in effect unless modified by a court of competent jurisdiction, and if any portion is held unenforceable, the provisions are deemed amended to the broadest enforceable scope and continue in effect. Additionally, the Administrator may require forfeiture or reimbursement of any portion of a DC SERP Account attributable to an incentive award if the Controlled Group seeks recovery under a clawback provision of a Cash Incentive plan. A Participant may elect the form and timing of distribution for their Extra Deferral Account, with the election required at the time of the first Extra Deferral Election. If a timely election is not made regarding timing, the Participant is deemed to have elected to receive payment in January of the first Plan Year following Separation from Service (subject to subsection (H)), and if no timely election is made regarding form, the Participant is deemed to have elected a lump sum. A Participant may change a distribution election (or deemed election) for the entire Extra Deferral Account after the initial election, subject to conditions in subsection (F). For the Restoration Account, a distribution election must be made at the time of the first Restoration Deferral Election or during the enrollment period immediately preceding the first year with a Company contribution, and applies to the entire account, including prior Restoration True-Up Contributions and Restoration SSP+ Company Contributions. If a timely election is not made regarding timing, the Participant is deemed to have elected to receive payment in January of the first Plan Year following Separation from Service (subject to subsection (H)), and if no timely election is made regarding form, the Participant is deemed to have elected a lump sum. A Participant may change a distribution election for the entire Restoration Account after the initial election, subject to conditions in subsection (F). For the Executive Benefit Account, no initial distribution election is required; the Participant is deemed to have elected a lump sum payable in January of the first Plan Year following Separation from Service (subject to subsection (H)), and may change this deemed election subject to conditions in subsection (F). The lump sum distribution option is a single payment made in the later of: (i) January of the first Plan Year following Separation from Service, or (ii) January of the first Plan Year following the Participant’s attainment of a specified age (subject to subsection (E)), as elected by the Participant (subject to subsection (H)). The amount equals the value of the Account as of the first business day of January of the Plan Year of payment (or a specified valuation date), with no additional interest or earnings credited thereafter. The installment payment option involves annual payments for a period between 2 and 15 years, beginning in the later of: (i) January of the first Plan Year following Separation from Service, or (ii) January of the first Plan Year following the Participant’s attainment of a specified age (subject to (E)), as elected by the Participant (subject to subsection (H)). Payments continue each January until the full amount is paid. The annual payment amount is calculated by dividing the Account balance as of the first business day of January of the Plan Year of payment (or a specified valuation date) by the number of years remaining in the distribution period, with no additional earnings or interest credited after the valuation date. If a Participant has elected installments and their remaining Account balance is $10,000 or less upon any scheduled payment date (excluding the DCP Account), the entire remaining balance is paid as a final lump sum at that time. A Participant may change a distribution election (or deemed election) for each of the Restoration Account, Executive Benefit Account, Extra Deferral Account, and DCP Account (Deferrals) and DCP Account (Match) only once, provided the new election changes the time of payment (consistent with clause (iii) below) and may change the form of payment (from lump sum to installments or vice versa). Such changes may be made at any time and do not need to occur during an annual enrollment period. If made during the annual enrollment period, the last change on file at the end of the period is irrevocable. If made outside the annual enrollment period or by a Participant who is not an Eligible Employee, the change is irrevocable upon making it. Changes that would defer commencement of any portion of the Restoration Account, Executive Benefit Account, Extra Deferral Account, or DCP Account beyond both age 70½ and Separation from Service are not effective. A new distribution election must be submitted at least 12 months before the existing scheduled distribution date under the applicable subaccount. The revised election must not take effect for at least 12 months after it is made. The new election must provide for an additional deferral period of at least 5 years beyond the original distribution date. Installment payments cannot be changed or revoked once they have begun. All payments are made in January (subject to subsection (H)). Benefits under this Plan begin no later than the first January following the calendar year in which the Participant both attains (or would have attained) age 70½ and is Separated from Service. For Participants actively employed beyond age 70½, benefits begin no later than the first January following the calendar year in which the Participant Separates from Service. Any election to the contrary is not effective. A Specified Employee will not receive any distribution during the six-month period immediately following Separation from Service. The Account of a Specified Employee will be distributed in the form elected (or deemed elected) under subsection (A), (B), or (C), as applicable, and will be made or commence as of the latest of: (1) the time elected (or deemed elected), (2) the month following completion of the six-month waiting period (for Separations from Service between July 1 and December 31), and (3) January of the first Plan Year following Separation from Service (for Separations from Service between January 1 and June 30). If a Participant has elected installments, subsequent payments are made in January of each successive year until the Account is exhausted. For payments occurring other than in January, the amount is based on the value of the Account as of the first business day of the month (or a specified valuation date), with no additional earnings or interest credited after the valuation date. In the event of a Specified Employee’s death during the six-month waiting period, the waiting period ceases, and benefits are distributed in accordance with Section 6.2 (Death Benefits). A Participant or Beneficiary may elect to receive a distribution of all or a portion of their Extra Deferral Account, Restoration Account, or other eligible account due to an unforeseeable emergency.

For Specified Employees who separate from service between July 1 and December 31, distributions will be made in January of the first plan year following separation; for those who separate between January 1 and June 30, distributions will be made in January of the first plan year following separation. Costco Wholesale Corporation and its subsidiaries (Costco or the Company) began operations in 1983 in Seattle, Washington. The Company operates membership warehouses in the United States, Puerto Rico, Canada, the United Kingdom, Mexico, Japan, Korea, Australia, Spain, France, Iceland, China, and through a majority-owned subsidiary in Taiwan. As of August 29, 2021, Costco operated 815 warehouses worldwide, 795 as of August 30, 2020, and 782 as of September 1, 2019. The Company operates e-commerce websites in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, the U.K., Korea, Taiwan, Japan, and Australia. Its common stock trades on the NASDAQ Global Select Market under the symbol “COST.” The Company reports on a 52/53-week fiscal year consisting of thirteen four-week periods, ending on the Sunday nearest the end of August. The first three quarters consist of three periods each, and the fourth quarter consists of four periods (five weeks in a 53-week year). The winter holiday season has a material seasonal impact, with increased net sales and earnings. References to 2021, 2020, and 2019 pertain to the 52-week fiscal years ended August 29, 2021, August 30, 2020, and September 1, 2019, respectively. Costco operates membership warehouses and e-commerce websites based on the concept of offering members low prices on a limited selection of nationally-branded and private-label products across a wide range of categories, resulting in high sales volumes and rapid inventory turnover. This is combined with volume purchasing, efficient distribution, and reduced handling in no-frills, self-service warehouse facilities, enabling profitable operations with significantly lower gross margins than most retailers. The Company generally sells inventory before paying for it, taking advantage of early payment discounts. Most merchandise is purchased directly from manufacturers and routed to cross-docking consolidation points (depots) or directly to warehouses. Depots receive large shipments and quickly ship goods to warehouses, creating freight volume and handling efficiencies that reduce distribution costs. For e-commerce, merchandise is shipped through depots, logistics operations for big and bulky items, and via drop-ship or other supplier delivery arrangements. The average warehouse space is approximately 146,000 square feet, with newer units slightly larger. Floor plans are designed for economy and efficiency in selling space, merchandise handling, and inventory control. Warehouses are not elaborate, as shoppers are primarily attracted by merchandise quality and low prices, and the Company strictly controls entrances and exits, resulting in inventory losses (shrinkage) well below typical retail levels. Warehouses operate on a seven-day, 70-hour week, with gasoline operations having extended hours. Due to shorter operating hours and operational efficiencies, labor costs are lower relative to sales volume. Merchandise is stored on racks above the sales floor and displayed on pallets with large quantities, reducing labor needs. In general, with country variations, warehouses accept certain credit cards, including Costco co-branded cards, debit cards, cash, checks, co-brand cardholder rebates, Executive member 2% reward certificates, and the Company’s proprietary stored-value card (shop card). The Company’s strategy is to provide members with a broad range of high-quality merchandise at prices believed to be consistently lower than elsewhere, limiting most items to fast-selling models, sizes, and colors. It carries less than 4,000 active stock keeping units (SKUs) per warehouse in its core business, significantly fewer than other broadline retailers, and averages between 9,000 and 11,000 SKUs online, some of which are also available in warehouses. Many consumable products are offered only in case, carton, or multiple-pack quantities. In line with member satisfaction, the Company generally accepts returns of merchandise, with a 90-day return policy for electronics and free technical support and extended warranties provided. Additional third-party warranty coverage is available on certain electronic items. Core merchandise categories include Foods and Sundries (including sundries, dry grocery, candy, cooler, freezer, deli, liquor, and tobacco), Non-Foods (including major appliances, electronics, health and beauty aids, hardware, garden and patio, sporting goods, tires, toys and seasonal, office supplies, automotive care, postage, tickets, apparel, small appliances, furniture, domestics, housewares, special order kiosk, and jewelry), and Fresh Foods (including meat, produce, service deli, and bakery). Warehouse ancillary businesses include gasoline, pharmacy, optical, food court, hearing aids, and tire installation, operating primarily within or next to warehouses to encourage more frequent shopping. The number of gas stations varies by country, and there is no gasoline business in Korea or China. At the end of 2021, Costco operated 636 gas stations, with gasoline net sales representing approximately 9% of total net sales in 2021. Other businesses include e-commerce, business centers, travel, and other services. E-commerce net sales represented approximately 7% of total net sales in 2021, excluding other online services such as business delivery, travel, same-day grocery, and other offerings. Business centers offer items tailored for food services, convenience stores, and offices, with walk-in shopping and deliveries, and are included in the total warehouse count. Costco Travel offers vacation packages, hotels, cruises, and other travel products exclusively for members in the U.S., Canada, and the U.K. The Company has direct buying relationships with many brand-name producers and does not rely on any single supplier. The COVID-19 pandemic caused unprecedented supply constraints, including disruptions and delays affecting product availability, and the Company seeks alternative sources when supply is unavailable. It also purchases and manufactures private-label merchandise when quality and member demand are high and the value to members is significant. Net sales increased 18% to $192,052 in 2021, driven by a 16% increase in comparable sales and sales from new warehouses opened in 2020 and 2021. Comparable sales grew 16%, resulting from higher shopping frequency and increased average ticket, with e-commerce comparable sales rising 44% in 2021, including an 80% increase in the first half of the year. Sales in non-foods and warehouse ancillary and other businesses, such as e-commerce and gasoline, were particularly strong. Net sales growth was also influenced by changes in foreign currencies relative to the U.S. dollar, which positively impacted net sales by $2,759 or 169 basis points, and by a 12% increase in the average price per gallon of gasoline, which added $1,636 or 100 basis points, along with a $1,469 or 90 basis point boost from a 10% volume increase in gasoline sales. The total gross margin percentage decreased seven basis points to 11.13%, primarily due to a shift in sales penetration toward warehouse ancillary and other businesses; however, excluding the impact of gasoline price inflation, gross margin percentage improved to 11.22%, up two basis points, driven by better performance in core merchandise categories, especially non-foods, and in warehouse ancillary and other businesses, as well as a three basis point positive impact from a 2020 inventory reserve that was not recorded in 2021. This was partially offset by a two basis point LIFO charge and a 2% increase in rewards. SG&A expenses as a percentage of net sales decreased 40 basis points to 9.61%, mainly due to leveraging increased sales and lower incremental wages related to COVID-19, with warehouse operations and other businesses contributing a 24 basis point reduction, while central operating costs, stock compensation, and acquisition-related costs also declined. Preopening expenses were $76 in 2021, compared to $55 in 2020, with a total of 22 warehouse openings and relocations, including 12 net new in the U.S., 4 in Canada, and 4 in Other International, compared to 16 in 2020. Membership fees increased 9% to $3,877, driven by sign-ups and upgrades to Executive membership, with renewal rates of 91% in the U.S. and Canada and 89% worldwide, and excluding foreign currency impacts, membership fees grew 8%. The effective tax rate was 24.0% in 2021, down from 24.4% in 2020. Net income rose 25% to $5,007, or $11.27 per diluted share, compared to $4,002, or $9.02 per diluted share in 2020. The company paid a special cash dividend of $10.00 per share in December 2020 and April 2021, and increased the quarterly cash dividend from $0.70 to $0.79 per share, totaling $5,748. A critical audit matter identified during the audit was the evaluation of the Company’s workers’ compensation self-insurance liabilities for its U.S. operations, which were estimated at $1,257 million as of August 29, 2021. Description of Business  
Costco Wholesale Corporation (Costco or the Company), a Washington corporation, and its subsidiaries operate membership warehouses based on the concept that offering members low prices on a limited selection of nationally-branded and private-label products in a wide range of merchandise categories will produce high sales volumes and rapid inventory turnover. At August 29, 2021, Costco operated 815 warehouses worldwide: 564 in the United States (U.S.) located in 46 states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico, 105 in Canada, 39 in Mexico, 30 in Japan, 29 in the United Kingdom (U.K.), 16 in Korea, 14 in Taiwan, 12 in Australia, three in Spain, and one each in Iceland, France and China. The Company operates e-commerce websites in the U.S., Canada, U.K., Mexico, Korea, Taiwan, Japan, and Australia.  
Basis of Presentation  
The consolidated financial statements include the accounts of Costco, its wholly-owned subsidiaries, and subsidiaries in which it has a controlling interest. The Company reports noncontrolling interests in consolidated entities as a component of equity separate from the Company’s equity. All material inter-company transactions between and among the Company and its consolidated subsidiaries have been eliminated in consolidation. The Company’s net income excludes income attributable to the noncontrolling interest in Taiwan. Unless otherwise noted, references to net income relate to net income attributable to Costco.  
Fiscal Year End  
The Company operates on a 52/53-week fiscal year basis with the year ending on the Sunday closest to August 31. References to 2021, 2020, and 2019 relate to the 52-week fiscal years ended August 29, 2021, August 30, 2020, and September 1, 2019, respectively.  
Use of Estimates

These estimates and assumptions take into account historical and forward-looking factors that the Company believes are reasonable, including but not limited to the potential impacts arising from the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) and related public and private sector policies and initiatives. Actual results could differ from those estimates and assumptions.

Short-Term Investments  
Short-term investments generally consist of debt securities (U.S. Government and Agency Notes), with maturities at the date of purchase of three months to five years. Investments with maturities beyond five years may be classified, based on the Company’s determination, as short-term based on their highly liquid nature and because they represent the investment of cash that is available for current operations. Short-term investments classified as available-for-sale are recorded at fair value using the specific identification method with the unrealized gains and losses reflected in accumulated other comprehensive income (loss) until realized. Realized gains and losses from the sale of available-for-sale securities, if any, are determined on a specific identification basis and are recorded in interest income and other, net in the consolidated statements of income. These available-for-sale investments have a low level of inherent credit risk given they are issued by the U.S. Government and Agencies. Changes in their fair value are primarily attributable to changes in interest rates and market liquidity. Short-term investments classified as held-to-maturity are financial instruments that the Company has the intent and ability to hold to maturity and are reported net of any related amortization and are not remeasured to fair value on a recurring basis.  
The Company periodically evaluates unrealized losses in its investment securities for credit impairment, using both qualitative and quantitative criteria.
