On December 22, 2017, the U.S. enacted the U.S. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (Tax Act), which reduced the U.S. federal corporate tax rate from 35% to 21%, required a one-time transition tax on certain unrecovered foreign earnings, eliminated U.S. federal income taxes on dividends from foreign subsidiaries, added a GILTI provision allowing foreign tax credits (FTCs) and up to 50% deduction to offset GILTI income, imposed limitations on deductible interest and executive compensation, and increased bonus depreciation. In accordance with Staff Accounting Bulletin No. 118 (SAB 118), a company must complete accounting under ASC 740 within one year of the Tax Act enactment, record a provisional estimate if a reasonable estimate is possible, and apply prior tax law if no estimate is possible. As of December 31, 2017, the Company’s accounting for the Tax Act was incomplete, but it recorded a provisional discrete non-cash net tax benefit of $1.4 billion, including $988 million from the corporate rate reduction and $438 million from a re-assessment of the FTC valuation allowance. The Company did not provide tax expense for the transition tax on unrepatriated earnings of $669 million, as it was fully offset by FTCs. The Company’s accounting for the Tax Act is now complete, with a non-cash income tax expense of $20 million in 2018, adjusting the valuation allowance on FTC carryovers due to guidance on FTC treatment under GILTI, increasing the effective tax rate by 3% for the year ended December 31, 2018. The Company also finalized accounting for indirect costs of employee fringe benefits subject to limitations under the Tax Act, with an immaterial impact on the effective tax rate. The Company has decided to treat future GILTI taxes as current period expenses, so no deferred tax liability is recorded. As of December 31, 2018, the Company has recorded a valuation allowance of $2.4 billion on its FTC carryover of $2.9 billion, resulting in a net deferred tax asset of $481 million. These FTCs are attributable to the Macau Special Gaming Tax, which is 35% of gross gaming revenue in Macau. Because MGM Grand Paradise is exempt from the Macau 12% complementary tax on gaming profits, the Company believes payment of the Macau Special Gaming Tax qualifies as a tax paid in lieu of a creditable U.S. income tax. The gaming industry is highly regulated, and operations require maintaining licenses and paying gaming taxes. Each casino is subject to extensive regulation under the laws, rules, and regulations of its jurisdiction, which generally address the responsibility, financial stability, and character of owners, managers, and persons with financial interest in gaming operations. Violations in one jurisdiction can lead to disciplinary action in others. Additional federal, state, and local laws and regulations apply, including those related to alcoholic beverages, smoking, environmental matters, employment and immigration, currency transactions, taxation, zoning and building codes, land use, marketing and advertising, timeshare, lending, privacy, telemarketing, Office of Foreign Asset Control, Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and anti-money laundering regulations. Changes or new laws could negatively impact business and operating results. In Nevada, casino operations are governed by the Nevada Gaming Control Act and its regulations, overseen by the Nevada Gaming Commission (Nevada Commission), the Nevada Gaming Control Board (Nevada Board), and local licensing agencies (local authorities), collectively known as the Nevada Gaming Authorities. These authorities enforce policies aimed at preventing unsavory individuals from being involved in gaming, ensuring responsible accounting, maintaining financial controls, providing reliable record-keeping, preventing cheating, and generating state and local revenues through taxes and licensing fees. All subsidiaries operating casinos in Nevada (Nevada casino licensees) must be licensed by the Nevada Gaming Authorities and pay periodic fees and taxes; licenses are not transferable. MGM Grand Hotel, LLC, New York-New York Hotel & Casino, LLC, Bellagio, LLC, MGM Resorts Manufacturing Corp., and Aria Resort & Casino, LLC are also licensed as manufacturers and distributors of gaming devices (Nevada manufacturer and distributor licensees). Certain subsidiaries are licensed or found suitable as shareholders, members, or general partners of these licensees. The Nevada registered corporations (including MGM and Mandalay Resort Group) and Mirage Resorts, Incorporated (as an intermediary) must be registered with the Nevada Commission and submit detailed financial and operating reports. No person may become a stockholder or receive profits from Nevada licensed subsidiaries without first registering (for ownership of 5% or less) or obtaining licenses and approvals from the Nevada Gaming Authorities. Local authorities may approve all persons owning or controlling stock in a corporation that controls a gaming licensee. The Nevada registered corporations, Mirage Resorts, Incorporated, and Nevada licensed subsidiaries have obtained necessary registrations, approvals, permits, and licenses. The Nevada Gaming Authorities may investigate individuals with material relationships to or involvement in Nevada registered corporations or licensed subsidiaries to determine suitability or licensing. Officers, directors, and key employees of Nevada licensed subsidiaries must file applications and may be required to be licensed; similarly, key employees of registered corporations involved in gaming activities may be required to be licensed or found suitable. A finding of suitability is equivalent to licensing and requires detailed personal and financial information and a thorough investigation, with the applicant paying all investigation costs. Changes in corporate positions must be reported, and the authorities may disapprove such changes. If an officer, director, or key employee is found unsuitable, the corporation must sever all relationships with that person, and the Nevada Commission may require termination of employment if a person refuses to file applications. Determinations of suitability or licensing are not subject to judicial review. Nevada registered corporations and casino licensees must submit detailed financial and operating reports. Substantially all material loans, leases, sales of securities, and similar financing transactions must be reported or approved by the Nevada Commission. If the Nevada Commission finds a violation of the Nevada Act, it may limit, condition, suspend, or revoke gaming licenses, subject to statutory procedures, and impose substantial fines per violation. A supervisor may be appointed, and earnings during such appointment (except for reasonable rental value) could be forfeited to the State of Nevada. Limitation, conditioning, or suspension of a license, or revocation, would materially adversely affect operations. Any beneficial holder of voting securities, regardless of share amount, may be required to file an application, be investigated, and have their suitability determined if the Nevada Commission believes ownership is inconsistent with state policy. The applicant pays all investigation costs. Any person who acquires more than 5% of a class of voting securities must report it to the Nevada Commission. Beneficial owners of more than 10% must apply for a finding of suitability within 30 days after the Chair of the Nevada Board sends a notice. An institutional investor (defined in the Nevada Act) acquiring between 10% and 25% may apply for a waiver if holding securities solely for investment purposes. Such an investor may own up to 29% for a limited time and maintain the waiver. An institutional investor is deemed to hold securities for investment purposes if acquiring and holding them in the ordinary course of business, not for purposes of influencing board elections, corporate policies, management, operations, or gaming affiliates. Activities not inconsistent with investment intent include voting on shareholder matters, making standard financial inquiries, and such other activities as the Nevada Commission determines appropriate. If a beneficial holder is a corporation, partnership, or trust, it must submit detailed business and financial information, including a list of beneficial owners, and pay all investigation costs. A person who fails or refuses to apply for a finding of suitability or license within 30 days or who refuses to pay investigation costs may be found unsuitable. The same applies to a record owner who fails to identify a beneficial owner. A stockholder found unsuitable and holding beneficial ownership beyond the period prescribed by the Nevada Commission may be guilty of a criminal offense. The company will face disciplinary action if, after receiving notice of unsuitability, it: pays dividends or interest, allows voting rights, pays remuneration, or fails to require the unsuitable person to relinquish voting securities, including through immediate purchase at fair market value. The Nevada Commission may require holders of debt securities of registered corporations to file applications, be investigated, and be found suitable. If a person is found unsuitable, the registered corporation may be sanctioned—including loss of approvals—if it pays dividends, recognizes voting rights, pays remuneration, or makes any payment (principal, redemption, conversion, exchange, liquidation, etc.) without prior approval. A current stock ledger must be maintained in Nevada and may be examined at any time. If securities are held in trust or by a nominee, the record holder must disclose the beneficial owner to the Nevada Gaming Authorities; failure to do so may result in being found unsuitable. The company must assist in identifying the beneficial owner. The Nevada Commission may require stock certificates to bear a legend indicating subjectivity to the Nevada Act, though no such requirement has been imposed to date. Nevada registered corporations may not make public offerings of securities without prior Nevada Commission approval if the securities or proceeds are intended for constructing, acquiring, or financing gaming facilities in Nevada, retiring or extending obligations for such purposes, or similar uses. Approval does not constitute a finding, recommendation, or approval of the prospectus or investment merits. Any contrary representation is unlawful. On July 27, 2017, the Nevada Commission granted prior approval for public offerings for three years, subject to conditions. Changes in control through mergers, consolidations, stock or asset acquisitions, management agreements, or acts resulting in control may not occur without prior Nevada Commission approval. Entities seeking to acquire control must meet stringent standards set by the Nevada Board and Commission, and controlling stockholders, officers, directors, or persons with material relationships may be required to be investigated and licensed. The Nevada legislature has declared that corporate acquisitions opposed by management, repurchases of voting securities, and corporate defensive tactics affecting Nevada gaming licensees or affiliated registered corporations may be injurious to stable corporate gaming. The Nevada Commission has established a regulatory scheme to mitigate adverse effects and promote financial stability, preserve corporate benefits, and ensure neutral, orderly governance. Approvals are required before exceptional repurchases above market price or before a management-opposed acquisition can be consummated. A plan of recapitalization proposed by a board in response to a tender offer to acquire control must receive prior Nevada Commission approval. License fees and taxes, calculated based on gaming type, are payable to the State of Nevada and local authorities, either monthly, quarterly, or annually, and are based on: a percentage of gross revenues, the number of gaming devices operated, or the number of table games operated. The tax on gross revenues is generally 6.75%, and a live entertainment tax is paid on admission charges for facilities offering live entertainment. Nevada manufacturer and distributor licensees also pay certain fees and taxes. Because the company operates outside Nevada, it is required to deposit and maintain a $10,000 revolving fund with the Nevada Board to cover investigation expenses related to foreign gaming operations, with the fund subject to increase or decrease at the Nevada Commission’s discretion. Under the Michigan Gaming Control and Revenue Act (the “Michigan Act”), the owners and operators of casino gaming facilities are subject to extensive state licensing and regulatory requirements. Local regulation by the City of Detroit is permitted under the Michigan Act, provided local ordinances are consistent with the Act and its implementing rules. The company is subject to the Michigan Act through its ownership interest in MGM Grand Detroit, LLC (the “licensed subsidiary”), which operates MGM Grand Detroit, and this ownership is held by its wholly-owned subsidiary, MGM Grand Detroit, Inc. The Michigan Act establishes the Michigan Gaming Control Board (the “Michigan Board”), which grants casino licenses to no more than three applicants who have entered into development agreements with the City of Detroit. The Michigan Board has broad authority to conduct background investigations and determine the suitability of applicants, affiliated companies, officers, directors, managerial employees, and persons or entities holding a one percent or greater direct or indirect interest in an applicant or affiliated company. Institutional investors holding less than 15% of the company’s debt or equity securities are exempt from suitability requirements because the company is publicly traded, provided the securities are held for investment purposes only and not to influence or affect the company’s affairs. Any person supplying goods or services directly related to, used in connection with, or affecting gaming, or supplying other goods or services on a regular and continuing basis, must obtain a supplier’s license from the Michigan Board. Similarly, any individual employed by the licensed subsidiary or a supplier licensee whose duties are related to or performed in a gaming or restricted area must obtain an occupational license. The applicant for a casino license bears the burden of proof to establish suitability in terms of integrity, moral character, reputation, business probity, financial ability, experience, responsibility, and other criteria deemed appropriate by the Michigan Board. A casino license is valid for one year and may be refused renewal if the licensee no longer meets licensure requirements. The Michigan Board may revoke, suspend, or restrict the licensed subsidiary’s casino license, impose fines or forfeit assets for violations of gaming or liquor control laws or rules, and if a license is revoked or suspended for more than 120 days, a conservator is appointed to preserve assets, operate the business in a sound manner, or, upon order of the Michigan Board, sell or transfer the assets to another entity meeting Michigan Act requirements, subject to certain approvals and consultations. The Michigan Board has adopted administrative rules with the force of law that impose detailed substantive and procedural requirements on licensing and operations, including licensing investigations and hearings, record keeping, contracting, reports, internal control and accounting, security and surveillance, extensions of credit to gaming patrons, conduct of gaming, and transfers of ownership interests. These rules also establish procedures for licensing, disciplinary, and other hearings. A person or company intending to acquire more than a 5% equity interest in a publicly traded holding company of a Michigan casino licensee must obtain Michigan Board approval. After acquisition, the acquirer and its “key persons” (generally officers, directors, managerial employees, and significant owners) must be determined by the Michigan Board to be “suitable” and “qualified.” Institutional investors with less than 15% ownership are generally exempt from these requirements if they hold shares for investment purposes only. Upon attaining 5% or more ownership or filing Schedule 13D or 13G with the SEC, the investor must notify the Michigan Board. Institutional investors acquiring less than 10% are entitled to an exemption from approval requirements but must file an institutional waiver application; those acquiring 10% or more must apply for an institutional waiver, providing information as outlined in Rule 504(3). Investors acquiring more than 15% must apply for approval within 45 days of acquisition, and both the investor and its key persons may be subject to suitability and qualification determinations. “Institutional investors” include financial institutions, insurance companies, pension funds, mutual funds, etc., and must hold shares solely for investment purposes. Activities deemed consistent with investment intent include voting by proxy from the board, serving on creditor or security holder committees during debt restructurings, nominating or being appointed to a board in connection with debt restructurings, serving until the end of a term, making financial inquiries for information purposes without seeking to change management, policies, or operations, and other activities the board deems consistent with investment intent. The Michigan Liquor Control Commission licenses, controls, and regulates the sale of alcoholic beverages by the licensed subsidiary under the Michigan Liquor Control Code of 1998, and the Michigan Act requires the licensed subsidiary to sell in a manner consistent with that code. The Detroit City Council enacted an ordinance titled “Casino Gaming Authorization and Casino Development Agreement Certification and Compliance,” which authorizes casino gaming only by operators licensed by the Michigan Board and party to a development agreement approved and certified by the City Council and currently in effect. The development agreement among the City of Detroit, MGM Grand Detroit, LLC, and the Economic Development Corporation of the City of Detroit has been approved and is in effect. Under the ordinance, the licensed subsidiary must submit periodic reports to the Mayor of Detroit and the City Council on compliance with the development agreement, including reasons for non-compliance and efforts to comply. The Mayor is required to monitor compliance, take enforcement action in case of default, and notify the City Council of such actions; if a development agreement is terminated, the City Council must notify the Michigan Board within five business days and request revocation of the operator’s casino license, and the Michigan Act requires the Michigan Board to revoke the license upon such request. The Michigan Board’s administrative rules prohibit the licensed subsidiary or the company from entering into a debt transaction affecting the capitalization or financial viability of MGM Grand Detroit without prior Michigan Board approval. The Michigan Act imposes a wagering tax equal to 19% of adjusted gross receipts from gaming operations, with proceeds shared between the State of Michigan and the City of Detroit. In addition, an annual municipal service fee equal to the greater of $4 million or 1.25% of adjusted gross receipts is paid to Detroit, and an annual assessment, initially set at approximately $8.3 million and adjusted annually based on a consumer price index, is paid to Michigan to cover regulatory and casino-related costs. The licensed subsidiary also pays 1% of its adjusted gross receipts to Detroit, increasing to 2% in any calendar year where adjusted gross receipts exceed $400 million. In Mississippi, gaming operations are conducted through two indirect subsidiaries: Beau Rivage Resorts, LLC, which operates Beau Rivage in Biloxi, and MGM Resorts Mississippi, LLC, which operates the Gold Strike Casino in Tunica County. The operation of casino facilities in Mississippi is subject to extensive state and local regulation, primarily under the licensing and regulatory control of the Mississippi Gaming Commission and the Mississippi Department of Revenue. The Mississippi Gaming Control Act (the “Mississippi Act”) legalized casino gaming in Mississippi, and the Mississippi Gaming Commission has adopted regulations to implement the Act, which aim to: prevent unsavory or unsuitable persons from having any direct or indirect involvement with gaming; establish and maintain responsible accounting practices; maintain effective financial controls, including minimum internal fiscal procedures, asset and revenue safeguards, reliable record keeping, and periodic reporting; prevent cheating and fraudulent practices; generate state and local revenues through taxation and licensing fees; and ensure that gaming licensees, to the extent practicable, employ Mississippi residents. The regulations are subject to amendment and interpretation by the Mississippi Gaming Commission, and changes could materially affect the types of gaming permitted and have a material adverse effect on the company and its Mississippi operations. The Mississippi Act allows legalized gaming in 14 counties bordering the Gulf Coast or the Mississippi River, but only if voters in those counties have not prohibited gaming; as of December 31, 2017, gaming was permitted in nine of the 14 eligible counties, with operations beginning in Adams, Coahoma, Hancock, Harrison, Tunica, Warren, and Washington counties. Prior to Hurricane Katrina, gaming vessels were required to be located on the Mississippi River or navigable waters in eligible counties along the Mississippi River or in waters south of the state in eligible Gulf Coast counties. After Hurricane Katrina, changes allowed land-based gaming facilities in three Gulf Coast counties, provided no portion of the facility is located more than 800 feet from the mean high water line of the Mississippi Sound or designated bays; the 800-foot limit does not apply to non-gaming facilities. The law permits unlimited stakes gaming on permanently moored dockside vessels or in land-based facilities on a 24-hour basis with no restrictions on the percentage of space used for gaming, and there are no limits on the number of gaming licenses that may be issued. The casino licensees are subject to licensing and regulatory control by the Mississippi Gaming Commission, which requires periodic payment of fees and taxes and does not allow transferability of licenses. Licenses are issued for a maximum term of three years and must be renewed. The current license for Beau Rivage Resorts, LLC is effective through April 20, 2019, and for MGM Resorts Mississippi, LLC through June 22, 2021. The company is registered with the Mississippi Gaming Commission as a publicly traded holding company of the casino licensees and is subject to licensing and regulatory control, required to submit detailed financial, operating, and other reports, and to furnish any other information the Commission may require. If the company fails to meet registration requirements, it and its casino licensees cannot own or operate gaming facilities in Mississippi. The casino licensees are also required to submit detailed financial, operating, and other reports to the Mississippi Gaming Commission and the Mississippi Department of Revenue and to furnish any other required information. With certain exceptions, no person may become a stockholder of or receive profits from the casino licensees without first obtaining licenses and approvals from the Mississippi Gaming Commission. Certain officers, directors, and employees must be found suitable or licensed by the Mississippi Gaming Commission; the company believes it has applied for all necessary findings of suitability, though the Commission may require additional persons to file applications. Any person with a material relationship or involvement with the company may be required to be found suitable, at which point they must pay associated investigation costs. A finding of suitability requires submission of detailed personal and financial information and a thorough investigation, and there is no assurance that a person will be found suitable; the Commission may deny an application for any reason it deems reasonable, and findings must be periodically renewed. Changes in licensed positions must be reported to the Mississippi Gaming Commission, and the Commission has the authority to disapprove such changes. The Commission may require the company to suspend or dismiss officers, directors, or key employees or sever relationships with persons who refuse to file appropriate applications or are found unsuitable. Employees associated with gaming must obtain work permits, which may be immediately suspended; the Commission will refuse to issue a work permit to a person convicted of a felony or to a gaming employee who has committed various misdemeanors or knowingly violated the Mississippi Act or for any other reasonable cause. At any time, the Mississippi Gaming Commission may investigate and require a finding of suitability of any of the company’s record or beneficial stockholders, regardless of ownership percentage. Mississippi law requires any person who acquires more than 5% of the company’s voting securities to report the acquisition to the Commission, and such a person may be required to be found suitable. Any person who becomes a beneficial owner of more than 10% of the company’s voting securities, as reported to the Commission, must apply for a finding of suitability. Applicants for a finding of suitability must pay the costs and fees incurred by the Commission in conducting the investigation. The Commission generally requires a finding of suitability for beneficial owners of more than 5% of a registered public or private company’s voting securities. However, the Commission has adopted a regulation permitting certain institutional investors to own up to 25% (or, under certain circumstances, up to 29%) of a registered or licensed company’s voting securities without a finding of suitability. An “institutional investor,” as defined, may apply to the Executive Director of the Mississippi Gaming Commission for a waiver of a finding of suitability if (i) it beneficially owns up to 25% (or up to 29% under certain circumstances) of the voting securities of a registered or licensed company, and (ii) holds the securities for investment purposes only. An institutional investor is not deemed to hold securities for investment purposes unless acquired and held in the ordinary course of business as an institutional investor and not for the purpose of causing, directly or indirectly, the election of a majority of the board of directors, changes in corporate charter, bylaws, management, policies, or operations, or any other action the Commission finds inconsistent with investment intent. Activities not deemed inconsistent with holding securities for investment purposes include: voting, directly or indirectly through a proxy from the board, on all matters voted upon by holders of such securities; and serving as a member of any committee of creditors or security holders.

An institutional investor is deemed to hold voting securities for investment purposes only if it beneficially owns up to 25% (or up to 29% under certain circumstances) of the voting securities of a registered or licensed company and holds them solely for investment purposes. Such holding is not considered inconsistent with investment intent if the securities were acquired and held in the ordinary course of business as an institutional investor, and not for the purpose of directly or indirectly causing a majority of the board of directors to be elected, changing the company’s corporate charter, bylaws, management, policies, or operations, or any action the Mississippi Gaming Commission finds inconsistent with investment intent. Activities that are consistent with holding voting securities for investment purposes include voting directly or indirectly through a proxy from the board, serving on a committee formed during a debt restructuring, nominating candidates in connection with a debt restructuring, accepting appointment to the board during a debt restructuring and serving until the term ends, making financial inquiries to management for informational purposes without seeking to change management or operations, and such other activities as the Mississippi Gaming Commission may determine to be consistent with investment intent. If a stockholder who must be found suitable is a corporation, partnership, or trust, it must submit detailed business and financial information, including a list of beneficial owners. The Mississippi Gaming Commission may at any time dissolve, suspend, condition, limit, or restrict a finding of suitability to own equity interests in a registered public company for any reason it deems reasonable. The Commission may require disclosure of the identities of holders of debt or other securities upon request, and may, at its discretion, require holders of debt securities to file applications, be investigated, and be found suitable to own such securities. Although the Commission generally does not require individual holders of notes to be investigated or found suitable, it retains the discretion to do so for reasons such as default or material influence over gaming operations. Any holder required to apply for a finding of suitability must pay all investigative fees and costs incurred by the Commission. A person who fails or refuses to apply for a finding of suitability or a license within 30 days of being ordered to do so may be found unsuitable. Any person found unsuitable and holding beneficial ownership of the company’s securities beyond the time prescribed by the Commission may be guilty of a misdemeanor. Upon receiving notice that a person is unsuitable to be a stockholder, holder of debt securities, or to have any other relationship with the company, the company will be subject to disciplinary action if it: pays the unsuitable person any dividend, interest, or other distribution; recognizes the exercise of voting rights through such securities; pays remuneration for services except in limited and specific circumstances; makes any payment by principal, redemption, conversion, exchange, or liquidation; or fails to pursue lawful efforts to require the unsuitable person to divest themselves of the securities, including immediate purchase at fair market value. Casino licensees must maintain in Mississippi a current ledger of equity security ownership, and the company must maintain a current list of stockholders reflecting record ownership of each outstanding share, which must be available for inspection by the Mississippi Gaming Commission at any time. If securities are held in trust by an agent or nominee, the record holder must disclose the identity of the beneficial owner to the Commission; failure to do so may result in the record holder being found unsuitable, and the company must render maximum assistance in determining the beneficial owner. The Mississippi Act requires that certificates of securities of a registered publicly traded corporation bear a legend stating that the securities are subject to the Mississippi Act and its regulations. On May 28, 2009, the Mississippi Gaming Commission granted a waiver of this legend requirement. The Commission retains the power to impose additional restrictions on the company and its security holders at any time. Substantially all loans, leases, sales of securities, and similar financing transactions by casino licensees must be reported to or approved by the Mississippi Gaming Commission. Licensed subsidiaries may not make a public offering of their securities but may pledge or mortgage casino facilities with prior Commission approval. The company may not make a public offering of its securities without prior Commission approval if any proceeds are used to finance construction, acquisition, or operation of gaming facilities in Mississippi or to retire or extend obligations for those purposes. Approval does not constitute a recommendation or approval of the prospectus or investment merits. Effective June 23, 2015, the Commission granted a three-year waiver of the prior approval requirement for securities offerings, subject to certain conditions, and this waiver includes a waiver of prior approval for guarantees, pledges, and restrictions on the casino licensees’ equity securities, also subject to conditions. The company cannot change control through merger, consolidation, acquisition of assets, management or consulting agreements, or any form of takeover without prior Commission approval. The Commission may require controlling stockholders, officers, directors, and other persons with material relationships to be investigated and licensed as part of the transaction approval process. The Mississippi Legislature has declared that corporate acquisitions opposed by management, repurchases of voting securities, and other corporate defensive tactics affecting corporate gaming licensees or affiliated publicly traded corporations may be injurious to stable and productive gaming. The Commission has established a regulatory scheme to mitigate adverse effects of such practices, to ensure financial stability of gaming operators and their affiliates, preserve the benefits of corporate governance, and promote a neutral environment for orderly corporate governance. The company may be required to obtain Commission approval before making exceptional repurchases of voting securities in excess of market price ("greenmail") or before consummating a corporate acquisition opposed by management. The Commission also requires prior approval if the company adopts a recapitalization plan proposed by the Board of Directors that opposes a tender offer made directly to stockholders. Prior Commission approval is required before the company, casino licensees, or persons found suitable conduct gaming operations outside the United States. The Commission may require access to information about foreign gaming operations. The company believes it has applied for all necessary waivers of foreign gaming approval for active or planned operations outside the United States. If the Commission determines that a casino licensee has violated a gaming law or regulation, it may limit, condition, suspend, or revoke the licensee’s license. The company, licensees, and involved persons may be subject to substantial fines for each separate violation. A violation under any of the company’s other operating subsidiaries’ licenses may be deemed a violation of the casino licensees’ gaming license. A violation could lead the Commission to appoint a supervisor to operate the facilities. Limitation, conditioning, suspension, or revocation of a casino license or the company’s registration as a publicly traded holding company, or the appointment of a supervisor, would materially adversely affect the company’s Mississippi gaming operations. Casino licensees must pay license fees and taxes to the State of Mississippi and to the county or city where operations are conducted, based on gross gaming revenues, number of slot machines, and number of table games. The State license fee is 8% of gross revenue, defined as cash receipts less cash payouts, and is credited against the company’s Mississippi income tax liability for the year paid. Local city and county fees, in addition to the state fee, are approximately 4% of gross revenue. In 1994, the Mississippi Gaming Commission adopted a regulation requiring a gaming establishment’s plan to include a 500-car parking facility near the casino and infrastructure facilities accounting for at least 25% of the casino cost. Infrastructure facilities include a hotel with at least 250 rooms, theme park, golf course, and similar facilities. Beau Rivage and Gold Strike Tunica are in compliance with this requirement. On January 21, 1999, the Commission amended the regulation to require 100% infrastructure investment, but this applies only to new casino projects and those not operating at the time of acquisition, thus not applying to Beau Rivage or Gold Strike Tunica, and they would still comply. On February 21, 2013, further amendments were adopted for new casino projects, but these do not apply to licensees licensed prior to December 31, 2013, so they do not apply to Beau Rivage or Gold Strike Tunica. Both local jurisdictions and the Alcoholic Beverage Control Division of the Mississippi Department of Revenue license, control, and regulate the sale of alcoholic beverages by casino licensees. Beau Rivage and Gold Strike Tunica are located in special resort areas, allowing 24-hour alcohol service. The Alcoholic Beverage Control Division requires key officers, managers, and owners of more than 5% of the casino licensees’ equity to submit detailed personal and financial information, be investigated, and be licensed. All such licenses are non-transferable. The Division has full power to limit, condition, suspend, or revoke any alcohol license or place a licensee on probation, and such actions could materially adversely affect operations. MGM Grand Paradise is regulated as a gaming operator under Macau law, and ownership of an interest in it is subject to continuing regulatory scrutiny. Ownership requires prior approval by the Macau government. Authorized gaming operators must pay periodic fees and taxes, and gaming rights are not transferable without Macau government approval. MGM Grand Paradise must submit detailed financial and operating reports and provide any other information required by Macau gaming authorities. No person may acquire rights over shares or assets of MGM Grand Paradise without prior Macau government approval. Transfers or encumbrances on shares or rights relating to shares, or the granting of voting rights or other shareholder rights to persons or entities other than original owners, require Macau government approval and subsequent reporting. The stock, casinos, assets, and equipment of MGM Grand Paradise shall not be subject to liens or encumbrances except under Macau government authorization. The subconcession contract requires Macau government approval for transfers of shares or rights in any direct or indirect stockholder of MGM Grand Paradise, including the company, if such shares or rights are equivalent to or greater than 5% of the share capital. This requirement does not apply to securities listed and traded on a stock market. Since MGM Grand Paradise’s securities are not listed or tradable, this approval requirement applies to transfers of its shares. Additionally, the contract requires notice to the Macau government of the creation of any encumbrance or grant of voting rights or other shareholder rights to persons other than original owners, if such shares or rights are equivalent to or greater than 5% of the share capital, except for securities listed and traded on a stock exchange. MGM Grand Paradise is prohibited from delegating management of gaming operations to a management company or entering into a management contract that transfers managing powers to a third party. Any assignment, transfer, alienation, or creation of liens or encumbrances on gaming operations to a third party is prohibited unless previously approved by the Macau government. The Macau gaming authorities may investigate any individual with a material relationship or involvement with MGM Grand Paradise to assess whether the operator’s suitability or financial capacity is affected. Shareholders with 5% or more of the share capital and directors must apply for and maintain a finding of suitability, accept ongoing inspection and supervision, and immediately notify the Macau government of any fact that may materially affect the qualification of any such shareholder, director, or key employee. Changes in approved corporate positions must be reported to the Macau gaming authorities. The Macau government may deny an application for a finding of suitability. Any person who fails or refuses to apply for a finding of suitability after being ordered to do so may be found unsuitable. A shareholder found unsuitable must transfer their shares to a third party within a term set by the Macau government; if not completed, MGM Grand Paradise must acquire those shares. If an officer, director, or key employee is found unsuitable, MGM Grand Paradise must sever all relationships with that person. Failure to act in accordance with this requirement subjects MGM Grand Paradise to administrative sanctions and penalties. The Macau government must give prior approval for changes in control of MGM Grand Paradise through merger, consolidation, stock or asset acquisition, management or consulting agreements, or any act by which a person obtains control. Entities seeking to acquire control must meet stringent standards set by the Macau government before assuming control. The Macau gaming authorities may also require controlling stockholders, officers, directors, and other persons with material relationships to be found suitable as part of the transaction approval process. The authorities have the power to supervise gaming operators to ensure financial stability of corporate gaming operators and their affiliates. The subconcession contract requires prior Macau government approval for any recapitalization plan, any increase in capital stock by public subscription, any issue of preferential shares, any creation, issue, or transformation of share types or series, or any change in the constituent documents (e.g., articles of association) of MGM Grand Paradise. The Chief Executive of Macau may require MGM Grand Paradise to increase its share capital if deemed necessary. MGM Macau and MGM Cotai were constructed and are operated under MGM Grand Paradise’s subconcession contract.

Entities seeking to acquire control of a registered corporation in Macau must meet stringent standards set by the Macau government before assuming control, and the Macau gaming authorities may require controlling stockholders, officers, directors, and other persons with a material relationship or involvement to be deemed suitable as part of the transaction approval process. The Macau gaming authorities have the power to supervise gaming operators to ensure the financial stability of corporate gaming operators and their affiliates. The subconcession contract for MGM Grand Paradise requires prior approval from the Macau gaming authorities for any recapitalization plan, public subscription of capital stock, issuance of preferential shares, creation or transformation of share types or series, or changes to the articles of association, and the Chief Executive of Macau may require an increase in share capital if deemed necessary. MGM Macau and MGM Cotai are operated under this subconcession, which excludes mutual bets, public gaming activities, interactive gaming, games of chance or other gambling on ships or planes, and is exclusively governed by Macau law, with disputes subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of Macau courts. The subconcession expires on March 31, 2020; unless extended, on that date, all casino operations and related equipment in MGM Macau will be automatically transferred to the Macau government without compensation, and MGM Resorts International will cease generating revenue from these operations. Beginning April 20, 2017, the Macau government may redeem the subconcession by providing at least one year’s prior notice and paying fair compensation or indemnity, calculated based on revenue from the prior tax year. The government may also unilaterally terminate the subconcession without compensation if MGM Grand Paradise fundamentally fails to comply with Macau laws or its basic obligations under the contract, provided that if the default is curable, the authorities must give prior notice to cure it, though no specific cure period is specified. MGM Grand Paradise has obligations under the contract to ensure fair and honest operation of casino games, employ qualified personnel, operate games without criminal influence, and safeguard Macau’s tax revenue interests. The company must maintain a minimum level of insurance and comply with reporting requirements to the Macau gaming authorities. It pays an annual premium consisting of a fixed portion of 30 million patacas (approximately $3.83 million at December 31, 2018) and a variable portion of 300,000 patacas per gaming table reserved for specific games or players, 150,000 patacas per gaming table not so reserved, and 1,000 patacas per gaming machine (including slot machines, approximately $38,304, $19,152, and $128 respectively at December 31, 2018), subject to a minimum of 45 million patacas (approximately $5.75 million at December 31, 2018). It also pays a 35% special gaming tax on gross gaming revenues and applicable withholding taxes, and contributes 1.6% and 2.4% of gross gaming revenue to a public foundation and to the Macau S.A.R. government, respectively, with a portion of the latter required for tourism promotion. Gross gaming revenue is calculated without deducting credit losses, so MGM Grand Paradise must pay taxes on winnings even if receivables from customers are uncollected. MGM Grand Paradise holds a land concession for a 10.67-acre parcel for MGM Macau (the “MGM Macau Land Contract”), which expires on April 6, 2031 and is renewable; the premium was paid in full before operations began, and annual rent is payable, with revisions every five years under Macau Land law. The company also holds a land concession for an approximately 18-acre site in Cotai Macau (the “MGM Cotai Land Contract”) for a second resort and casino, expiring on January 8, 2038 and renewable; the premium was paid in full before opening, and annual rent is payable, with revisions every five years under Macau Land law. MGM Grand Paradise received a five-year corporate income tax exemption on casino profits starting January 1, 2007, extended for an additional five years in October 2011, and further extended through March 31, 2020. In Maryland, the owners and operators of video lottery facilities are subject to the Maryland VLT Law and its regulations through MGM National Harbor, LLC, which operates in Prince George’s County. The Maryland Lottery and Gaming Control Commission (Maryland Commission) and Maryland Lottery and Gaming Control Agency (Maryland Agency) regulate video lottery terminals and table games, with the Maryland Video Lottery Facility Location Commission (Maryland Location Commission) awarding up to six licenses based on business, economic development, and location factors. The Maryland Commission determined on October 10, 2013 that MGM National Harbor, LLC and its principals were qualified, and on December 23, 2013, awarded it the sixth and final license. On December 7, 2016, the Maryland Commission issued a 15-year video lottery operation license with an initial fee of $21 million based on 3,600 proposed terminals, which the Commission determined could be operated at up to 3,600 terminals. On August 17, 2016, the Commission temporarily reduced the terminal count to 3,321, which became permanent if 3,600 terminals were not in operation by December 8, 2017. On June 29, 2017, a further temporary reduction to not less than 2,700 terminals was approved while preserving the 3,600 terminal authorization until December 8, 2018. On November 15, 2018, a continued temporary reduction to not less than 3,130 terminals was approved until December 8, 2019, with the final authorized number set at the actual number of terminals in operation on that date. Video lottery terminals must have an average payout of at least 87%, operations are permitted 24 hours a day, patrons must be 21 years old, and alcohol may not be offered free of charge. The law restricts check cashing, debit and credit card usage, ATMs, and other transactions. The Maryland Commission conducts background investigations and determines qualification of applicants, affiliated companies, directors, officers, key employees, and persons with 5% or greater ownership interests. Institutional investors may be exempt from certain requirements via a waiver application, which is discretionary and based on factors such as securities holdings, involvement in operations, and gaming history in other jurisdictions. After a license is awarded, the Maryland Commission regulates the licensee and its officers, directors, and designated persons, may suspend, revoke, or restrict licenses, levy civil penalties, and requires annual updates of licensing information. The Commission may conduct unannounced inspections and investigations, and collects fees, reviews complaints, and enforces regulations. Regulations include requirements for licensing investigations, marketing controls, internal controls, facility design, surveillance, promotions, responsible gaming, junket enterprises, minority business participation, employee health and retirement benefits, and hiring preferences for employees within ten miles of the facility. A video lottery license may not be transferred, assigned, or pledged without Commission approval, and a licensee cannot sell or transfer more than 5% of its legal or beneficial interests without notification and Commission approval, with automatic revocation of the license if requirements are not met. Entities and individuals are prohibited from owning more than one video lottery facility, and applicants must submit a divestment plan for any additional license. Applicants must make serious, good-faith efforts to solicit and interview minority investors before a license is awarded and must do so again in future capital raises. The Maryland Commission may recommend or propose changes to the Maryland VLT Law or amend regulations, which could negatively impact the gaming industry and operations. In New Jersey, ownership of Borgata is subject to extensive regulation under the New Jersey Casino Control Act and related regulations. The New Jersey Casino Control Commission (NJ Commission) and the New Jersey Division of Gaming Enforcement (NJ Division) regulate gaming and non-gaming activities and approve ownership and financial structures of casino licensees, holding, and intermediary companies. The NJ Commission issues casino and key employee licenses, while the NJ Division issues other licenses, including intrastate Internet gaming approvals, sports wagering pool approvals, and registrations for service providers. The NJ Division investigates license applications and monitors compliance. On June 24, 2010, Borgata’s casino license was renewed effective July 1, 2010, with an indefinite term by operation of law. No later than five years after issuance and approximately every five years thereafter, licensees and qualifying entities must submit information to demonstrate continuing qualification. The NJ Commission may reopen a license hearing at any time, especially at the request of the NJ Division. In September 2014, the Company and certain subsidiaries were found qualified as holding companies of Borgata. Under the NJ Act, no entity may hold a casino license unless each officer, director, beneficial owner, or person with the ability to control or elect a majority of the board (except licensed lending institutions) and all holding, intermediary, or subsidiary companies obtains and maintains qualification approval. Persons holding 5% or more of equity securities are presumed to have control and must individually qualify unless rebutted by clear and convincing evidence or waived. Equity securities include voting stock or any security with direct or indirect profit participation. Passive “institutional investors,” as defined, may be exempt from qualification under certain circumstances. Casino licensees must also qualify any financial backer, investor, mortgagee, bondholder, or holder of debt instruments (25% or more) related to casino operations or premises, except that in cases of default, persons holding 10% may be subject to qualification.

Equity securities of a holding or intermediary company are presumed to have the ability to control the company or elect one or more of its directors and, unless this presumption is rebutted by clear and convincing evidence or the qualification requirement is waived, are required to be individually qualified. Equity securities are defined under the NJ Act as any voting stock or any other security that provides direct or indirect participation in the profits of the issuer. Despite the presumption of control for holders of 5% or more of equity securities in a holding company or the requirement for casino licensees to qualify certain holders of debt securities, the NJ Act allows for a waiver of qualification for passive “institutional investors,” as defined by the NJ Act, under certain circumstances. Casino licensees must establish and maintain the qualifications of any financial backer, investor, mortgagee, bondholder, or holder of indentures, notes, or other evidences of indebtedness—whether in effect or proposed—that relates to the casino operation or casino hotel premises, if such holder owns 25% or more of such instruments; however, in cases of default, persons holding 10% of such instruments are required to establish and maintain their qualifications. Holders with less than these thresholds may be required to qualify at the discretion of the Director of the NJ Division. Banks and licensed lending institutions are exempt from qualification requirements when acting in the ordinary course of business. The NJ Act restricts the issuance, ownership, and transfer of securities of a casino licensee and its holding or intermediary companies, defining “security” to include instruments that evidence direct or indirect beneficial ownership or creditor interest, such as stock (common and preferred), mortgages, debentures, security agreements, notes, warrants, options, and rights. If the NJ Commission determines a holder of such securities is not qualified under the NJ Act, it has the right to take any remedial action deemed appropriate, including forcing the divestiture of such securities by the disqualified holder. If disqualified holders fail to divest, the NJ Commission may revoke or suspend the casino license or licenses related to the issuing company. It is unlawful for a disqualified holder to directly or indirectly exercise any rights conferred by such securities or to receive dividends, interest, or any remuneration from its affiliated casino licensee for services or otherwise. The NJ Act requires the certificate of incorporation to state that if a holder is found disqualified by the NJ Commission, such holder must dispose of their interest in the company. Accordingly, the certificate of incorporation requires holders of our securities to dispose of such securities if found disqualified under the NJ Act, and also provides that we may redeem the stock of any holder found disqualified. A lender’s ability to foreclose on pledged assets, including gaming equipment, is subject to compliance with the NJ Act. Generally, no person may hold an ownership interest in or manage a casino or own gaming assets, including gaming devices, without being licensed. Thus, any lender seeking to enforce a security interest must file necessary licensure applications, be investigated, and either be found qualified by the NJ Commission or obtain interim casino authorization (“ICA”) before acquiring any ownership interest. Similarly, any prospective purchaser of an ownership interest in a casino or gaming assets must file licensure applications, be investigated, and either be found qualified by the NJ Commission or obtain ICA before acquiring such interest or assets. The Massachusetts Expanded Gaming Act (“Massachusetts Act”) imposes extensive state licensing and regulatory requirements on owners and operators of gaming establishments. The Company is subject to the Massachusetts Act and its regulations through its ownership interest in Blue Tarp reDevelopment, LLC (“Blue Tarp”), which operates a gaming establishment in Springfield, Massachusetts. The Massachusetts Gaming Commission (“Massachusetts Commission”) is responsible for issuing licenses under the Massachusetts Act and ensuring that licenses are not issued or held by unqualified, disqualified, or unsuitable persons. The Investigations and Enforcement Bureau (“IEB”), a bureau within the Massachusetts Commission, conducts administrative investigations of applicants and licensees and enforces the Massachusetts Act and its regulations, coordinating with the Massachusetts State Police, Attorney General, and the Alcoholic Beverage Control Commission. The Massachusetts Act also establishes a Gaming Enforcement Division within the Attorney General’s Office to investigate and prosecute criminal violations. The Massachusetts Commission may award up to three Category 1 licenses (table games and slot machines) and one Category 2 license (slot machines only) to qualified applicants within the Commonwealth. On December 23, 2013, the Massachusetts Commission determined that Blue Tarp and all applicable principal individuals and entities were qualified. On November 6, 2014, the Massachusetts Commission awarded the sole Category 1 license in Region B of Massachusetts to Blue Tarp, effective November 7, 2014. Blue Tarp received its operations certificate from the Massachusetts Commission on September 13, 2018, which is conditioned on Blue Tarp continuing to meet applicable licensing, registration, qualification, and other regulatory requirements. The initial license term is 15 years, commencing upon the Massachusetts Commission’s approval of the operation’s commencement on August 23, 2018. The initial license fee for Category 1 licenses is $85,000,000, as determined by the Massachusetts Commission and authorized by the Massachusetts Act, which Blue Tarp has paid. All Category 1 and Category 2 licensees are subject to additional annual fees under the Massachusetts Act. Category 1 licensees must make ongoing annual capital expenditures equal to a minimum of 3.5% of net gaming revenues. Gaming establishments may operate 24 hours a day, and patrons must be 21 years of age to wager. Gaming beverage licenses may be granted for the sale and distribution of alcoholic beverages at the establishment, except between 2 a.m. and 8 a.m. outside the gaming area and between 4 a.m. and 8 a.m. within the gaming area. The Massachusetts Act and regulations also specify procedures and restrictions for check cashing, debit and credit card usage, ATMs, and other transactions. The Massachusetts Commission, particularly the IEB, has broad authority to conduct background investigations and determine whether applicants for Category 1 and Category 2 licenses, affiliated holding or intermediary companies, subsidiaries, directors, managers, officers, financiers, debt holders, associates, key gaming executives and employees, and other persons or entities holding a five percent or greater direct or indirect interest in the applicant are qualified (with certain exemptions for institutional investors at the discretion of the Massachusetts Commission). After a Category 1 license is awarded, the Massachusetts Commission and IEB are responsible for the continuing regulation and licensing of the licensee and its officers, directors, employees, and other designated persons. The Massachusetts Commission may suspend, revoke, or condition a Category 1 license or any other license issued under the Massachusetts Act, and the IEB may levy civil penalties for regulatory or other violations. All licenses issued under the Massachusetts Act are expressly revocable privileges, conditioned on the licensee fulfilling all licensure conditions, complying with applicable laws and regulations, and maintaining qualification and suitability. The Massachusetts Commission is responsible for collecting application, license, and other fees, conducting investigations of and monitoring applicants and licensees, reviewing and ruling on complaints, and may conduct inspections of gaming establishment premises or licensee records and equipment. Regulations implementing the Massachusetts Act impose detailed substantive and procedural requirements related to licensing and ongoing operations, including, but not limited to, employee and vendor licensing, accounting procedures and internal controls, surveillance and security requirements, gaming equipment and device registration and testing, self-exclusion, ongoing reporting on construction, approvals, and operations, temporary licensure, marketing and affirmative marketing plans, notification requirements for new or changes in shareholders, executives, and other qualifiers, notification and/or approval of certain material events and transactions, complimentary services, ongoing capital expenditures, political contributions, credit issuance and customer transactions, auditing and record retention, facility design and gaming floor plans, slot machine possession and transportation, table game rules and procedures, employee credentials, vendors and junkets, and count room and cage procedures. Generally, interests in a gaming establishment and Category 1 licenses may not be transferred without notification and approval of the Massachusetts Commission. The sale, assignment, transfer, pledge, or other disposition of any security issued by a corporation holding a gaming license is conditional and will be ineffective if disapproved by the Massachusetts Commission. Category 1 licensees may not change their business governing structure without notification and approval of the Massachusetts Commission, and may not operate, invest in, or own, in whole or in part, another gaming licensee’s license or gaming establishment. The Massachusetts Commission retains the authority to promulgate, amend, or repeal regulations concerning the Massachusetts Act, which could adversely affect the gaming industry and the Company’s ability to operate in Massachusetts. Additionally, certain regulations are currently in draft form and subject to further review, revision, and final approval.

CityCenter Holdings, LLC is a Delaware limited liability company that owns and operates CityCenter in Las Vegas, Nevada, a mixed-use development located between the Bellagio and Park MGM (formerly Monte Carlo) resorts, both owned by MGM Resorts International. The Company is a joint venture, 50% owned by a wholly owned subsidiary of MGM Resorts International and 50% owned by Infinity World Development Corp, which is wholly owned by Dubai World, a Dubai United Arab Emirates government decree entity. The Company’s governing document is the Third Amended and Restated Limited Liability Company Agreement dated December 22, 2015. The Board of Directors, composed of six members—three selected by each Member—has exclusive authority for managing the Company, and compensation for board duties is borne by the Members. The Company has no employees and relies on agreements with MGM Resorts for day-to-day management. CityCenter includes the Aria Resort & Casino, a 4,004-room casino resort with approximately 140,000 square feet of casino space, 500,000 square feet of conference and convention space, and numerous restaurants, nightclubs, pools, and spas; the Vdara Hotel and Spa, a luxury condominium-style hotel with 1,495 units; and the Veer Towers, 669 luxury residential condominium units, all of which were sold and closed by the end of the year ended December 31, 2016. In August 2018, the Company closed the sale of Mandarin Oriental Las Vegas, and in April 2016, it closed the sale of The Shops at Crystals. The consolidated financial statements include the Company and its subsidiaries, with all intercompany balances and transactions eliminated in consolidation. The Company uses accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America, which require management to make estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities and revenues and expenses. Fair value measurements are based on a hierarchy of Level 1 (quoted prices in active markets), Level 2 (observable inputs for similar assets), and Level 3 (unobservable inputs), with the Company using Level 2 inputs for interest rate swaps. Cash and cash equivalents include investments with maturities of ninety days or less, carried at cost. Accounts receivable, primarily from casino customers, include approximately 53% of receivables from foreign countries, where enforceability and economic conditions could affect collectability. Trade receivables are non-interest bearing and initially recorded at cost, with an allowance for doubtful accounts maintained based on specific reviews, historical experience, and current conditions. Inventories consist of food and beverage, retail merchandise, and operating supplies, valued at the lower of cost or market. Residential real estate includes capitalized costs of completed condominium units available for sale, less impairments, with the last units sold in 2016. Property and equipment are depreciated on a straight-line basis over estimated useful lives: buildings and improvements (20 to 40 years), land improvements (10 to 20 years), furniture and fixtures (3 to 20 years), and equipment (3 to 15 years). In December 2015, the Company closed the Zarkana show at the Aria Resort & Casino, shortened the useful lives of related assets, and recognized $82 million in accelerated depreciation during the year ended December 31, 2016; the assets were disposed of in April 2016, and construction of the conference and expansion space began in May 2016, opening in the first quarter of 2018. Interest costs associated with development projects are capitalized and cease when the project is substantially complete or development is suspended for more than a brief period. Long-lived assets are evaluated for impairment when indicators exist, with impairment recorded if undiscounted future cash flows do not exceed carrying value, based on fair value typically measured using a discounted cash flow model. Indefinite-lived intangible assets are reviewed annually in the fourth quarter for impairment, with no impairments recorded. Debt issuance costs are capitalized and amortized straight-line to interest expense over the debt’s contractual term. Revenue is recognized from casino wager transactions based on net win, with discounts on markers recorded as a reduction of casino revenue. For transactions involving discretionary goods and services, revenue is allocated based on stand-alone selling price (SSP), with the remainder recorded to casino revenue. For loyalty program incentives, a portion of net win is deferred and recognized when redeemed, with revenue recognized in the relevant department. Redemption at third-party outlets reduces the loyalty liability and results in payments to third parties, with discounts recorded as other revenue. Commissions and incentives to gaming customers totaled $212 million, $190 million, and $194 million for the years ended December 31, 2018, 2017, and 2016, respectively. Revenue from rooms, food and beverage, and retail is recognized when the good or service is transferred to the customer. The accompanying notes are an integral part of these consolidated financial statements.

Services provided by the Company and supplied by third parties are recognized as operating expenses. For casino wager transactions that include incentives earned by customers under the Company’s loyalty program, the Company allocates a portion of net win based on the sales price of such incentive (less estimated breakage), and this allocation is deferred and recognized as revenue when the customer redeems the incentive. When redeemed, revenue is recognized in the department that provides the goods or service. Redemption of loyalty incentives at third-party outlets reduces the loyalty liability and amounts owed are paid to the third party, with any discount received recorded as other revenue. Commissions and incentives provided to gaming customers were $212 million, $190 million, and $194 million for the years ended December 31, 2018, 2017, and 2016, respectively. The transaction price for rooms, food and beverage, and retail contracts is the net amount collected from the customer, and revenue is recognized when the good or service is transferred to the customer over their stay at the hotel or when delivery is made for food and beverage and retail and other contracts. Sales and usage-based taxes are excluded from revenues. For some arrangements, the Company acts as an agent, primarily arranging entertainment shows and customer rooms through online travel agents. The Company also has contracts that include multiple goods and services, such as packages bundling food, beverage, or entertainment with hotel stays or convention services. For such arrangements, revenue is allocated to each good or service based on its relative sales price, which is primarily determined by the amount the Company charges when selling separately in similar circumstances to similar customers. Contract and contract-related liabilities may arise due to timing differences between cash receipts and revenue recognition, resulting in three types of liabilities: (1) outstanding chip liability, representing amounts owed in exchange for gaming chips held by customers, (2) loyalty program obligations, representing deferred allocations of revenue related to loyalty incentives, and (3) customer advances and other, primarily consisting of funds deposited by customers before gaming play occurs (“casino front money”) and advance payments on goods and services not yet provided, such as advance ticket sales or deposits on rooms and convention space or for unpaid wagers. These liabilities are generally expected to be recognized as revenue within one year of being purchased, earned, or deposited and are recorded within “Other accrued liabilities” on the Company’s consolidated balance sheets. As of December 31, 2022, MGM Resorts had three reportable segments: Las Vegas Strip Resorts, Regional Operations, and MGM China. Las Vegas Strip Resorts includes Aria (including Vdara), Bellagio, The Cosmopolitan, MGM Grand Las Vegas (including The Signature), Mandalay Bay (including Delano and Four Seasons), The Mirage (until its disposition in December 2022), Luxor, New York-New York (including The Park), Excalibur, and Park MGM (including NoMad Las Vegas). Regional Operations includes MGM Grand Detroit, Beau Rivage, Gold Strike Tunica (until its disposition in February 2023), Borgata, MGM National Harbor, MGM Springfield, Empire City, and MGM Northfield Park. Over half of the net revenue from Las Vegas Strip Resorts comes from non-gaming operations such as hotel, food and beverage, entertainment, and other amenities, while the majority of net revenue from Regional Operations is derived from gaming operations. The company’s long-term strategy focuses on marketing to diverse customer segments and utilizing its convention and meeting facilities to maximize hotel occupancy and customer volumes, which improves labor utilization. Operating results are highly dependent on customer volume, which affects room pricing and other amenity charges. Casino operations offer a variety of slots and table games, with premium players accessing high-limit rooms and lounge experiences. MGM Resorts owns approximately 56% of MGM China, which owns and operates MGM Macau and MGM Cotai through MGM Grand Paradise, holding the relevant gaming and land concessions. Although visitation in 2020, 2021, and 2022 was significantly reduced by the COVID-19 pandemic, long-term growth in the Asian gaming market is expected to drive future visitation. MGM China’s revenues are primarily from gaming operations under a concession administered by the Macau Government. VIP gaming at MGM China uses special purpose nonnegotiable gaming chips, with commissions based on rolling chip turnover, recorded as a reduction of casino revenue; however, VIP gaming was not a significant source of revenue in 2022 and is not expected to be in future years. The company’s primary business involves operating casino resorts offering gaming, hotel, convention, dining, entertainment, retail, and other resort amenities. Most revenue is cash-based, and the company relies on operating cash flow to pay rent, fund capital expenditures, repay debt, and return capital to shareholders. The company leases domestic resort real estate under triple-net lease agreements and invests in property improvements, including new hotel rooms, restaurants, entertainment, and amenities. It also offers online gaming and sports betting through LeoVegas and BetMGM. Results of operations are influenced by capital allocation, access to capital, and cost of capital, with a focus on maintaining a strong balance sheet and returning capital while pursuing strategic development. Operations are not highly seasonal, though results can vary due to major conventions, Far East baccarat volumes, marketing timing, holiday play, and customer segments, particularly high-end gaming customers. The spread of COVID-19 significantly impacted the company’s business, financial condition, and operations in 2020, 2021, and 2022. In March 2020, all domestic properties were temporarily closed due to government restrictions, with re-openings occurring through the second and third quarters of 2020, followed by gradual removal of restrictions by the end of 2021. By December 31, 2022, all domestic properties were open, though early 2022 saw reduced visitation due to the omicron variant. In Macau, operations resumed on February 20, 2020, with health safeguards, and travel restrictions remained in place, including visa requirements and quarantines, which limited visitation. In the third and fourth quarters of 2021, local cases led to a state of immediate prevention, mass testing, and closures, with gaming suspended on July 11, 2022, resuming on July 23, 2022, under health safeguards. Adjusted Property EBITDAR is the reportable segment GAAP measure used as the primary profit measure, defined as earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, preopening and start-up expenses, property transactions, net, gain on REIT transactions, net, restructuring costs, rent expense related to triple-net operating leases and ground leases, income from unconsolidated affiliates, and excluding gain on consolidation of CityCenter, net, gain from CityCenter’s Harmon land sale, corporate expenses (including CEO transition and October 1 litigation settlement), and stock compensation expenses. Same-Store Adjusted Property EBITDAR excludes Adjusted Property EBITDAR from acquired or disposed segments, and is provided as a supplemental disclosure for period-to-period comparisons of operating performance, not as an alternative to GAAP measures or overall operating performance.

Adjusted EBITDAR is a non-GAAP financial measure used by management to provide useful information to analysts, lenders, financial institutions, and investors when valuing MGM Resorts International or comparing its results to other gaming companies, as it excludes rent expense related to triple-net operating leases and ground leases. This exclusion is intended to eliminate differences in capital structure and leasing arrangements, since not all gaming companies have such leases. However, Adjusted EBITDAR should not be viewed as a measure of overall operating performance, an indicator of performance in isolation, or as an alternative to operating income, net income, or cash flows from operating activities, as it is not presented on a GAAP basis and excludes certain expenses, including triple-net lease and ground lease rent. Additionally, other companies in the gaming and hospitality industries may calculate Adjusted EBITDAR differently, and such differences may be material. The measure does not reflect significant cash uses, including capital expenditures, interest payments, triple-net lease and ground lease payments, and debt principal repayments. Long-lived assets, goodwill, and indefinite-lived intangible assets are evaluated for impairment based on whether they are held for sale or to be held and used. For assets held and used, undiscounted future cash flows are compared to carrying value; if cash flows do not exceed carrying value, an impairment is recorded based on fair value, typically measured via discounted cash flow models. The audit identified the determination of the unit of account and the revision of the useful life of the MGM Grand Paradise gaming subconcession intangible asset as a critical audit matter. This assessment involved challenging, subjective, and complex judgments under Accounting Standard Codification (ASC) 350-30, Intangibles–Goodwill and Other: General Intangibles Other than Goodwill. The gaming subconcession was acquired by MGM Grand Paradise on April 19, 2005, pursuant to an agreement with SJM Resorts S.A., granting the right to operate games of chance and other casino games. On June 23, 2022, an addendum extended the subconcession to December 31, 2022. A new gaming law, approved by the Macau Legislative Assembly on June 21, 2022, discontinued and prohibited gaming subconcessions after expiration and introduced material changes to the rights and obligations under new concessions, limiting future awards to a maximum of six concessions with a term not exceeding 10 years and potentially extendable by three years. As a result, the Company concluded that the MGM Grand Paradise gaming subconcession and the new gaming concession are separate units of account. The useful life of the gaming subconcession intangible asset was revised from its original basis tied to the expiration of the MGM Cotai land concession in January 2038 to align with the cessation of subconcession rights on December 31, 2022. Amortization of the subconcession was therefore recognized on a straight-line basis over its reduced useful life and was fully amortized as of December 31, 2022. Audit procedures included testing controls over management’s assessment of the unit of account, application of ASC 350-30, revision of the useful life, and calculation of accelerated amortization expense; inspecting the June 2022 gaming law and related agreements; and, with technical accounting specialists, evaluating the reasonableness of management’s application of accounting guidance and judgments. The audit also involved recalculating the accelerated amortization expense from June 21, 2022, through December 31, 2022, based on the revised useful life. The Company has served as the auditor since 2002. The consolidated financial statements, including the balance sheets, statements of operations, statements of comprehensive income, and statements of cash flows, reflect these changes and related financial data for the years ended December 31, 2022, 2021, and 2020.
