The report includes an extract of the Concession Contract for the operation of games of fortune and chance in casinos in the Special Administrative Region of Macau, which specifies that the concession covers operations in Macau SAR casinos, excluding mutual betting, public operations not permitted by law, interactive games, and games on ships or aircraft except as provided in specific legal provisions. The concession is subject exclusively to Macau SAR law, and the Concessionaire waives jurisdiction outside Macau SAR, recognizing Macau SAR courts as having exclusive jurisdiction. The Concessionaire must comply with Macau SAR legislation and may not invoke external laws to avoid obligations. The Concessionaire must obtain prior authorization from the Chief Executive to operate in other jurisdictions or regions, and must submit required documents or data to the Macau SAR Government. The concessions regime is governed by Law No. 7/2022, Law No. 16/2001, Administrative Regulation No. 26/2001, and other applicable legal provisions, along with the current contract. The Concessionaire must operate in accordance with applicable laws and the terms of the contract, with a concession period of ten years from January 1, 2023, to December 31, 2032, and the contract’s clauses may extend beyond this period. Authorized sites are “MGM Casino Macau” and “MGM Casino Cotai.” The Concessionaire may operate games authorized under Law No. 7/2022 and those approved by the Secretary for Economy and Finance, and must submit an annual list of gaming tables and slot machines by December, with changes subject to prior communication to the DICJ. The Concessionaire must maintain casinos open 24 hours a day, with exceptions authorized by the Chief Executive and reported to DICJ, including emergency suspensions due to serious accidents or natural disasters, with a 10-day notice and a 24-hour emergency communication mechanism established. The Concessionaire must install high international standard electronic surveillance and control equipment approved by DICJ, both in casinos and adjacent areas as requested, and report any criminal or illegal acts immediately. The Concessionaire’s corporate purpose includes operating games of fortune or chance in casinos, with any expansion of activities requiring prior authorization from the Secretary for the Economy and Finance. The Concessionaire must maintain its head office in Macau SAR and be incorporated as a limited company. The share capital must not be less than MOP 5,000,000,000, with net worth maintained at that level, and any increase in share capital, issuance of preferred shares, or creation of new share types or series requires Government authorization. Public subscription or transfer of shares requires Government authorization, and all share transfers or encumbrances, including mortis causa transfers, require authorization from the Secretary for Economy and Finance. The Concessionaire must report any such transfers to DICJ within 15 days and notify the Concessionaire within 30 days of registration, providing copies of documents and details of any terms. The Concessionaire also ensures that all shareholdings, down to final shareholders, are represented exclusively by nominal shares, except for shares listed on stock exchanges.

The holder of ownership or other rights to the shares representing the Concessionaire’s share capital must immediately notify the Concessionaire of any transfer or encumbrance of such shares, or any act involving the granting of voting rights or other corporate rights to third parties, and the Concessionaire is required to report this to the DICJ within 30 days of registration in the share register or equivalent formalities, providing a copy of the legal documents and detailed information on any terms or conditions established. The Concessionaire must ensure that any inter vivos transfer of ownership or rights over shares held by shareholders—whether individuals or companies—directly or indirectly amounting to 5% or more of the Concessionaire’s share capital, and extending up to the final shareholders, is authorized by the Secretary for Economy and Finance, except for legal persons listed on a stock exchange for tradable shares. Similarly, mortis causa transfers of shares held by individuals or companies representing 5% or more of the Concessionaire’s share capital, or of shares in companies holding 5% or more of such shareholders’ holdings, up to the final holders, must be communicated to DICJ as soon as known. The Concessionaire must also notify DICJ promptly of any encumbrance on shares of shareholders or holders of shares in those shareholders, down to the final shareholders, where such holdings indirectly reach or exceed 5% of the Concessionaire’s share capital, excluding shares of companies listed on a stock exchange for tradable shares. This obligation also applies to any attribution of voting rights or corporate rights to a third party, except for listed legal entities. The provisions of paragraph four apply to transfers of shares referred to in paragraph five, with necessary adjustments. Decisions on major financial initiatives—such as internal fund movements exceeding 50% of the share capital, salary or benefit payments exceeding 10% of the share capital, or other financial decisions exceeding 10% of the share capital—are considered major financial initiatives under Section 22(1)(12) of Law No. 16/2001, and the Concessionaire must notify the Chief Executive at least five working days in advance, unless justified. Transfers of real and credit rights by the Concessionaire exceeding MOP 100,000,000 or loan agreements as borrower of equal or greater value require authorization from the Secretary for Economy and Finance. The issuance of debt securities by the Concessionaire requires the Chief Executive’s authorization. The Concessionaire or a company in which it is a controlling shareholder may not be listed on a stock exchange; if shareholders directly or indirectly holding 5% or more of the Concessionaire’s share capital are listed, the Concessionaire must inform DICJ within 15 days and submit relevant documentation, and it must endeavor to prevent such companies from seeking listing without prior government notification. The Concessionaire must submit annually in December a detailed report on its shareholding and capital structure, including those of companies holding 5% or more of its share capital and their respective shareholders, down to the final holders, except for listed companies regarding their shares; it must also provide a declaration if no changes have occurred, accompanied by a certified copy of the shares and a signed declaration from each shareholder and relevant party confirming ownership and registration. It must also ensure that no individual holds functions in corporate bodies of the Concessionaire, junkets, or management companies simultaneously, except in general meetings, and must notify DICJ promptly of any appointment to a board or supervisory body. The government must inform the Concessionaire if an appointed individual is part of another Concessionaire, gaming promoter, or management company’s corporate body, and any acts or resolutions violating paragraph one are voidable; DICJ shall request the removal of such violators within a set period. The Concessionaire’s board must delegate management to a managing director who must be a permanent resident of Macau SAR and hold at least 15% of the share capital; the delegation, including appointment, powers, term, and any replacement, requires Chief Executive authorization and must be submitted to DICJ in draft form. If the government does not approve, the Concessionaire must submit a new draft within 15 days and, if the person is not accepted, provide a completed copy of Annex II to Administrative Regulation No. 26/2001. The Concessionaire agrees not to issue mandates or powers of attorney granting board-level powers to conduct business, except for expedient acts at public offices or services, without government authorization. Any changes to the Concessionaire’s articles of association or shareholder agreements require DICJ’s approval and are voidable without it; proposals must be submitted to DICJ at least 30 days before the annual shareholders’ meeting, and a certified copy must be delivered within 30 days of approval. The Concessionaire must inform DICJ of any shareholder agreements, including those on voting rights, by conducting inquiries with shareholders 15 days before an annual meeting or during a general meeting and reporting the results. DICJ must notify the Concessionaire within 60 days whether it approves changes to statutes or shareholder agreements. The Concessionaire must notify DICJ promptly of any circumstances affecting its operations, such as liquidity or solvency issues, legal proceedings, or criminal acts in its gaming areas; it must also report any events that could impair compliance or lead to concession termination; it must report all director, investor, and key employee remunerations, profit-sharing mechanisms, existing or proposed perks, and management/service contracts, and submit certified copies of relevant documents; it must inform DICJ of any imminent serious economic or financial changes, including those of its controlling shareholders, associated entities, and shareholders holding 5% or more who have committed to financing obligations; it must notify DICJ when average annual turnover with third parties reaches or exceeds MOP 500,000,000; it must submit annually in January a document showing all bank accounts and balances; it must provide any additional information requested by DICJ and submit required details to DICJ and the Financial Services Bureau for their functions. DICJ may determine that obligations in subparagraphs 3 and 4 are annual. The Concessionaire must submit management company contracts to the Chief Executive for authorization and submit a draft contract for approval; it may only pay the management company remuneration for management and may not share casino revenues or pay commissions. The management company is subject to Law 16/2001 and other applicable legislation. The Concessionaire must remain trustworthy throughout the concession period and is subject to continuous government monitoring and supervision; it must bear the costs of verifying its good standing as set by DICJ, with DICJ issuing a document certifying these costs. Shareholders holding 5% or more of the Concessionaire’s share capital, its directors, and key employees must remain trustworthy and are subject to continuous government monitoring; the Concessionaire must ensure their trustworthiness and must require them to notify DICJ promptly of any facts affecting trustworthiness, and must inquire every six months whether they are aware of any relevant facts, with immediate notification required upon awareness. The Concessionaire must also ensure that management companies and its shareholders and key employees remain of good standing throughout the concession, and the verification procedures for good standing apply to shareholders, directors, and key employees of both the Concessionaire and management companies. The Concessionaire must provide the government with any documents, information, or materials necessary to verify its suitability. The Concessionaire must notify DICJ within 15 days of becoming aware of any of its directors or shareholders holding 5% or more of its share capital participating in licensing or operations of games in other jurisdictions, or being investigated by a foreign regulatory authority for gaming operations.

The Concessionaire shall maintain sufficient financial capacity to operate the concession and fully comply with all contractual obligations, including those related to investments as specified in the Investment Plans annexed to the concession contract. The Concessionaire and its shareholders holding 5% or more of its share capital are subject to continuous and permanent monitoring and supervision by the Government in accordance with the law. The Concessionaire is responsible for bearing the costs of verifying its financial standing and that of its major shareholders, with DICJ issuing a document stating such costs as valid proof. The Concessionaire must notify the Government of any loan or similar contract exceeding MOP 60,000,000, and if the value exceeds MOP 100,000,000, such a transaction requires prior authorization from the Secretary for Economy and Finance. The Concessionaire must not grant loans or enter into similar contracts with its directors, shareholders, or key employees without such authorization and must not enter into legal transactions with entities that have step-in rights to manage the Concessionaire. The Concessionaire assumes full and exclusive responsibility for all financial and financing risks related to the concession, without prejudice to Clause 42, and the Macau SAR is not liable for any financing obligations. The Concessionaire must secure financing necessary to meet its obligations under the concession contract, including the Investment Plans, and no exceptions or defenses can be used against the Macau SAR in contractual relations with third parties, including financing entities or shareholders. The Concessionaire must maintain reserve funds as required by law. It must immediately provide the Government with any documents, information, or data necessary to verify its financial capacity and notify the Government promptly of any loans, mortgages, debt declarations, guarantees, or other obligations of MOP 16,000,000 or more. The Concessionaire must submit certified copies of such documents and obtain and submit a statement signed by each of its controlling shareholders, including the last one, agreeing to cooperate and provide requested documents or information. The Concessionaire must implement the Investment Plans annexed to the concession contract and those included in the award proposal submitted during the public tender, in accordance with the terms stated in those plans and proposals. It must use qualified labor, give preference to local permanent residents or residents when contracting companies or workers, comply with Macau SAR technical norms and regulations, attach construction projects to the Land and Urban Construction Bureau (DSSCU) with a plan of works, execute works in strict compliance with approved projects and international standards, use certified and internationally recognized high-quality materials, systems, and equipment, maintain high international quality standards for all projects and commercial establishments, ensure modern and efficient management, and notify the Government of any situation that alters or may alter the normal development of construction or operations, including structural anomalies, with a detailed and reasoned report and proposed measures. The Concessionaire is liable to the Macau SAR and third parties for losses arising from serious deficiencies, errors, or omissions in design, construction, maintenance, or operation of projects under the Investment Plans. The Government undertakes to facilitate the Concessionaire’s ability to execute the projects listed in the Investment Plans. The Government may require documents or impose changes to ensure compliance with standards and quality, but may not impose changes that increase the overall amount specified in Clause 41. The Concessionaire must submit by 30 September each year a proposal for the following year’s investment projects, including investment details and deadlines, for Government approval, which will be decided within sixty days, with possible adjustments based on socio-economic needs or agreement. In cases of force majeure or special circumstances not attributable to the Concessionaire, it may request amendment or partial or total suspension of approved projects, submitting a detailed report and supporting documents. The Concessionaire must submit by 31 March each year a report on the previous year’s implementation, including project status, investment amounts, deadlines, and results, and any additional information requested. If the Investment Plans or specific projects are not authorized due to legal, urban planning, or public interest reasons, the Concessionaire must reallocate the funds to projects related to its activity or to public interest projects designated by the Government. The Concessionaire must cooperate with the Government in monitoring the execution of the Investment Plans and submit required documents, information, or evidence. The Government, through DSSCU, will monitor construction work, including compliance with the plan of works and quality of materials, systems, and equipment, and the Concessionaire must submit detailed written reports every two months on work progress, progress control, and measures taken to ensure compliance, as per Section 38 of Administrative Regulation No. 38/2022. The Concessionaire must submit extraordinary reports when work progress is compromised. It must provide, upon request, all relevant written and drawn documents and any clarifications or information requested. If there is doubt about work quality, the Government may order additional tests, with the Concessionaire bearing the costs of such tests and any repairs found. The Government may issue orders, notices, or notifications to the project manager directly through DSSCU, and the project manager must monitor work diligently and be present at the site when required. The Government may suspend or halt construction work if nonconformity or violations of legal, regulatory, or contractual provisions are detected, and such supervisory powers do not impose liability on the Macau SAR, as the Concessionaire is solely responsible for all design, execution, or operational imperfections, except those resulting from Government decisions. The Concessionaire is not exempt from legal or contractual obligations due to hiring or subcontracting third parties. If the total expenditure on the Investment Plans is less than the committed amount in the award proposal, the Concessionaire must spend the remaining funds on projects related to its activity, designated by the Concessionaire and accepted by the Government, or on public interest projects designated by the Government. The Concessionaire is obligated to maintain up-to-date insurance covering risks inherent in the concession activities, with policies taken out with insurers authorized in Macau SAR or, if not feasible, with foreign insurers authorized by the Government. The required insurance includes workplace accident and occupational illness insurance, motor vehicle liability insurance, civil liability insurance for ships or aircraft, advertising installations, general civil liability for casino operations, insurance for damage to buildings and property, and construction insurance (all risks, including civil liability). The coverage for civil liability insurance (subparagraph 6) must include fire, lightning, explosion, pipe bursting, floods, typhoons, earthquakes, aircraft crashes, vehicle collisions, theft, strikes, riots, and other similar events. The insurance limits are set according to existing legislation for the first four types, by the Government for the fifth, equal to the net value of insured goods (gross value minus accumulated depreciation) for the sixth, and equal to the value of the construction work for the seventh. The Concessionaire must ensure that any contracting entity covers labor accidents and occupational diseases. It must provide the Government with a copy of insurance policies upon signing or renewal and must not begin any construction work without first submitting such copies. Without Government authorization, the Concessionaire may not cancel, suspend, modify, or replace any insurance policies, except in case of a change in insurer, in which case it must inform the Government immediately. The Government may directly pay insurance premiums on behalf of the Concessionaire if it fails to do so, using the bond provided by the Concessionaire to secure compliance with obligations. The Concessionaire must ensure the conservation or replacement of Macau SAR assets used in the concession through the temporary transfer of its usufruct, fruition, and use as instructed by DICJ, and must ensure the conservation of land, soil, or natural resources for which the Government is responsible under Section 7 of the Macau SAR Basic Law.

The Concessionaire must not begin any construction projects or work without first sending copies to the Government as referenced in the previous paragraph. Unless authorized by the Government, the Concessionaire may not cancel, suspend, modify, or replace any insurance policies, except in the case of a change in the insurance company, for which the Concessionaire must inform the Government as soon as possible. The Government may, on behalf of the Concessionaire, make direct payment of insurance premiums if the Concessionaire fails to do so, using the bond provided to secure compliance with legal or contractual obligations. Regarding property, the Concessionaire undertakes to ensure the conservation or replacement, as instructed by DICJ, of Macau SAR assets used in the concession operation through the temporary transfer of its usufruct, fruition, and use. The Concessionaire must also ensure the conservation of land, soil, or natural resources managed by the Government under Section 7 of the Macau SAR Basic Law and allocated to the concession operation by lease or concession. Casinos must be located on property owned by the Concessionaire, except as prescribed in Section 5 of Law No. 7/2022 and Sections 5(4) and 37 of Law 16/2001. The Concessionaire shall not encumber casinos, equipment, or utensils allocated to games without Government authorization. Upon expiry of the concession, the casinos and associated equipment and utensils, even if outside the premises, must be free of any onus or encumbrance. When new casinos are authorized, they must be located in buildings or complexes under strata title, operated in one or more autonomous units with clearly identified and delimited areas. The Concessionaire must submit to the Government, as soon as possible, a certificate from the Property Registry describing all autonomous units, including their by-laws, accompanied by a floor plan defining and delimiting the respective areas. Any alteration to the ownership of autonomous units must be registered, and the Concessionaire must send to the Government through DSF the respective land registry certificate as soon as possible. The Concessionaire must also submit condominium regulations relating to horizontal property to the Government for approval. Upon termination or extinction of the concession, the casinos and gaming equipment and utensils, even if located outside their premises, will revert gratuitously and automatically to the Macau SAR, except for those temporarily transferred to the Concessionaire under Clause 49. The Concessionaire must deliver these properties in a perfect state of repair and operation, without prejudice to normal wear and tear. For registration purposes, a public deed record will serve as the transfer title, even if the land concession is provisional. If the Concessionaire fails to hand over the properties, the Government shall immediately take administrative possession, and the expenses will be covered by the bond for compliance with legal or contractual obligations. DICJ shall conduct an inspection of the properties referred to in Clauses 43 and 44, which may be attended by Concessionaire representatives, to verify conservation and maintenance, resulting in an inspection report. In the event of dissolution or liquidation, properties may not be divided until the Government certifies, through a compulsory inventory, that the reversionable properties are in a perfect state of conservation and operation or that no sums are due to the Macau SAR as compensation, with any such debt shown to be owing. The terms of Clause 45, paragraph two, do not affect the normal renovation of allocated gaming equipment and utensils. The Concessionaire must prepare in triplicate and maintain an updated inventory of all Macau SAR properties and rights allocated to the concession and all properties revertible to the Macau SAR, submitting an annual update of maps showing all alterations to DICJ and DSF by 31 May each year. Regardless of the number of tables operated, the variable premium amount cannot be less than that resulting from 500 gaming tables and 1,000 gaming machines. The fixed part of the premium must be paid by 10 January of each year, and the Government may require it to be paid in monthly installments. The variable part must be paid monthly, by the tenth day of the following month, for tables and machines operated during the previous month. The gaming industry is highly regulated, requiring compliance with laws and regulations in each jurisdiction where operations occur, including restrictions on ownership, financial stability, responsible gaming practices, recordkeeping, employee licensing, payment of taxes and fees, and adherence to community benefits agreements. Regulatory agencies have broad authority to interpret and enforce gaming laws, including adopting regulations, investigating violations, imposing sanctions such as fines, and reviewing the character and fitness of individuals involved in gaming operations. Changes in laws, regulations, or interpretations could negatively impact the Company’s business and operating results.

Effective controls over licensees include establishing minimum internal control procedures for fiscal affairs, safeguarding assets and revenues, maintaining reliable recordkeeping and filing periodic reports with gaming regulators, preventing cheating and fraudulent practices, qualifying, licensing, or registering employees, vendors, and other persons with financial interests in or control over gaming operations, paying gaming taxes, licensing fees, and other regulatory fees, maintaining responsible gaming programs, and complying with community benefits agreements where applicable. Regulatory environments in operating jurisdictions are established by legislation and administered by agencies with authority to interpret laws and regulations, which have broad discretion to regulate owners, managers, and those with financial interests. These regulators adopt regulations, investigate and enforce laws, impose sanctions such as fines, review character and fitness for licensure, grant licenses, collect and review reports, review and approve transactions like acquisitions or change-of-control events, securities offerings, and debt transactions, and establish and collect taxes and fees. Changes in gaming laws, regulations, or supervisory procedures could negatively impact business and operating results. Licensing, suitability, and qualification are required for us, our subsidiaries, certain directors, officers, employees, and in some cases, shareholders or debt holders, based on criteria such as good character, honesty, financial stability, facility quality, investment amount, community impact, revenue potential, and minority and local hiring practices. Regulators evaluate individuals based on personal and financial history, associations, and criminal records. Many jurisdictions limit the number of gaming licenses, including per operator, such as Maryland’s restriction to one video lottery operation; licenses are generally not transferable, though some allow transfer with regulatory approval, and are typically granted for limited durations requiring renewal, with no assurance of renewal. Licenses are revocable; for example, under New Jersey law, a conservator may be appointed by the NJCCC to take full control of a casino and its hotel and may sell or dispose of the property. Regulators may investigate individuals or entities with material relationships to gaming operations and require changes in directors or officers to be approved. Officers, directors, and key employees must file applications, pay investigation costs, and may be denied licensure or have conditions placed on their approval. Shareholders or debt holders may also be required to apply for suitability, such as Nevada’s requirement for any beneficial holder of voting securities to file an application if ownership is inconsistent with state policy or if the person engages in proscribed activities; applicants must pay investigation costs. A person found unsuitable cannot hold beneficial ownership of voting or non-voting securities or debt securities of public corporations registered with the regulator, and such unsuitability affects their ability to associate with gaming licensees in that jurisdiction and potentially others. Jurisdictions require reporting of ownership of more than 5% of voting securities, with Nevada requiring reporting of over 5% and a suitability application within 30 days for over 10%. Some jurisdictions permit “institutional investors” to acquire up to 15% without applying, provided they meet specific definitions—such as public employee retirement funds, investment companies, insurance companies, banks, or investment advisors—and hold securities in the ordinary course of business for investment purposes only, with a certification under oath. Even with a waiver, investors cannot take actions inconsistent with their status without reapplying. A change in investment intent must be reported immediately. Failure to apply for suitability or cooperation with investigations, or failure to pay investigation costs, may result in being found unsuitable, and record owners who fail to identify beneficial owners face similar consequences. A person found unsuitable who holds voting securities beyond the prescribed period may be guilty of a criminal offense. If a person is found unsuitable, the company may face disciplinary action if it pays dividends, allows voting rights, pays remuneration, or fails to require the person to relinquish securities, including through immediate purchase at fair market value. Debt security holders may also be required to apply for suitability, and if found unsuitable, regulators may limit dividend or interest payments. Manufacturers and distributors of gaming equipment and suppliers of goods and services must be registered or licensed, and only properly registered suppliers may be used. Lenders’ ability to foreclose on pledged gaming assets is subject to gaming laws; for example, under New Jersey law, no person may own or manage a casino or hold gaming assets without a license, so lenders must file for licensure, be investigated, and obtain either a finding of qualification or interim casino authorization (ICA) before acquiring ownership. Similarly, prospective purchasers of casino ownership or gaming assets must file for licensure and obtain qualification or ICA. Violations of gaming laws may result in license limitations, suspensions, or revocations, substantial fines, and appointment of trustees or conservators to operate or take title to gaming assets, with earnings forfeited or assets sold if licenses are revoked. Violations in one jurisdiction may trigger disciplinary action elsewhere, materially affecting financial condition, prospects, and operations. We are required to submit periodic financial and operating reports and provide other information requested by regulators; some jurisdictions can compel document production or inspections. Under federal law, we must record and report currency transactions over $10,000 and file Suspicious Activity Reports when warranted. Some jurisdictions require logs of aggregate cash transactions in specific amounts. A current stock ledger must be maintained and examined by regulators at any time. Record holders must disclose beneficial owners, and failure to do so may result in being found unsuitable. Regulators may require stock certificates to bear legends indicating compliance with gaming laws or transfer restrictions. In certain jurisdictions, regulators may impose additional restrictions on security holders at any time. Substantially all material loans, leases, sales of securities, and similar financing transactions by us or subsidiaries must be reported or approved by regulators. Public offerings of securities are prohibited without prior regulatory approval if proceeds are intended for constructing, acquiring, or financing gaming facilities or retiring or extending obligations for such purposes; such approval does not imply investment merit. Changes in control through mergers, acquisitions, or other means require prior regulatory approval. Entities seeking to acquire control must meet stringent standards and may require investigation and licensing of controlling stockholders, officers, directors, or other key persons. In some jurisdictions, corporate acquisitions opposed by management, repurchases of voting securities above market price, or corporate defensive tactics may be deemed injurious to stable gaming operations and require prior approval. Certain jurisdictions also require prior approval of a board-proposed recapitalization in response to a tender offer for control. Because gaming licenses are generally not transferable, we cannot grant security interests in gaming licenses, and security interests in gaming assets are limited and may require prior regulatory approval. Pledging stock or equity in a subsidiary holding a gaming license and foreclosing on such pledge may be ineffective without prior approval. Subsidiaries holding gaming licenses may not guarantee securities issued by affiliated or parent companies or pledge assets to secure obligations without prior regulatory approval. Some jurisdictions require filing a report or notice with the gaming regulator within a prescribed time after certain financial transactions or transfers or offerings of securities. Were they to deem it appropriate, certain gaming regulators may take further action.

Netflix, Inc. is the world’s leading internet television network, serving over 117 million streaming memberships in more than 190 countries, with members watching over 140 million hours of TV shows and movies daily, including original series, documentaries, and feature films. Members can stream content anytime, anywhere, on nearly any internet-connected screen, with the ability to play, pause, and resume viewing without commercials or commitments. In the United States, members also receive DVDs delivered quickly to their homes. The company launched its streaming service in 2007 and has since built an ecosystem for internet-connected screens, expanding its content offerings to enhance consumer engagement. Its core strategy focuses on growing its streaming membership business globally while maintaining profit margin targets, by improving the member experience through expanded content—particularly original programming—and by enhancing the user interface and extending service availability to more devices. Members can download selected titles for offline viewing. Netflix began its international expansion in Canada in 2010 and has since launched services globally, excluding The People's Republic of China and territories where U.S. companies are not permitted to operate. The company operates in three reportable segments: Domestic streaming, International streaming, and Domestic DVD. Domestic streaming generates revenue from monthly membership fees for streaming content in the United States, International streaming from streaming content outside the U.S., and Domestic DVD from DVD-by-mail services. As of December 31, 2017, Netflix had approximately 5,500 total employees, of which about 5,400 were full-time, including around 600 temporary workers. The company was incorporated in Delaware in August 1997 and completed its initial public offering in May 2002. Its principal executive offices are located at 100 Winchester Circle, Los Gatos, California 95032, and its telephone number is (408) 540-3700. The company is a well-known seasoned issuer and is not required to file reports under Section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. It has filed all required reports during the prior 12 months and has been subject to such filing requirements for the past 90 days. It has submitted and posted electronically all required Interactive Data Files. The registrant has not elected to use the extended transition period for complying with new or revised financial accounting standards. The registrant is not a shell company. The document includes forward-looking statements regarding business strategy, financial performance, membership growth, content investments, competition, and risks, which are subject to uncertainties and risks that could cause actual results to differ materially. A detailed discussion of these risks is included in Item 1A: "Risk Factors."

The entertainment video market is highly competitive and rapidly evolving, with consumers having increasing access to content through various distribution channels that operate under subscription, transactional, ad-supported, or piracy-based models. Piracy poses a significant threat due to its appeal of offering virtually all content for free, leading to rapid global growth and challenging traditional providers such as broadcasters, cable operators, and internet-based entertainment companies. These established competitors benefit from long operating histories, large customer bases, strong brand recognition, and substantial financial, marketing, and operational resources, enabling them to secure favorable supplier terms, adopt aggressive pricing, and invest heavily in product development, technology, infrastructure, content acquisition, and marketing. New entrants or existing providers may introduce unique services or business combinations to strengthen their positions. If the company fails to compete effectively or profitably, it could suffer adverse effects on market share, revenues, and profitability. The company’s content commitments—typically multi-year agreements with studios and content providers, including non-cancelable talent agreements—are characterized by fixed costs not tied to membership usage or size, and are included in the Contractual Obligations section and related financial notes. These long-term, fixed commitments may limit operational flexibility and negatively impact liquidity and results of operations if membership growth or revenue does not meet expectations. Content produced directly by the company often requires larger upfront cash payments than other licensed content, further straining cash flow. If content is not well received by consumers or cannot be shown in certain territories, the company may face difficulties in acquiring or retaining members, and due to the fixed nature of these commitments, it may not be able to quickly adjust its content offerings. As a producer and distributor, the company faces risks of liability for negligence, copyright or trademark infringement, or claims related to marketing materials. The expansion of original programming—such as TV series and movies—is intended to differentiate the service, enhance the brand, and attract members, but if such programming fails to meet expectations in terms of cost, viewing, or popularity, the business, brand, and operations could be harmed. The company also bears production risks, including completion and talent risks, and may face increased costs or delays due to changes in collective bargaining agreements. If the company creates or licenses merchandise based on original programming, it could face product liability, intellectual property, or other claims. Content may be removed from the service or production discontinued if it is not well received or could damage the brand. Failure to anticipate costs or mitigate risks—such as content not being used or being removed—could harm the business, and litigation to defend claims could be costly and damaging to operations. The company may not be indemnified or fully insured against such claims. If studios or rights holders refuse to license content on acceptable terms, the company’s ability to offer streaming content will be compromised, and costs could rise. Certain licenses allow rights holders to withdraw content quickly, and as competition increases, programming costs may rise. The company focuses on securing exclusive rights and maintaining a cost-efficient, compelling mix of content, and if the mix fails to delight members, membership acquisition and retention could suffer. Music and performance rights require licenses from collection management organizations (CMOs); failure to reach mutually acceptable terms could lead to litigation or injunctions, and ongoing disputes among CMOs could result in rights being unilaterally withdrawn, increasing costs or limiting content availability. The company’s international expansion involves managing diverse content, cultural practices, legal environments, and consumer behaviors, and faces risks such as staffing challenges, political instability, compliance with U.S. and local laws, regulatory actions, weaker intellectual property protections, tax changes, currency fluctuations, profit repatriation restrictions, differing payment systems, censorship, low device penetration, data protection laws, broadband availability, integration challenges, and more lenient views on piracy. Failure to manage these risks could harm international operations and overall business performance. The company is subject to taxation in multiple U.S. and foreign jurisdictions, requiring significant judgment in assessing global tax positions, with potential for reversal by tax authorities and increased obligations due to new laws or changes in interpretation, including recent U.S. tax reform and EU or OECD tax proposals. Changes in how the company markets its service—such as curtailment of marketing channels due to rising costs or perceived brand damage—could reduce member acquisition and increase marketing expenses. Partnerships with cable, satellite, and telecommunications providers are essential for delivering content via set-top boxes and mobile devices; if these partnerships expire or are not renewed on acceptable terms, or if partners fail to update devices, service delivery and member retention could be harmed. Devices are manufactured by third parties, and performance issues or consumer dissatisfaction with the connection between devices and the service could lead to claims or reputational damage. Cybersecurity risks—including cyber-attacks, denial of service, data breaches, and unauthorized access—pose a threat to the reliability and security of the company’s systems and those of third parties, potentially resulting in service disruptions, data loss, intellectual property theft, and reputational harm. The company has implemented safeguards but has experienced unauthorized data releases in the past. The reliability and security of its systems are critical to maintaining member trust and service availability.

Interruptions in computer systems or internet access could make the service unavailable, degraded, or hinder the delivery of streaming content or DVD selections, reducing the appeal of the membership service to current and potential members. The company’s computer systems and those of third parties are vulnerable to cybersecurity risks, including cyber-attacks from state-sponsored or individual actors such as computer viruses, denial of service attacks, and physical or electronic break-ins, which may lead to service disruptions, data or intellectual property loss, misuse, or theft. Although the company has implemented systems and processes to prevent such attacks, unauthorized releases of digital content assets have occurred, though they have not had a material impact to date. There is no guarantee that future attacks would not have a material effect, and the company’s insurance does not cover expenses related to such disruptions or unauthorized access. Preventing such intrusions is costly and may limit service functionality or negatively impact the service offering. Any significant disruption to service or access to systems could result in lost memberships and harm business operations. The company uses its own communications and computer hardware, either in its facilities or through third-party web hosting providers, and also relies on third-party cloud computing services, including Amazon Web Services (AWS), which provides a distributed computing infrastructure. The company has architected its software and systems to utilize AWS, currently running the vast majority of its computing on AWS, and due to the lack of easy alternatives, any disruption to AWS would adversely impact operations. While Amazon competes in retail, the company does not believe AWS use would give Amazon a competitive advantage. If the technology used in operations fails, is unavailable, or underperforms, business and operational results could be negatively affected. The company uses a mix of proprietary and third-party technology for content recommendations, merchandising, and content delivery, including its own content delivery network (CDN); however, if ISPs do not interconnect with the CDN or if the CDN operates poorly, streaming delivery could be impaired. Similarly, if recommendation technology fails to predict or suggest content members will enjoy, member acquisition and retention could suffer. Third-party technology used for marketing, payments, and daily operations, if it fails or operates improperly due to software bugs, could impair service delivery and member retention. Harm to members’ personal devices from software used in operations could also negatively affect business outcomes. Changes in government regulations related to the internet or other business areas could require business model changes or increase operating expenses. As the company expands internationally, governments are introducing or extending regulations related to broadcast media and tax, and consumer protection laws may become stricter, imposing additional burdens. Laws affecting net neutrality, such as those implemented in the European Union or recently repealed in the U.S., create uncertainty, and network operators may engage in discriminatory practices that could impede growth or increase costs. If network operators block, restrict, or impair access to the service, or implement usage-based pricing, bandwidth caps, or tiered access, the company could face higher expenses and reduced membership acquisition and retention. Network operators, who also provide multichannel video programming, have incentives to treat their own data preferentially, which could harm the company’s growth, especially if such discriminatory practices are implemented. Privacy concerns may limit the company’s ability to collect and use membership data, and disclosures of such data could damage reputation and lead to legal claims. The company collects and uses member data, including billing data, stored on its own systems and third-party systems, with encryption and authentication used to protect billing data like credit card numbers. Despite these measures, unauthorized intrusions into member or employee data could occur, leading to reluctance from members to provide necessary information, legal claims, regulatory fines, or reputational harm. The company is subject to payment processing risk, relying on internal and third-party systems to process payments via credit/debit cards, gift cards, direct debit, and online wallets, subject to rules, fees, and regulations. Disruptions, increased fees, changes in the payment ecosystem, delays in payments, or regulatory changes could harm revenue and operating expenses. In some cases, the company uses cable and other partners to bill subscribers; if these partners stop processing payments, alternative collection methods would be needed, negatively affecting member acquisition and retention. Fraudulent use of payment methods could also impact results and damage consumer perception. If trademarks and other proprietary rights are not adequately protected, brand value and competitive position could decline, and competitors might mimic the service. The company relies on confidentiality agreements, licenses, and legal protections such as trademarks, copyrights, patents, and trade secrets, and has filed trademark and patent applications. However, these may not be approved, third parties may challenge existing rights, or infringement may occur, requiring costly legal actions or changes to business practices. The company holds domain names like Netflix.com, and failure to protect them could harm brand reputation and user access. Third parties may acquire similar domain names, which could be costly or impossible to prevent. Intellectual property claims, including from third parties alleging infringement, could be expensive and result in loss of rights to websites, streaming technology, recommendation systems, content selection, or marketing. The company uses third-party intellectual property in content creation and marketing, and disputes could require costly litigation, diversion of personnel, removal of content, development of non-infringing technology, or changes to content, merchandising, or marketing. Legal proceedings, including copyright, patent, consumer, and securities class actions, are costly and time-consuming, potentially leading to content unavailability, service disruptions, and diversion of management attention. The company may seek additional capital through equity, equity-linked, or debt securities due to negative operating cash flows over the past three years, primarily from investments in original streaming content. If capital is raised through equity, stockholders may experience dilution, and new securities could have rights senior to common stockholders, potentially negatively impacting the stock price. The company has substantial indebtedness and obligations, including $6.5 billion in senior notes as of December 31, 2017, a $500 million unsecured revolving credit facility (with no borrowings as of that date), and approximately $7.5 billion in total content liabilities, not including significant streaming content commitments not yet recognized as liabilities. This debt and obligation burden may make it difficult to meet financial obligations, limit borrowing capacity, restrict cash flow use, reduce flexibility in responding to business changes, place the company at a competitive disadvantage, and increase vulnerability to economic downturns. Streaming content obligations are long-term and multi-year, so the company may not be able to reduce them in response to economic downturns or reduced cash flow, potentially forcing access to capital markets at unfavorable times, which could negatively affect the stock price.

This Annual Report on Form 10-K highlights that the company’s substantial indebtedness and other obligations, including long-term streaming content commitments, may hinder its ability to meet financial obligations such as scheduled principal and interest payments on its Notes and other debts. These obligations could limit the company’s capacity to borrow funds for working capital, capital expenditures, acquisitions, or general business purposes, restrict the use of cash flow or access to additional financing, require a significant portion of operating cash flow to be allocated to debt service and other obligations, reduce flexibility in responding to business or industry changes, place it at a competitive disadvantage compared to less leveraged competitors, and increase vulnerability to adverse economic or industry conditions. The streaming obligations are large and multi-year, so the company cannot reduce them in the near term during an economic downturn or decline in operating cash flow, potentially forcing it to access the capital markets at an unfavorable time, which could negatively impact its stock price. The company may not generate sufficient cash to service its debt and other obligations, as payment ability depends on financial and operating performance, which is influenced by economic, competitive, and uncontrollable factors. Over the past three years, cash flows from operating activities have been negative, and the company may not achieve sufficient positive cash flow to meet debt and streaming obligations. If cash flows are insufficient and refinancing or restructuring is not possible on commercially reasonable terms, the company could face substantial liquidity issues, leading to delays or reductions in investments and capital expenditures, or the need to sell material assets or operations—measures that may not be feasible on satisfactory terms or at all, and could materially and adversely affect its business, operations, or financial condition. The company relies on the continued service of key personnel, including its Chief Executive Officer and co-founder Reed Hastings, and executive team members, and faces significant competition in hiring and retaining skilled employees, which could disrupt operations. The Domestic DVD segment is experiencing a decline in memberships, and although the company believes this segment will continue to generate significant contribution profit, a faster-than-anticipated decline could harm the business. The company does not plan to increase resources or improve technology for DVD operations, and service interruptions or degradations could lead to increased member cancellations and reduced satisfaction. If the U.S. Postal Service increases delivery rates or implements service reductions, such changes could negatively affect customer satisfaction and the segment’s contribution profit. The company’s charter documents and Delaware law include provisions that may discourage, delay, or prevent a takeover that shareholders might consider favorable, such as the ability to issue up to 10,000,000 shares of undesignated preferred stock without shareholder approval, a classified board, restrictions on written consent, advance notice requirements for shareholder proposals, and prohibitions on calling special meetings. Delaware law also prevents a business combination with a shareholder owning 15% or more of the stock unless the shareholder has held it for three years or the board approves the transaction, and such a merger could trigger retention payments to executives under the Amended and Restated Executive Severance and Retention Incentive Plan, increasing transaction costs. The company’s stock price has been highly volatile due to factors such as variations in operating results, analyst expectations, business announcements, competition, market volatility, demand for the stock, and competitor performance, and investors may not be able to resell shares at or above their original purchase price. Following periods of volatility, the company has faced securities litigation, which may continue and result in substantial costs and management distraction. Financial forecasting requires management judgments and estimates, which may differ materially from actual results, including estimates of content asset usage and amortization periods; revisions to these estimates could lead to impairment charges or increased expenses, causing the company to miss earnings guidance or negatively impact reported results and stock price. The company’s corporate headquarters are located in Los Gatos, California, with approximately 600,000 square feet of leased space, and it leases additional offices in the U.S., including about 400,000 square feet in Los Angeles, California for content acquisition, marketing, and administrative functions, and in Fremont, California for DVD operations, as well as office space in other countries to support international streaming. The company believes its current facilities are adequate and that suitable additional or substitute space will be available as needed. Information on legal proceedings is included in Note 5, Commitments and Contingencies in the financial statements. The company’s common stock is traded on the NASDAQ Global Select Market under the symbol “NFLX.” As of January 25, 2018, there were approximately 327 stockholders of record, though there are many more beneficial owners. The company has not declared or paid any cash dividends and has no current intention to do so. The selected financial data for the years ended December 31, 2017 through 2013 shows revenues of $11,692,713 in 2017, increasing from $8,830,669 in 2016 to $6,779,511 in 2015, with operating income rising to $838,679 in 2017 from $379,793 in 2016, and net income reaching $558,929 in 2017. Earnings per share were $1.29 (basic) and $1.25 (diluted) in 2017, with weighted-average common shares outstanding of 431,885 (basic) and 446,814 (diluted). Net cash (used in) provided by operating activities was negative at $1,785,948 in 2017, compared to $1,473,984 in 2016, and free cash flow was $2,019,659 in 2017. Cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments totaled $2,822,795 as of December 31, 2017, and total content assets, net, were $14,681,989. Working capital was $2,203,662 in 2017, and total assets were $19,012,742. Long-term debt was $6,499,432, and non-current content liabilities were $3,329,796, resulting in total content liabilities of $7,502,837. Total stockholders’ equity was $3,581,956 as of December 31, 2017. The data has been adjusted for the company’s seven-for-one stock split that occurred in July 2015.

As of December 31, 2017, Netflix had 117,582 global streaming memberships, an increase of 25% from 93,796 in 2016 and 25% from 74,762 in 2015. Net global streaming membership additions during the period were 23,786 in 2017, up from 19,034 in 2016 and 17,371 in 2015. Global streaming average monthly revenue per paying membership was $9.43 in 2017, up 10% from $8.61 in 2016 and 6% from $8.15 in 2015. Consolidated revenues for the year ended December 31, 2017, were $11,692,713, a 32% increase from $8,830,669 in 2016 and a 30% increase from $6,779,511 in 2015. International revenues accounted for 44% of consolidated revenue in 2017, up from 36% in 2016. The revenue growth was driven by membership growth, particularly in international memberships, which accounted for 49% of total average paid streaming memberships as of December 31, 2017, up from 43% in 2016. The increase in operating income was due to higher revenues, partially offset by increased content expenses, including a $39.1 million expense related to abandoned unreleased content, and higher headcount costs for streaming service improvements, international expansion, and content production. Net income increased 199% to $558,929 in 2017 from $186,678 in 2016 and 52% from $122,641 in 2015, primarily due to higher operating income and a tax benefit from the adoption of ASU 2016-09 in the first quarter of 2017, partially offset by higher interest expense from increased notes outstanding and foreign exchange losses from remeasuring euro-denominated senior notes. Netflix offers three membership plans: basic (standard definition, one screen), standard (high definition, two screens), and premium (high and ultra-high definition, four screens). Pricing in the U.S. ranged from $7.99 to $13.99 per month for basic to premium, and internationally from approximately $4 to $20 per month (U.S. dollar equivalent). In the Domestic streaming segment, memberships at the end of 2017 were 54,750, up 11% from 49,431 in 2016 and 10% from 44,738 in 2015. Paid memberships were 52,810 in 2017, up 10% from 47,905 in 2016 and 10% from 43,401 in 2015. Average monthly revenue per paying membership was $10.18 in 2017, up 11% from $9.21 in 2016 and 8% from $8.50 in 2015. Revenues were $6,153,025 in 2017, up 21% from $5,077,307 in 2016 and 21% from $4,180,339 in 2015. Cost of revenues increased by $463,441 (16%) and $368,596 (15%) respectively, primarily due to a $419.0 million increase in content amortization and $44.4 million in other costs. Marketing expenses rose by $170,499 (45%) and $65,186 (21%), mainly due to increased advertising and partner payments. Contribution margin improved to 37% in 2017 from 36% in 2016 and 33% in 2015. In the International streaming segment, memberships at the end of 2017 were 62,832, up 42% from 44,365 in 2016 and 48% from 30,024 in 2015. Paid memberships were 57,834 in 2017, up 40% from 41,185 in 2016 and 50% from 27,438 in 2015. Average monthly revenue per paying membership was $8.66 in 2017, up 11% from $7.81 in 2016 and 4% from $7.48 in 2015. Revenues were $5,089,191 in 2017, up 58% from $3,211,095 in 2016 and 64% from $1,953,435 in 2015. Cost of revenues increased by $1,226,541 (42%) and $1,130,995 (64%), primarily due to a $990.3 million increase in content amortization and $236.2 million in other costs. Marketing expenses rose by $116,445 (19%) and $101,800 (20%). Contribution profit increased by $535.1 million to $226,589 in 2017 from a loss of $308,521 in 2016 and $333,386 in 2015, with a contribution margin of 4% in 2017, up from (10)% in 2016 and (17)% in 2015. The increase in international revenues was due to a 43% growth in paid memberships and an 11% increase in average monthly revenue per paying membership, with foreign exchange fluctuations reducing revenues by approximately $21.9 million in 2017 compared to 2016. In 2016, international revenues grew 57% in paid memberships and 4% in average revenue per paying membership, with foreign exchange unfavorably impacting revenues by approximately $174.0 million. Cost of revenues increased by $998.5 million in 2016 due to content expenses and $132.5 million in other costs, partially offset by exchange rate fluctuations. Marketing expenses increased due to higher advertising and partner payments. The International streaming segment's contribution profit improved significantly due to profitability in mature markets offsetting investments in new markets.

The increase in international revenues was driven by a 57% growth in the average number of paid international memberships and a 4% increase in average monthly revenue per paying membership, which resulted from price changes and plan mix, partially offset by unfavorable foreign exchange rate fluctuations. The company estimates that international revenues would have been approximately $174.0 million higher in the year ended December 31, 2016 if foreign exchange rates had remained consistent with those in the year ended December 31, 2015. If foreign currency exchange rates fluctuate beyond expectations, revenues and average revenue per paying membership may differ from projections. The increase in international cost of revenues was primarily due to a $998.5 million rise in content expenses related to existing and new streaming content, including more exclusive and original programming, and a $132.5 million increase in other costs, mainly from higher streaming delivery expenses, customer service call center costs, and payment processing fees, all driven by a growing member base, partially offset by exchange rate fluctuations. International marketing expenses rose due to expenses for territories launched in the last eighteen months. International contribution losses decreased by $24.9 million year over year as growth in paid memberships and revenue outpaced marketing spending growth. In the Domestic DVD segment, net losses were $(731) thousand in 2017 compared to $(790) thousand in 2016 and $(863) thousand in 2015, with a 7% decrease in memberships at the end of the period and an 18% decline in memberships from 2016 to 2017, and a 16% decline from 2015 to 2016. Paid memberships declined by 17% from 2016 to 2017 and 16% from 2015 to 2016. Average monthly revenue per paying membership decreased by $0.05 from 2016 to 2017 and by $0.08 from 2015 to 2016. Revenues declined by $91,770 thousand (17%) from 2016 to 2017 and by $103,470 thousand (16%) from 2015 to 2016. Cost of revenues decreased by $60,217 thousand (23%) and $61,166 thousand (19%) respectively, leading to a $31,553 thousand (11%) decrease in contribution profit, with contribution margin rising to 55% in 2017 from 52% in 2016 and 50% in 2015, due to reduced DVD usage and lower content expenses. Technology and development expenses increased to $1,052,778 thousand in 2017 from $852,098 thousand in 2016 and $650,788 thousand in 2015, representing a 24% and 31% increase respectively, with a 9% share of revenues in 2017 compared to 10% in 2016 and 2015. The increase was primarily due to a $131.1 million rise in personnel-related costs, including stock-based compensation, from higher employee compensation and a 3% headcount growth to support streaming improvements and international expansion, plus $39.1 million in third-party expenses (cloud computing) and $30.1 million in facilities-related costs, mainly for the expanded Los Gatos, California headquarters. General and administrative expenses rose to $863,568 thousand in 2017 from $577,799 thousand in 2016 and $407,329 thousand in 2015, an increase of 49% and 42% respectively, with a 7% share of revenues in both 2017 and 2016, up from 6% in 2015. The increase was due to a $184.7 million rise in personnel-related costs, including stock-based compensation, from a 56% headcount increase to support international expansion and original content production, and higher compensation for existing employees, plus $49.9 million in facilities-related costs from new Los Angeles, California facility and expanded Los Gatos headquarters, and $49.4 million in third-party expenses (contractors and consultants). Interest expense increased to $238,204 thousand in 2017 from $150,114 thousand in 2016 and $132,716 thousand in 2015, a 59% and 13% increase respectively, with a 2% share of revenues each year. The increase in 2017 was primarily due to higher long-term debt, with $229.2 million in interest on notes. Interest and other income (expense) decreased to $115,154 thousand in 2017 from $30,828 thousand in 2016 and $31,225 thousand in 2015, a 474% and 199% decrease respectively, primarily due to foreign exchange losses. In 2017, the $127.9 million foreign exchange loss was mainly from a $140.8 million loss in remeasuring €1,300 million Senior Notes, partially offset by gains from remeasuring cash and content liabilities in other currencies. In 2016, interest and other income (expense) increased by $62,053 thousand due to foreign exchange gains, primarily from remeasuring significant content liabilities in currencies other than functional currencies. The provision for income taxes decreased to $73,608 thousand in 2017 from $73,829 thousand in 2016 and $19,244 thousand in 2015, a 200% and 284% decrease respectively, with an effective tax rate of (15)% in 2017, 28% in 2016, and 14% in 2015. The decline in the effective tax rate was due to excess tax benefits from adopting ASU 2016-09 and increased foreign income taxed at rates below the U.S. statutory rate, with a $243.5 million difference between the 15% rate and the 35% federal statutory rate in 2017, partially offset by state taxes and non-deductible expenses and the provisional impact of tax law changes. On December 22, 2017, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act was enacted, which reduced the corporate tax rate from 35% to 21% for tax years beginning after December 31, 2017, transitioned U.S. international taxation to a territorial system, and imposed a one-time transition tax on the deemed repatriation of foreign earnings as of December 31, 2017. The company recorded $79.1 million in additional income tax expense in the fourth quarter of 2017, including a $46.9 million provisional adjustment for deferred tax assets and liabilities based on expected reversal rates, and a $32.2 million provisional adjustment for the one-time transition tax on $484.9 million in foreign earnings. A $66.5 million benefit was also recorded for foreign taxes expensed in prior years that may now be claimed as foreign tax credits, based on sufficient projected foreign source income. The effective tax rate increased in 2016 to 28% from 14% in 2015, mainly due to a $13.4 million release of tax reserves in 2015 and higher foreign taxes, with a $17.3 million difference between the 28% rate and the 35% federal statutory rate in 2016, primarily due to Federal and California R&D credits, partially offset by state income taxes, foreign taxes, and non-deductible expenses. Cash and cash equivalents and short-term investments increased by $1,089.0 million in the year ended December 31, 2017 to $2,822,795 thousand from $1,733,782 thousand in 2016, primarily due to cash received from debt issuance, partially offset by increased cash used in operations. As of December 31, 2017, foreign subsidiaries held $611.3 million in cash and cash equivalents. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act included a one-time transition tax on unremitted foreign earnings, resulting in a $32.2 million tax expense recorded in 2017. Long-term debt, net of debt issuance costs, increased by $3,135.1 million due to €1,300.0 million note issuances in May 2017 and $1,600.0 million in October 2017. The earliest maturity date for outstanding long-term debt is February 2021. In July 2017, the company entered into a $50 million agreement.

As of December 31, 2017, cash and cash equivalents held by our foreign subsidiaries amounted to $611.3 million. The Tax Cut and Jobs Act of 2017 included a one-time transition tax on unremitted foreign earnings, and as a result, we recorded a tax expense of $32.2 million related to the transition tax on the one-time mandatory deemed repatriation of all our foreign earnings as of that date. Long-term debt, net of debt issuance costs, increased by $3,135.1 million due to long-term note issuances of €1,300.0 million in May 2017 and $1,600.0 million in October 2017. The earliest maturity date for our outstanding long-term debt is February 2021. In July 2017, we entered into a $500.0 million unsecured revolving credit facility (“Revolving Credit Agreement”), with an uncommitted incremental facility to increase the amount by up to an additional $250.0 million subject to certain terms and conditions. As of December 31, 2017, no amounts had been borrowed under the Revolving Credit Agreement. We anticipate financing our capital needs in the debt market, as we believe our after-tax cost of debt is lower than our cost of equity. Our ability to obtain additional financing will depend on, among other things, our development efforts, business plans, operating performance, and the condition of the capital markets at the time we seek financing. We may not be able to obtain such financing on terms acceptable to us or at all. If we raise additional funds through the issuance of equity or debt securities, those securities may have rights, preferences, or privileges senior to the rights of our common stock, and our stockholders may experience dilution. Our primary uses of cash include the acquisition, licensing, and production of content, streaming delivery, marketing programs, and personnel-related costs. For licensed content, cash payment terms have historically been in line with the amortization period. Investments in original content, and in particular content that we produce and own, require more cash upfront relative to licensed content. For example, production costs are paid as the content is created, well in advance of when the content is available on the service and amortized. We expect to significantly increase our investments in global streaming content, particularly in original content, which will impact our liquidity and result in future negative free cash flows for many years. We currently anticipate that cash flows from operations, available funds, and access to financing sources, including our revolving credit facility, will continue to be sufficient to meet our cash needs for at least the next twelve months. Free cash flow is defined as cash provided by (used in) operating and investing activities excluding non-operational cash flows from purchases, maturities, and sales of short-term investments. We believe free cash flow is an important liquidity metric because it measures, during a given period, the amount of cash generated that is available to repay debt obligations, make investments, and for certain other activities or the amount of cash used in operations, including investments in global streaming content. Free cash flow is considered a non-GAAP financial measure and should not be considered in isolation of, or as a substitute for, net income, operating income, cash flow used in operating activities, or any other measure of financial performance or liquidity presented in accordance with GAAP. In assessing liquidity in relation to our results of operations, we compare free cash flow to net income, noting that the three major recurring differences are excess content payments over amortization, non-cash stock-based compensation expense, and other working capital differences. Working capital differences include deferred revenue, taxes, and semi-annual interest payments on our outstanding debt. Our receivables from members generally settle quickly and deferred revenue is a source of cash flow. For the year ended December 31, 2017, net cash used in operating activities was $1,785,948 thousand, an increase of $312.0 million from the prior year, primarily due to increased investments in streaming content requiring more upfront payments. Payments for streaming content assets increased from $6,880.6 million to $8,905.8 million, or 29%, while amortization of streaming content assets increased from $4,788.5 million to $6,197.8 million, or 29%. Additionally, higher operating expenses, primarily related to increased headcount costs to support improvements in our streaming service, international expansion, and increased content production activities, contributed to the increased cash use. This was partially offset by a $2,862.0 million or 32% increase in revenues. Cash provided by investing activities decreased by $15.4 million, primarily due to a $65.6 million increase in purchases of property and equipment, largely due to the expansion of our Los Gatos, California headquarters and new office space in Los Angeles, California. The company acquires, licenses, and produces content, including original programming, to provide members with unlimited access to TV shows and films. Content licenses are paid at a fixed fee and are tied to specific windows of availability, with payment terms requiring upfront cash payments that are higher than amortization expenses. Payments for content, including additions to streaming assets and changes in related liabilities, are classified under "Net cash used in operating activities" on the Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows. For licensed content, the fee per title is capitalized, and a corresponding liability is recorded at the gross amount when the license period begins, the cost of the title is known, and the title is accepted and available for streaming. The portion available for streaming within one year is reported as "Current content assets, net," and the remainder as "Non-current content assets, net" on the Consolidated Balance Sheets. For produced content, costs such as development, direct costs, and production overhead are capitalized and included in "Non-current content assets, net." Participations and residuals are expensed in line with the amortization of production costs. Content assets are amortized over the shorter of the title’s contractual window of availability or estimated period of use, or ten years, beginning in the month of first availability, on an accelerated basis due to expected higher upfront viewing from marketing and merchandising. This amortization is regularly reviewed, and estimates require significant management judgment. The business model is subscription-based, so content assets are reviewed in aggregate at the operating segment level when an event or change in circumstances suggests a change in expected usefulness. To date, no such event has been identified; if one were to occur, the assets would be stated at the lower of unamortized cost, net realizable value, or fair value, and unamortized costs for abandoned assets would be written off.
